sources.title: How Adam Robinson would take a SaaS from 0 to 1,000+ customers: discovery, manual MVP, then the magic triangle
sources.originalTitle: If I Started a SaaS in 2026, I’d Do This (0 to 1,000+ Users)
sources.summary: Adam lays out his zero-to-1,000-customers system from building RB2B and two other software companies. Validate with 50+ discovery calls and prepayment, ship a manual MVP, prove product market fit with three signals, then run content, outreach and retargeting together as a "magic triangle".

principles.text: Do at least 50 discovery calls and look for prepayment before writing any code.
principles.quote: Before writing a single line of code, commit to 50 discovery calls minimum. Your only goal is to find people who will pay you for something that you haven't built yet.

sources.title: LinkedIn course: how Adam Robinson grew from 4K to 100K+ followers and built RB2B to $3M ARR
sources.originalTitle: How to Go From 0 to 100,000 Followers on LinkedIn (FREE COURSE)
sources.summary: Adam lays out a six-step LinkedIn framework: develop an authentic story, perfect your profile, write hook-driven posts, run connect campaigns, build community through comments, then add video. His core claim is that personal brands beat company pages because people connect with people, and that organic content gives small companies free ads that big competitors can't buy.

principles.text: Personal profiles beat company pages: people do business with people, so show up as your authentic self.
principles.quote: Today, people do business with people, not companies. People are on social media to connect with people, not companies.

principles.text: Great organic content works as free ads that large companies must pay for, leveling the field with a solo founder.
principles.quote: If you can create great organic social content that your target market loves and consumes daily, those are free ads. Large companies have to pay for those impressions.

principles.text: Be clear, consistent and constantly reinforce your story; vulnerability and candor cut through where big brands can't.
principles.quote: If you can say things to LinkedIn that you would say to your spouse behind closed doors, it will do better than anything any large company could ever post.

principles.text: Stand out by being polarizing: sit between mainstream and crazy so your side loves you and the other side hates you.
principles.quote: If you can find a sweet spot between mainstream and crazy where people on your side love you but on the other side hate you, that's where the prolific content lives.

principles.text: Pick content pillars tangential to the problem you solve, so your prospects share those problems too.
principles.quote: I like to focus on topics that are tangential to the problem that you're solving. Meaning, all the prospects who have the problem you're solving also have the problems you're talking about.

principles.text: Be patient after connecting: let prospects see your content for about 60 days before asking for a meeting.
principles.quote: Don't start pitching. Wait 60 days. This patience is what will separate you from the people who connect and then pitch 10 minutes later.

sources.title: How Adam Robinson turned LinkedIn into RB2B's only channel: pillars, hooks, credibility
sources.originalTitle: Turn LINKEDIN Into a $30M ARR GROWTH Machine | Adam Robinson (Retention.com, RB2B)
sources.summary: Adam explains how a year of posting on LinkedIn before seeing any direct revenue built a founder brand that became RB2B's sole acquisition channel (about $5M ARR in 13 months). He covers content pillars and content-market fit, hook writing, credibility signals, why video deepens trust, and why he skips AI-written posts and viral-for-followers tactics.

principles.text: Posting on LinkedIn means building a public figure: repeat the same few content pillars in many different ways.
principles.quote: what you are doing when you are consistently posting on LinkedIn is you are creating a public figure as a PR agency would have created a public figure in the media 50 years ago.

principles.text: Find content-market fit: pick 2-3 authentic, non-mainstream pillars that resonate with your market.
principles.quote: you've got to come up with two or three things that are authentic to you that resonate with the market that are not down the middle mainstream.

principles.text: The hook matters most; a mediocre post with a great hook beats a great post with a weak hook. Use numbers.
principles.quote: a mediocre post with a great hook will do far better than a great hook, sorry, a great post with a weak hook.

principles.text: Treat every post as if no one knows you and build credibility into each one, since audience overlap between posts is low.
principles.quote: you have to treat each post as though no one has ever heard of you before. So each post has to maximize the credibility of you every time.

principles.text: Optimize for trust within your ICP, not raw follower count; broad viral topics build a crowd, not buyers.
principles.quote: I'm trying to maximize the trust in like the real audience that I have within my ICP, right?

principles.text: Early posting is about finding your voice, not engagement or deals; keep going through the no-revenue stretch.
principles.quote: starting to post on social is not about engagement and deals and dollars. It's about being one day closer to finding your voice.

sources.title: How Adam Robinson scaled Retention.com to $22M with six people and launched RB2B on LinkedIn
sources.originalTitle: Adam Robinson Shares Profit and Loss, $22m Revenue, Strategy behind Linkedin and Lawsuit
sources.summary: Adam Robinson walks through Retention.com's P&L (about 87% gross margin, roughly $6M net income run rate), his failed 2023 push to scale like a funded rival, and how a candid LinkedIn post about a vendor's cease and desist gave RB2B 1,600 pre-launch leads. He also discusses RB2B's credit-based pricing, high free-to-paid conversion, and his open concerns about churn.

principles.text: A data business can hold high margins at scale by turning data costs into a fixed cost.
principles.quote: you compile a lot of data at SAS margins and then you don't really have to increase the spend on that data if you do it the right way and you kind of make the cost fixed

principles.text: Funded peers and vanity metrics tempt bootstrappers into overspending; staying disciplined is hard on the ego.
principles.quote: it just takes a lot for your ego to withstand everything that's trying to make you a bigger vanity metric company

principles.text: Honest, unpolished founder storytelling beats PR-filtered brand content for building resonance.
principles.quote: you end up with fluffy crap at the end that no one can resonate with

principles.text: Organic social works when it is mostly value and story, with only the occasional hard CTA.
principles.quote: hardly any of it is sales content you know maybe one out of every 10 post I'll put some like hard CTA at the bottom of it

principles.text: Run heavy customer discovery calls before launch so you know what to build.
principles.quote: SOS and I were getting on the phone with like 10 people a day between the two of us for like six months so we really had a good idea of what we wanted to deliver at launch

principles.text: Content aimed at a tight audience drives unusually strong activation and free-to-paid conversion.
principles.quote: the content is targeting such a tight audience of the right people on LinkedIn and it's just leading to that

sources.title: Adam Robinson's free course: take a SaaS from $0 to $10M ARR bootstrapped with a tiny team
sources.originalTitle: How to Grow Your SaaS From $0 to $10M ARR (1+ Hour FREE COURSE)
sources.summary: Adam Robinson lays out the "sell before you build" framework: pre-sell with a sizzling one-liner and quick pitch, build a manual MVP, find product-market fit through hundreds of calls, and stay tiny. The second half covers getting unstuck from $1M to $10M, hiring almost nobody, inbound-led outbound, and refusing VC money.

principles.text: Sell before you build: pre-sell the idea to real buyers first.
principles.quote: Elite founders do not start developing anything before they have buyers of what they're about to build.

principles.text: Do things that don't scale until you have PMF; skip growth hacking, ads, SEO and partnerships.
principles.quote: Nothing will work if you don't have product market fit. Everything will work if you do have product market fit.

principles.text: Money is the honest signal; getting people to pay beats nice words about your idea.
principles.quote: The single best way to figure out if someone actually likes your idea is get them to hand you money.

principles.text: Do not hire anyone before $1M ARR; aim for $10M ARR with no more than 10 employees.
principles.quote: Do not hire anybody before 1 million ARR. Co-founders only.

principles.text: When stuck above $1M, go all in on your lowest-churn segment and ignore everyone else.
principles.quote: If you can identify a segment with significantly lower churn, go all in on them. That's your new ICP.

principles.text: Pipeline comes from creating original demand, then selling only to people who visited your site.
principles.quote: These STRs don't create demand. They were only capturing demand created elsewhere.

sources.title: How Adam Robinson bootstrapped three SaaS companies to $1M ARR, faster each time
sources.originalTitle: Bootstrapped SaaS: From $0 to $1M ARR - 3 Times! (Adam Robinson)
sources.summary: Adam walks through reaching $1M ARR with Robly (17 months), Retention.com (27 weeks) and RB2B (16 weeks). Each used a distribution channel with little competition, and RB2B was built audience-first via founder-led LinkedIn content. He is candid about the failures, high churn and layoffs behind the wins.

principles.text: Customer acquisition is expensive because of competition; find an uncontested channel with a good offer.
principles.quote: what makes acquiring customers expensive is competition and if you have a channel that you don't have any competition in and you have a good offer is going to be incredibly inexpensive for you to acquire those customers.

principles.text: Do things that don't scale early: manual onboarding to the activation moment keeps customers sticking.
principles.quote: We knew the magic moment was getting someone to hit send on their first campaign. If we could do that, they stuck 100% of the time.

principles.text: A fast-payback ad channel can still bring bad customers; for SaaS, Facebook ads often attract high-churn wannabes.
principles.quote: I think for SAS, it very rarely works to do Facebook ads because you bring in these wannabes that, you know, it's like a 15% per month churn customer

principles.text: Sell before you build; building for a launch nobody wants wastes a year.
principles.quote: how I advocate building for building companies now, like sell before you buy.

principles.text: Distribution channels decay; build for how go-to-market works now, not what worked before.
principles.quote: it's like product and distribution and what is available at the time, you know, that determines what grows, right?

principles.text: Treat yourself as being in the edutainment business; great organic social content is the most efficient trust-builder.
principles.quote: My job is to make entertaining, educational, and highly compelling content about how I am building my SAS and about how you can do it, too.

sources.title: How Adam Robinson grew LinkedIn to 140k followers and RB2B to $4M ARR with a six-step framework
sources.originalTitle: How I Grew My LinkedIn From 0 to 140k Followers in 2 Years
sources.summary: Adam Robinson breaks down his LinkedIn playbook: define a clear, consistent character, take polarizing and vulnerable positions, optimize your profile, write hook-driven posts, run patient connect campaigns, and build community through comments. He credits it with 140k followers in 2 years and RB2B reaching $4M ARR from LinkedIn alone.

principles.text: Build a personal character with three Cs: be clear, be consistent, and constantly reinforce it.
principles.quote: You must be incredibly clear about who you are. The market knows me. Adam Robinson is a bootstrapped SAS founder who builds in public with radical transparency.

principles.text: Live in the prolific zone: polarizing takes between mainstream noise and crazy; being loved by 80% and hated by 20% is fine.
principles.quote: If you're far enough out to the right where 80% of the people on the right are going to love you and 20% of the people on the left are going to absolutely hate you, that's a great place to live.

principles.text: Vulnerability is an unfair advantage small players have; big companies can't be candid about real problems.
principles.quote: If you can say things on LinkedIn that you might only say to your spouse behind closed doors, it will do better than anything any larger company could ever post.

principles.text: Write for the audience, not the algorithm; the algorithm serves the audience, so better content is the only durable fix.
principles.quote: You are not writing for an algorithm. You're writing for an audience.

principles.text: Hooks should build maximum credibility fast, assume no one knows you, and use numbers, since the hook's only job is getting the 'see more' click.
principles.quote: Always write like no one's ever heard of you before and try to build the most credibility possible because most people seeing your post don't have any idea who you are.

principles.text: Be patient after connecting: wait about 60 days of content exposure before messaging, which yields an 80% reply rate.
principles.quote: After 60 days of seeing your content and possibly even engaging with it, this person thinks you're a celebrity. Once you reach out to them, when they've been reading your stuff, there's an 80% reply rate.

sources.title: How Adam Robinson grew RB2B to $1M ARR with founder-led LinkedIn content
sources.originalTitle: $1 Million ARR in 13 Weeks | How Adam Robinson, RB2B did it with Linkedin Organic Content!
sources.summary: Adam Robinson explains why founder-brand content on LinkedIn replaced outbound for RB2B. He covers the sales motion around it, how to write hooks, handling backlash, using paid thought-leadership ads, and why AI should not write your posts.

principles.text: People connect with people, so build a founder brand instead of a company page.
principles.quote: people are not on social media to connect with companies people are on social media to connect with people period even on LinkedIn right like period

principles.text: A person builds audience affinity at a fraction of the cost and time of a brand.
principles.quote: you can create the Affinity around a person that you could create around a brand in like one1 100th of the time with one1 100th of money because we're set up to feel that way

principles.text: The founder-brand motion: connect with ICP, post for 60 days, then ask for a demo.
principles.quote: in the beginning it's outbound connection campaign to your ICP you get them to accept you post great content you wait 60 days you ask for a demo it's 80% conversion rate because they think you're some sort of a celebrity

principles.text: Commit to posting until you find your voice; expect it to take about a year.
principles.quote: for me it took a year I put I'm I'm a very Focus foced and maniacal person in many ways I put a lot yeah I put a lot into this and it took me a year

principles.text: Build credibility in the hook with specifics, numbers and bold claims, and spend most idea time on hooks.
principles.quote: you have to treat LinkedIn as though this person who's reading it has never heard of you and you have to build however you can as much credibility as possible in the hook

principles.text: A polarizing view you truly believe is a gift; expect haters but never fake controversy.
principles.quote: if you have a polarizing view that you believe in that the world has not yet accepted that's one of the best gifts that's ever been given in social media

sources.title: How Adam Robinson used founder edutainment on LinkedIn to take RB2B from $1MM to $2MM ARR in six weeks
sources.originalTitle: How Adam Robinson took RB2B to hit $2MM ARR just 6 weeks after crossing $1MM ARR
sources.summary: Adam Robinson explains why he treats his company as an "edutainment" media brand with software at the bottom of the funnel. He covers writing for people with his own pain, saying the uncomfortable truth, building a warm audience above sales, using LinkedIn comments for networking, and bootstrapping to $10MM ARR.

principles.text: Run the company as an edutainment media brand; software sits at the bottom of the funnel.
principles.quote: I view myself in the edutainment business and I happen to sell SAS at the bottom of the funnel but like I'm not competing with my competitors on SAS and features

principles.text: Write for people who share your exact pain right now, not an audience you only serve.
principles.quote: What if I started writing to people who were basically me and not like writing to Shopify store owners

principles.text: Great content says what everyone feels but no one admits, including your own struggles.
principles.quote: when you say things that connect with people so deeply because they're feeling it and no one is willing to admit it to themselves like that's that's what I think makes great content

principles.text: Build the awareness layer above outbound; reps only capture warmth that content created.
principles.quote: what that rep's really doing is just capturing the machine of warmth that you created above it

principles.text: Treat website-visit leads as warm: filter to ICP and push them through every channel quickly.
principles.quote: of the leads that we would give you filter out the ICP leads throw away all the rest of them and just stick them into that tumbler

principles.text: Use LinkedIn comments to get known by the right people; a small targeted following is enough.
principles.quote: if you can just get in people's comments constantly like they they will know you after a few months

sources.title: How Adam Robinson grew RB2B to $6.7M ARR with a founder brand on LinkedIn
sources.originalTitle: How to Scale a SaaS From $0 to $6.7M in 2 Years (Marketing Strategy Revealed)
sources.summary: Adam Robinson explains how RB2B started as a pivot from LinkedIn content, how a crude Slack mockup proved demand, and how he built a founder brand by repeating a few ideas. He also covers the risk of depending on one channel and the churn ceiling that pushes him to widen the product.

principles.text: Test a crude version fast: if people pay for something rough, pursue it.
principles.quote: if you give something to somebody that sucks and they pay you for it, that's like indicator one that you should probably pursue it.

principles.text: How data is presented can change demand dramatically; a Slack feed with headshots beat a spreadsheet of identical data.
principles.quote: the enthusiasm was like 11 out of 10 for the Slack thing and like 2 out of 10 for this other experience of of the same data, right?

principles.text: Products usually come from stumbling onto something that works better, not from audience-first planning.
principles.quote: you're kind of doing one thing that's working okay and then there's this other thing that you kind of stumble along that it's clear that it will work much better and so you like go all in on that

principles.text: Become known for something by repeating the same few ideas from many angles on every channel.
principles.quote: You say the same couple things over and over again in a thousand different ways on every single possible channel. And then you're the guy that is that, right?

principles.text: Reverse-engineer high-performing posts: map your story onto the structure of proven winners.
principles.quote: just kind of put them all in a row and like see the architecture of the post. See if you can put your story on that architecture

principles.text: Single-channel dependence is a risk; he is diversifying and widening the product because churn caps growth and extra features make it stickier.
principles.quote: you can beg people to not cancel and you'll maybe get 10% of them, but like you start building other stuff, and it just gets stickier.

sources.title: How Adam Robinson scaled retention.com past $25M ARR and rB2B to $4M ARR
sources.originalTitle: How to Make $1M/Month from a SaaS
sources.summary: Adam Robinson walks through Robly, retention.com and rB2B: validating go-to-market before building, why word of mouth makes every channel work, and why churn and buyer persona decide a SaaS. He also covers keeping teams lean, a layoff, and using a public founder brand as the main acquisition channel.

principles.text: Develop customers in parallel with the product; validate the go-to-market before you build.
principles.quote: you are developing your customers in parallel of developing your product and that is what reduces risk of startups because your intuition your Market intuition is often just bad

principles.text: Product-driven word of mouth is what makes ads, email and every other channel work.
principles.quote: if your product is good enough to have Word of Mouth there's like a million things you can do to accelerate that but if it doesn't have Word of Mouth all of those things that you would do to accelerate the word of mouth are going to be like you know one/ 100th is effective

principles.text: Category and buyer persona drive churn; selling to low-stickiness buyers caps the business.
principles.quote: it is a high churn product category with a high churn buyer Persona

principles.text: A lean company reaching $10M ARR gives you total optionality; outside money pushes you off that path.
principles.quote: if you can get a lean company to 10 million AR that is the promised land

principles.text: Stay the smallest team you can be, and do less but only what matters, rather than overstaffing for a bigger future.
principles.quote: you want to be as a startup I think you want to be the smallest possible version of what you can be at that time right

principles.text: A founder brand works because the founder shares the real numbers, including failures, that others won't.
principles.quote: I'm a guy who's at 25 million AR who's working in public there's no one else right

sources.title: How Adam Robinson used LinkedIn reach and a free product to launch RB2B
sources.originalTitle: 53: Adam Robinson - The power of LinkedIn for B2B from zero to one
sources.summary: Adam Robinson explains how organic LinkedIn video built an audience that shaped RB2B's go-to-market: a massive free offer, paid features added over time, and patience on revenue. He also covers why churn depends on product category and why free users are worth keeping.

principles.text: Let your distribution advantage dictate go-to-market: a big audience makes a massive free offer work far better.
principles.quote: the LinkedIn thing was working so well I'm like you know what if I had a massive free offer and like tried to execute one of these MailChimp go to markets the free thing is going to work way better for me with this megaphone

sources.title: Adam Robinson on founder-led LinkedIn growth: content schedule, ghostwriters, and inbound-led outbound
sources.originalTitle: Maja Voje and Adam Robinson: Founder-Led Growth on LinkedIn | GTM Strategist Podcast
sources.summary: Adam walks through his actual weekly calendar, showing most of a CEO's week going to content and podcasts. He explains why organic founder content beats paid ads, how to start (ghostwriter, study creators, comment thoughtfully), why he runs on gut over metrics, and how to follow up with website visitors.

principles.text: Organic founder content can beat any ad budget for building awareness and trust, when your buyers live on that platform.
principles.quote: I have developed more trust and the awareness is higher than any AD campaign or sponsorship or whatever I could have done with that money

principles.text: Get a ghostwriter first and learn by watching; only take over writing once you catch the content bug.
principles.quote: start with a Ghost Rider work with them for a few months they can help you with some of this stuff right like if they understand what you do what might what might you write about

principles.text: Make people feel they know you like a friend; that human connection is what survives commoditized software.
principles.quote: I believe that it's making people feel like they know me like a friend so I'm trying to use that as like a fundamental principle in how I'm presenting myself on LinkedIn

principles.text: Early on, run content on gut; the most important things can't be measured and metrics-driven teams overweight the measurable.
principles.quote: I do worry that like the most important things cannot be measured and when you get people in who are running your entire company on metrics the most important things uh lose relative value to the things that are far less important but you can measure

principles.text: Study top creators in your own space to learn why posts work, and comment thoughtfully on a small list of ecosystem peers.
principles.quote: I think if you have a list of 10 people in your space and you spend a few days a week commenting on their stuff they might start commenting on your stuff and you will slowly become known in the ecosystem that way

principles.text: Follow up with website visitors within single-digit hours, using the same playbook you use for outbound demos.
principles.quote: I think there's some magic amount of time you should wait like in the number in the single digit hours right and you can automate all of this

sources.title: Audience-first GTM: how Adam Robinson built RB2B demand through LinkedIn founder content
sources.originalTitle: GTM 114: Audience-First GTM, Fueling Startup Growth via LinkedIn with Adam Robinson
sources.summary: Adam Robinson explains how he built an audience on LinkedIn first and then built RB2B for it, using organic founder content, radical transparency and podcast cross-pollination as a low-cost, bootstrapped demand engine. He also shares stories of starting from zero three times, why VC doesn't accelerate sub-$10M ARR companies, and why a clear one-liner can launch a product.

principles.text: Build the audience first, then build the product they already want to buy.
principles.quote: we hadn't even really decided to make the B2B product until we saw how effective this content vehicle was

sources.title: How Adam Robinson bootstrapped Retention.com to $22M ARR and pivoted to B2B via LinkedIn co-creation
sources.originalTitle: How I Bootstrapped $22m ARR in 4 Years With LinkedIn
sources.summary: Adam Robinson recounts taking Retention.com from zero to $22M ARR with a tiny team, using outrageous Facebook ads, cold email and word of mouth. He covers the stalls, the failed 2023 scale-up, and the pivot to B2B, where LinkedIn content let him build a waitlist of ideal buyers before the product shipped.

principles.text: With strong product and one or two channels plus word of mouth, you can get much further with far fewer people.
principles.quote: with the right combination of product and then just one or two channels and word of mouth, you can get way farther than you think that you can get with way fewer bodies.

principles.text: Without word of mouth nothing accelerates growth; with it, many tactics work.
principles.quote: If you do not yet have word of mouth nothing that you do will work.

principles.text: Early on, be outrageous to cut through the noise; a young company has no brand to damage.
principles.quote: you can do aggressive and outrageous things, uh you know, months into creating your company because there's no brand to destroy.

principles.text: Build the buyers while you build the product, so you launch with customers or stop early.
principles.quote: you need to be building the buyers at the same time. And it just de-risks your startup journey tremendously

principles.text: Founder brand lifts every other channel, so treat it as a long-run commitment rather than judging it by monthly demos.
principles.quote: the biggest determinant of the of an open rate of an email is who sends it.

principles.text: Bootstrap discipline should not be dropped when scaling; acting like a VC-backed CEO and hiring seniors without processes hurt badly.
principles.quote: I totally lost that, and I started behaving like a venture-backed CEO.

sources.title: How Adam Robinson built a brand-led content engine for a bootstrapped SaaS (Retention.com)
sources.originalTitle: The Content Engine Behind a $22m Bootstrapped SaaS Startup | Adam Robinson, CEO of Retention.com
sources.summary: Adam Robinson explains why brand and community are the real moats in SaaS without network effects. He covers how he built a LinkedIn audience by working in public, and why he pairs a big free offer with a paid upsell. He also gives his view on churn, premium media content and creator-led distribution.

principles.text: Without network effects, brand and community are a SaaS company's only moats, so invest in them early and for the long haul.
principles.quote: brand and Community are the only Moes you have if you don't have Network effects

principles.text: Working in public only grabs attention when your numbers are impressive. Proof of success earns the audience.
principles.quote: somebody shows up and they're like I have 12 million I with six people and I'm gonna tell you everything I'm doing it's like wow

principles.text: Start on the less crowded social network. LinkedIn had far fewer creators than Twitter, so it gave more reach per effort.
principles.quote: only one to two% of people create content versus Twitter is like almost 5050

principles.text: Keep testing posts until you know what great looks like. After that you can run the content machine indefinitely.
principles.quote: if I'm right about this and I know what great is like I can keep this machine going forever

principles.text: Pair a big free product with a paid time-saving upsell. Free users who already got value will pay to skip the work.
principles.quote: I'm trying to sell this idea that if you want to save time with Integrations pay 500 bucks if you don't knock yourself out with a free app forever

principles.text: A premium content series builds a deep bond with viewers that no ad can match, even if it costs real money.
principles.quote: that person is connected to everything that I am doing in a way that they could not have been any other way

sources.title: How RB2B prices below competitors' cost of acquisition and runs $9M ARR on near-zero human time
sources.originalTitle: Why Adam Robinson Prices RB2B Below His Competitors' Cost of Acquisition
sources.summary: Adam Robinson explains how cheap thought-leadership awareness plus near-zero marginal fulfillment cost let RB2B price below rivals' CAC and unit costs, freezing the product at a simple $79 offer. He also covers skipping VC for lean sub-VC-scale businesses and his plan to build Moltsets, a contact-data brand for Claude Code users, on top of existing content and data assets.

principles.text: Combine near-zero customer acquisition cost with zero marginal fulfillment cost and you can price below competitors' economics.
principles.quote: the incredibly cheap awareness I was getting from my thought leadership, and the fact that we are already a data company with two other product lines, and we have data scientists, and we had this data asset

principles.text: Rivals with higher unit costs and investor pressure can't match a low-price simple product, so they flee upmarket.
principles.quote: their unit economics of fulfilling these contacts were literally higher than my subscription price.

principles.text: Once rivals move upmarket, own the cheap, simple, fast-start slot and freeze the product to stay lean.
principles.quote: If you want to get started in 60 seconds for 79 bucks, we're the only game in town, right? And we have decided to just leave the product frozen in time

principles.text: Design for the leanest operation: freemium PLG SMB funnel, accepting a revenue cap in exchange for AI-amplified low headcount.
principles.quote: it's got to be freemium PLG SMB funnel. And you're kind of accepting a cap on the revenue, but the trade-off is that eventually you should be able to run that with virtually no human input.

principles.text: Sub-VC-scale businesses are attractive: no well-funded competitors chase them, and a portfolio of lean ~$10M ARR products is a great outcome.
principles.quote: If I could just keep creating lean 10 million ARR businesses that are like it's a portfolio of these sub VC scale things.

principles.text: Create product pull before spending money; capital raised too early gets spent on channels before there is pull.
principles.quote: you need to create this pull. You know, and then once you have the pull of product out of you, then you can spend money on channels to speed that up.

sources.title: Adam Robinson on bootstrapping vs VC, founder-led LinkedIn brand, and why outbound spam is dying
sources.originalTitle: Adam Robinson ROASTS VC Culture, why founders are broke, and the $25M bootstrapped blueprint
sources.summary: Adam argues that a lean, profitable bootstrapped business beats the VC treadmill, and explains how a founder-led LinkedIn brand plus a novel product took RB2B to about $5M ARR with a handful of people. He also says SDR-style outbound has lost its arbitrage while thought leadership and real-world events gain power.

principles.text: A stalled but lean business that banks millions a year can be easier and better than chasing an IPO-scale outcome.
principles.quote: he was like the sole founder and he was banking $20 million every year. And I just like had never heard that, you know, but like to me that actually seemed easier to do than create something that's just growing indefinitely and you IPO it.

principles.text: Word of mouth is the prerequisite for growth; with it many tactics can accelerate you, without it nothing works.
principles.quote: without word of mouth, nothing else that you do will work. With word of mouth, there's a million things you can do to speed it up, right?

principles.text: Founder-led LinkedIn thought leadership is the only brand marketing that works for a zero-revenue startup.
principles.quote: I just don't think there's any other type of brand marketing that would work for a startup with zero revenue other than the type that I'm doing on LinkedIn for this audience.

principles.text: Validate demand through content first: test topics on your audience, then build the product for the people who engage.
principles.quote: the funny thing about RB2B was we built the product after it became clear that I was going to be able to build this audience.

principles.text: Write to your earlier self; content must both entertain and teach, in equal measure.
principles.quote: if I stopped entertaining, zero. If I stopped teaching, zero. It's like 50/50.

principles.text: Mass cold outbound has lost its arbitrage; when it was rare it worked, once 100,000 companies did it, it stopped.
principles.quote: When there were 10 and 100 companies doing that, it worked beautifully. when there was a 100,000 companies doing that same thing. Uh that's just not the arbitrage anymore, right?

sources.title: Adam Robinson's 8 SaaS marketing strategies that work: founder brand, inbound-led outbound, UGC, word of mouth
sources.originalTitle: Best SaaS Marketing Strategies For 2026
sources.summary: Adam Robinson, who has scaled three SaaS companies to 35M combined ARR, walks through eight marketing strategies he uses at RB2B: founder brand, inbound-led outbound, cold email, LinkedIn DMs, paid ads as an accelerator, UGC, and word of mouth. His core argument is that product-market fit and word of mouth come first, and every other tactic only works well once you have them.

principles.text: Build a founder brand by being vulnerable and clear about who you are; big companies can't copy that.
principles.quote: Be incredibly clear about who you are. For me, it's a bootstrapped SAS founder who builds in public.

principles.text: Content is the ultimate leverage: it drives inbound leads at almost no cost beyond your time.
principles.quote: As a founder, you need to realize that content is the ultimate leverage.

principles.text: Combine inbound and outbound: drive traffic, identify ICP visitors, then follow up with them like warm prospects.
principles.quote: They've already shown intent by visiting your website. Our conversion rates are 10 times higher than traditional cold outreach.

principles.text: Cold email at volume works only with a clean list: pull from multiple data sources, verify every email, and rotate many sending domains.
principles.quote: Don't just use one tool, use five or six. And always validate your emails before sending.

principles.text: On LinkedIn, run connect, then value, then follow-up: no pitch in the connection request, and stop after three follow-ups.
principles.quote: The goal here is just to get the connection, not to book a meeting.

principles.text: Paid ads are an accelerator, not a foundation; use them to retarget engaged people and ABM lists, with authentic selfie-video creatives.
principles.quote: They're an accelerator. They're not the foundation. You need other things working for you first before ads will be effective at all.

sources.title: How Adam Robinson scaled Get Emails/Retention.com to $13M ARR in 36 months with manual ABM
sources.originalTitle: How I Used ABM to Scale to $13M ARR in 36 Months
sources.summary: Adam breaks down the lean outbound machine behind $13M ARR with six employees: a $3k/month Philippines team manually building target lists, a four-email sequence, a three-step LinkedIn flow, and ads to the same list. He also says what he would change today (multiple domains, sequencers, LinkedIn content) and why the 2020-21 conditions mattered.

principles.text: Build lists manually instead of pulling from Apollo/ZoomInfo; shared databases get hammered and reply rates collapse.
principles.quote: everyone else is using those same databases with those same emails. The problem is with the database platforms. Those email addresses get absolutely smashed.

principles.text: Target companies via technographics, then multi-thread 3-5 relevant people per account, always including the CEO.
principles.quote: We identified three to five potentially relevant people at each company.

principles.text: Cheap offshore labor works when you give them repeatable activity, not decisions or problems to solve.
principles.quote: We loaded them up with activity, not problems to solve.

principles.text: Run email, LinkedIn and ads against the same list so prospects feel you are everywhere.
principles.quote: combined with email LinkedIn, it created the impression that we were absolutely everywhere.

principles.text: High-volume outbound only accelerates a business that already has product-market fit; it cannot save one without word of mouth.
principles.quote: If you don't have word of mouth, which is the equivalent of product market fit, this will not save you.

principles.text: Today: still build lists manually, but send from separate domains, use a sequencer, and build organic LinkedIn content.
principles.quote: I'd set up multiple sending domains to protect the main brand domain.

sources.title: How Adam Robinson scaled RB2B to $5M ARR in 13 months with five people
sources.originalTitle: How Adam Robinson Scaled RB2B to $5M ARR in 13 Months
sources.summary: Adam tells the years-long backstory behind RB2B: a stuck email app, a feature customers loved, and a pivot found through LinkedIn posts. He covers validating demand with 300 discovery calls, a free Slack integration, pricing mistakes, founder-brand distribution, radical transparency, and keeping the team tiny.

principles.text: Overnight success is years of head-banging; the unlock then arrives all at once.
principles.quote: it was the two years before it and banging my head against the wall that actually like allowed for that unlock. But the unlock happened all at once.

principles.text: Test a new audience with posts before building, then confirm with discovery calls.
principles.quote: I know exactly how to write a post for a B2B revenue leader that will crush.

principles.text: In discovery, ask about the current workflow and what people complain about, not about your idea.
principles.quote: like how are you using website identity right now? Like how is that information getting to your reps, right? Like what are some things that they complain about?

principles.text: Give away the magic moment for free and charge for the rest; the free Slack integration drove virality.
principles.quote: if you really want this to go viral, I think we need to give the Slack integration for free. because that's the magic moment

principles.text: In a distrusted category, build trust by sharing everything publicly, including money numbers.
principles.quote: if I'm inherently in an inherently untrustworthy product category, how do I build the maximum amount of trust? It's like, well, I share literally everything about what I'm doing, right?

principles.text: Keep the team small on purpose; set a headcount rule so everyone wears many hats and focus is forced.
principles.quote: We literally just declared it. We're like, we're not going to hire anyone until we're above 10.

sources.title: How Adam Robinson bootstrapped Retention.com to $22M ARR and rebuilt with a free product and LinkedIn
sources.originalTitle: Adam Robinson: Bootstrapping Retention.com to $22 Million ARR
sources.summary: Adam describes his journey from failed email products to a free, plg tool (RB2B), and why personal-brand distribution beats outbound. He covers category creation, a weekly LinkedIn/Zoom event as a feedback loop, word of mouth as a prerequisite, and why outbound response rates are collapsing.

principles.text: Word of mouth is the gate: without it no channel works; with it, everything amplifies.
principles.quote: if you don't have Word of Mouth nothing works you know like we're sitting here picking channels right it's like well what's the maximum low hanging fruit that we can execute on

principles.text: Personal brand content compounds; a founder's face on an event outperforms company branding.
principles.quote: it may be 10x on any individual thing that you do but these this all this stuff compounds so if everything is 10x then in a year it's 10,000x

principles.text: Run a weekly recurring event to take the market's temperature and sharpen narrative.
principles.quote: the best feedback loop is this weekly event

principles.text: Coin and own a category or workflow; saying you're part of a new workflow helps even if it isn't fully real.
principles.quote: it's so helpful to just do this category creation thing I think even if it's not real right it's like so helpful to say that you're part of some new workflow that people are not doing

principles.text: Build your buyers while building the product; talk to many prospects early so you quit cheaply if it's wrong.
principles.quote: you have got to be building your buyers as you're building your product before you have it because software is so hard to get right

principles.text: A free offer can be a positioning moat; a small megaphone-backed company gains more from free than from midmarket sales.
principles.quote: I have this huge megaphone and it's got scale but a mid-market sales operation does not have the advantages a scale has if I had a free offer it would help me a lot more

sources.title: How RB2B hit $1.9M ARR from cold email: infrastructure, three campaigns, 4-month testing
sources.originalTitle: This Cold Email Strategy Makes $160k/mo for My SaaS (Copy This)
sources.summary: Adam Robinson explains how cold email drives about a third of RB2B's $6M+ ARR. Most founders fail by ignoring infrastructure, emailing only truly cold lists, and quitting early. RB2B ran three strategies: waitlist launch emails, pure cold outbound, and AI-personalized retargeting of site visitors, which converted best.

principles.text: Build deliverability infrastructure before writing copy; a perfect message in spam is worthless.
principles.quote: Your perfect message means nothing if it lands in a spam folder.

principles.text: Warm your audience first. Post on LinkedIn for months before emailing so cold contacts already know you.
principles.quote: We spent 3 months posting on LinkedIn generating awareness of me and what we were going to do at RB2B before we sent a single email.

principles.text: Build a waitlist in public with a simple CTA, then email it on launch day as warm outreach.
principles.quote: Then by launch day, 3,000 people were already waiting to sign up for RB2B.

principles.text: Write short, punchy cold emails in your own voice, with the benefit in the first line and one clear call to action.
principles.quote: It's short, punchy copy. It captured my actual voice. It's not corporate speak or formal business language.

principles.text: Commit to a multi-month testing window; early results mislead and most founders quit too soon.
principles.quote: Most founders give up after sending only 500 emails. We committed to 4 months of testing to find message market fit.

principles.text: Retarget website visitors fast with simple, contextual email; timing at peak interest beats generic cold outreach.
principles.quote: Hey, saw you on our site via RB2. Do you have any questions?

sources.title: How Adam Robinson runs RB2B at $8.6M ARR with a simple product, personal brand and AI support
sources.originalTitle: $8.6M ARR, Nobody's Touched It In A Month — Adam Robinson (RB2B) #004
sources.summary: Adam Robinson explains how a LinkedIn personal brand, a deliberately simple product, AI-run customer support and a fixed-cost data asset let RB2B reach $8.6M ARR with almost no hands-on work. He argues real moats today are distribution, unique data and network effects, and that bootstrapped cash-flow businesses beat chasing VC scale.

principles.text: Build a personal brand, not a company page: people follow people, so it's the fastest way to create awareness.
principles.quote: فالناس يتواجدون على وسائل التواصل الاجتماعي لمتابعة الأشخاص وليس الشركات.

principles.text: Write honestly about your real founder struggles; that content can beat audience-targeted pitches by 100x on engagement.
principles.quote: كانت تحصل على تفاعل يعادل مائة ضعف أي شيء أكتبه لمحاولة جذب انتباه متاجر التجارة الإلكترونية هذه.

principles.text: Keep the product radically simple so AI support can resolve nearly every ticket from good docs and account data.
principles.quote: حافظنا على بساطة منتجنا إلى أقصى درجة ورفضنا إضافة أي تعقيدات إليه

principles.text: Cheap awareness plus a fixed-cost data asset lets you price below competitors' customer acquisition cost.
principles.quote: لذا فإن الجمع بين الوعي منخفض التكلفة وأصل البيانات ذي السعر الثابت ورغبتي في الحفاظ على هذا الشيء بسيطاً بشكل لا يصدق.

principles.text: When anyone can copy your product, defensibility comes from cutting through noise with marketing, unique data, or network effects.
principles.quote: إذا كان بإمكان أي شخص نسخ كل ما تفعله، فإن الميزة تكمن إما في قدرتك على اختراق الضجيج من منظور تسويقي، أو أنك تمتلك بيانات فريدة يمكن لوكلاء الذكاء الاصطناعي استخدامها لاتخاذ إجراء

principles.text: Aim for cash flow and a portfolio of bootstrapped businesses in niches too small for VCs, rather than one venture-scale bet.
principles.quote: هدفي هو التدفق النقدي. أنا مهتم حقًا بحقيقة أنني أستطيع متابعة هذه الفرص التي لا تصل لمستوى الاستثمار الجريء (VC)

sources.title: How Adam Robinson built an organic LinkedIn engine as a founder, from vulnerability to RB2B
sources.originalTitle: The Secret to Organic LinkedIn Growth with Adam Robinson
sources.summary: Adam explains how he built a large organic LinkedIn following as a founder, and why it works for him. He stresses authentic, vulnerable pain-point writing over AI-generated content, picking the platform where your ICP lives, ghostwriters for the early stage, and using conflict like a 6sense cease-and-desist as marketing for RB2B.

principles.text: AI makes mediocre content abundant, so authentic, vulnerable, human point-of-view content stands out more.
principles.quote: the LIE of AI is thinking that it can actually offer perspective right it's like you saw these tools and you're like oh that can do X for me and then a lot of people they're like oh I'll start using it to post on LinkedIn but it's like people don't want that crap

principles.text: Articulate real pain in detail with transparency, sharing things you'd tell a best friend, not wins and announcements.
principles.quote: I'm like in excruciating detail like articulating only the pain that a CEO of a 20 million r r SAS could experience right like in in a very clear way with a lot of transparency and a lot of vulnerability

principles.text: Content-market fit is as hard as product-market fit; expect to experiment for months before it clicks.
principles.quote: Devin Reed has this idea of content Market fit in getting content Market fit I think is as hard as product Market fit for a startup and it just takes the same amount of dedication and perseverance and curiosity

principles.text: Choose the platform by where your ICP lives; if you sell to hospitals, don't go all-in on LinkedIn, though a founder profile still helps hiring.
principles.quote: if you selling to hospitals I would not recommend going psychotic like I did in trying to be literally the best content creator on LinkedIn not worth it okay it is worth I think having a profile for other reasons

principles.text: Founder thought leadership attracts opt-in employees, because candidates arrive already knowing how you think.
principles.quote: if you can explain have a steady stream of things coming out of you that are like why you are doing things and how you think about all of the different aspects of what you're dealing with in your company

principles.text: Write for a specific audience and earn meaning-based trust rather than chasing viral reach; use LinkedIn as both distribution and trust platform.
principles.quote: the alternative is you are using LinkedIn to be your distribution and Trust platform and I am trying to like I know exactly who what I write is going to attract

sources.title: How Adam Robinson tried to grow a bootstrapped SaaS like a VC-backed company, and what broke
sources.originalTitle: Adam Robinson’s Lessons from When a Bootstrapper Tries to Grow like a Venture Backed Company
sources.summary: Adam Robinson recounts scaling retention.com to $21M ARR, then trying to build a unicorn in a year after watching Jasper's rise, missing targets on churn, competition and spending discipline. He also explains why LinkedIn founder content, free products, and stacking bootstrapped businesses are his core growth bets.

principles.text: Bootstrapping a profitable SaaS to ~$10-20M ARR lets you stack new ventures with fat free cash flow and freedom.
principles.quote: there is a point that you reach as a bootstrapper I don't know where it is maybe it's like 10 15 maybe 20 million AR if you've run it properly where it's so profitable

principles.text: Churn depends on product category; a system of record churns far less than a lead-gen tool, so don't assume a segment shift fixes churn.
principles.quote: if you're a CRM if you're a system of record that is the lowest churn product there is

principles.text: Being loud about early success invites competitors who undercut you at renewal, turning expansion into contraction.
principles.quote: all of a sudden we got five comp competitors and then renewals come around and the competitors are just like using builtwith hitting everybody up

principles.text: Bootstrappers who copy VC-style spending lose fiscal discipline; hiring 50 people in 60 days without processes failed.
principles.quote: I was just spending like a sailor setting a poor example everybody who worked for us spending like a sailor hiring super expensive employees

principles.text: Founder-led LinkedIn content, honest and in video, builds parasocial trust and is the most capital-efficient channel when buyers live there.
principles.quote: there could not possibly be a more Capital efficient way to spread awareness in in your buyers

principles.text: When stuck, the fix is a better product, not copying tactics; nothing works with a weak product.
principles.quote: everything works when your product is not good nothing works right so like the art of getting unstuck is the art of making everything that you're doing better

sources.title: How Adam Robinson bootstrapped three SaaS companies to $1M ARR, faster each time
sources.originalTitle: 3 Startups to $1M ARR - Faster Every Time | SaaS Club
sources.summary: Adam walks through Robly (17 months), Retention.com (27 weeks) and RB2B (16 weeks), all without outside funding. The thread: find an acquisition channel with no competition, and eventually build an audience first, since cold email no longer works.

principles.text: Acquiring customers is expensive because of competition; an uncontested channel with a good offer is cheap.
principles.quote: what makes acquiring customers expensive is competition. And if you have a channel that you don't have any competition in and you have a good offer, it's going to be incredibly inexpensive for you to acquire those customers.

principles.text: A channel can carry a weak product only briefly; once the list is used up, a non-competitive product stalls.
principles.quote: our product wasn't actually competitive outside of that channel

principles.text: Cold email and BDR-style outbound no longer work; pick a go-to-market that is future-proofed against it.
principles.quote: There is no way that we could have done what we did with get emails in the way that we did it today. It would be impossible.

principles.text: Make the product free and lead with founder content so the offer spreads on its own instead of paying for sales people.
principles.quote: It's this hundred million dollar value proposition that just punches you in the face. That's literally free.

principles.text: Vulnerable, honest posts about your own failures beat polished generic content on LinkedIn.
principles.quote: I'm talking about my own problems now and my own failures to revenue leaders like me in SaaS, which is very different angle.

principles.text: Treat the job as edutainment and use thought leadership ads to amplify posts that already won organically.
principles.quote: my job is edutainment. My job is to make entertaining, educational and highly compelling content about how I am building my SaaS and about how you can do it too.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Adam lays out his zero-to-1,000-customers system from building RB2B and two other software companies. Validate with 50+ discovery calls and prepayment, ship a manual MVP, prove product market fit with three signals, then run content, outreach and retargeting together as a "magic triangle".

chunks.heading: Discovery before building: 50 calls and real prepayment
chunks.text:
- Adam says most founders fail because they "fall in love with their idea instead of their customers' problems." They build for 12 to 18 months before talking to anyone and confuse building something with building something people want.
- He cites that 90% of startups never reach $1M ARR.
- Before writing code, he commits to at least 50 discovery calls. The goal is to find people who will pay for something not yet built. He means actual prepayment, not "Yeah, that sounds interesting."
- His favorite example is BarkBox. Matt Meeker owned a Great Dane in NYC, where stores sold tiny toys for tiny dogs (2010, pre-Amazon Prime). He took a Photoshop mockup of a monthly delivery of five large toys for $29 to Washington Square Park and swiped cards on a Square reader on his phone. He got 50 purchases on day one, before he had a website.

chunks.heading: Getting the first discovery calls
chunks.text:
- Start with your personal network on LinkedIn and other social platforms, targeting people who match your ideal customer profile (ICP).
- He shares Andy Mowat's outreach message for Distribute: "I was at Outreach.io and now I'm building a HubSpot and Seismic competitor, three times cheaper and 10 times more user-friendly, and we currently have around 4,000 active users that love us. Would you be open to giving honest feedback about the product I'm building?" Andy offers a $100 gift card for their time. Adam says this still works.
- Another tactic he has used: offer paid advisory roles to people who don't make much money (director level and below) but are still in the ICP.
- The "Alina Vanderberg approach" (Chili Piper, now around $40M ARR): go to industry events with a notepad sketch of the product vision and ask influential people, "Would you buy something like this? And if not, what would we have to change for you to buy it?"
- To spot the most influential person in a room, watch who people walk toward to hug. The recipient of the hug is who Alina talks to.

chunks.heading: What to say on discovery calls
chunks.text:
- Lead with a "sizzling one-liner" that makes eyes light up. For RB2B it was "person level website visitor identification," because before that only company-level identification existed.
- Questions he asks:
  1. Do you understand the problem I'm trying to solve?
  2. Do you have the problem?
  3. How are you solving it today?
  4. Would you pay for the solution I'm describing if I could get it to you tomorrow?
  5. What else would the solution need for you to pay for it?
  6. I'm thinking of charging X per month, would you pay that?
- The goal is to understand their pain so deeply that you can solve it better than anyone.

chunks.heading: Build the minimum product and stay manual
chunks.text:
- Build only what is needed to deliver the core value proposition. If it takes more than 4 to 6 weeks, "you're probably building too much."
- Anything that could be done manually should be done manually first. At RB2B, they sent spreadsheets over email manually for five full months before putting up a website.
- Why manual is an "unfair advantage":
  - You stay close to customers and learn things automation would hide.
  - You iterate about 10 times faster than competitors trying to automate everything.
  - You reach the market months earlier and get real feedback.

chunks.heading: Product-market fit signals and inbound velocity
chunks.text:
- Three signals of product-market fit, and he says you need all three:
  1. At least one referral per week from paying customers.
  2. Customers would be genuinely upset if you took the product away.
  3. Organic growth without any marketing.
- Until you have these, do nothing except pursue product-market fit, "because nothing you do will work." He equates PMF with strong word of mouth: people sharing and bragging about the product unprompted, prospects saying "I heard about you from X," and customers creating content that drives signups.
- Inbound velocity (a steady daily flow of prospects) is not required to move forward but makes everything easier. Start by posting on LinkedIn from day one, sharing the wins, failures and pivots in real time.
- Signs it is working: website visits without outreach, inbound connection requests from your ICP, and prospects DMing about the product.
- Example: he built in public on LinkedIn for months before launching RB2B. At launch they had a 1,600-person waitlist and 300 discovery meetings booked with high-value customers, and hit $1M ARR in 6 weeks post-launch.

chunks.heading: The "magic triangle" and founder-led LinkedIn content
chunks.text:
- Phase two is the magic triangle: content, outreach and retargeting. Each feeds the other two. Content drives awareness and traffic, outreach converts warm visitors, and retargeting brings back people who weren't ready.
- Only activate it after product-market fit (at least one referral per week). Doing it earlier wastes money scaling something that doesn't work.
- Why all three are needed:
  - Content alone is too slow ("you can't wait 2 years to build an audience," but start building today).
  - Outreach alone converts terribly; "cold email alone is essentially dead."
  - Retargeting alone generates no new pipeline.
- LinkedIn is the foundation. Personal profiles grow about 10 times faster than company pages, and the human connection works like free ads.
- Founder content strategy:
  - Post at least three times a week.
  - Pick three pillars. His are building in public with real numbers, the future of his industry (a polarizing stance on go-to-market), and contrarian takes (bootstrapping vs VC, where he advocates taking as little money as possible).
  - Follow the "three C's": be clear about who you are, consistent, and keep reinforcing the story.
  - Share failures as well as wins. Authenticity is the edge because big companies have to sound like corporate brands.

chunks.heading: Outreach: email, LinkedIn and website visitors
chunks.text:
- Do two types of outreach: cold outreach only to ICP people, and follow-up with people who visited your website. For the cold list, they use Apollo to build a list of founders and marketers at SaaS companies with 5 to 200 employees, reaching out to three people per company. For website visitors, he built RB2B to identify them at person level (name, job title, LinkedIn, business email).
- Email infrastructure:
  - Use Instantly or Smartlead (they switch between them depending on what works).
  - Rotate hundreds of domains (e.g. tryyourproduct.com, getyourproduct.com).
  - Two inboxes per domain, sending 2 to 10 emails per day per inbox, to get past Gmail and Outlook spam filters.
  - Validate every address with NeverBounce and LeadMagic.
  - Copy should be clear and concise, state the problem you solve, and end with a clear call to action.
- LinkedIn connection requests:
  - Use the same ICP list plus RB2B visitors. Start at 10 to 20 per day, working up to at most 50.
  - Send requests with no message. Acceptance is high, and near 100% for website visitors. It rises as your audience grows.
  - Be careful with automation: he has seen warnings, and you can get permanently banned. He names HeyReach and Lemlist-style tools (he says "Log Growth Machine," i.e. La Growth Machine) for automation.
- LinkedIn follow-up:
  - Wait for them to like or comment on your content, then DM: "Hey, [first name]. Thanks for the like or comment. How are things going at [company]?" Response rate is usually north of 60%.
  - If there is no engagement after 60 days, send a soft touch such as "What caught your attention?" followed by "How are things going at [company]?"
  - Don't pitch in the first message. "You're not actually selling. You're building rapport so that you can get someone on a call to sell." Never sell on LinkedIn.
- Combining email and LinkedIn hits the same prospects on two channels, and some people respond better on one than the other.

chunks.heading: Retargeting as the multiplier
chunks.text:
- Install pixels from LinkedIn, Meta, Google and Twitter on the website.
- Build custom audiences from website visitors, lookalike audiences from paying customers and prospect lists, and matched-audience ads that go straight to prospect lists.
- Ad creative uses Russell Brunson's who/what/why/how framework: who are you, what do you have, why do they need it, how can they get it. Keep it authentic. Most of the time it is a selfie video from his phone, and phone-recorded content performs best.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Adam lays out a six-step LinkedIn framework: develop an authentic story, perfect your profile, write hook-driven posts, run connect campaigns, build community through comments, then add video. His core claim is that personal brands beat company pages because people connect with people, and that organic content gives small companies free ads that big competitors can't buy.

chunks.heading: Why personal profiles beat company pages on LinkedIn
chunks.text:
Adam argues that "people do business with people, not companies," and that LinkedIn lets a founder scale human-to-human connection in a way a company's ad cannot.

- He grew from 4,000 to 140,000 followers in 24 months. He says he reached 100,000 in 18 months.
- He took RB2B from 0 to $3M ARR in about 6 months, with five people and no funding, which he credits to LinkedIn.
- Organic content works as free ads. Large companies have to pay for the impressions.
- He says personal profiles grow about 10x faster than company pages and get far more engagement.
- His comparison: a post from competitor and market leader 6sense versus one of his own. His own post won on engagement.
- Don't copy big-company branding. He says not to build a slick, sterile brand or a logo in the same colors as everyone else, and he mocks 6sense's line that it "reimagines the way revenue teams create, manage, and convert pipeline."
- Your humanity, flaws, adversity and beliefs are the advantage a big company can't match.

chunks.heading: The three C's: clarity, consistency, constant reinforcement
chunks.text:
Adam's framework for building a personal brand has three parts.

- Be incredibly clear about who you are.
- Be consistent about who that person is.
- Constantly reinforce that story.
- The more vulnerable, flawed and relatable the message, the more it cuts through. He says very few creators on LinkedIn will talk about real problems, and doing so puts you in the top 1%.
- Example: he posted about a layoff and admitted the company had fallen out of product-market fit and failed to fix churn for 18 months. His executive team begged him to soften it. He refused.
- His test: "If you can say things to LinkedIn that you would say to your spouse behind closed doors, it will do better than anything any large company could ever post." He notes that investors or co-founders may limit how far you can go.
- A tip he credits to Devin Reid: people behave on LinkedIn like they behave at work, so being a little inappropriate stands out.
- Sharing financial numbers makes building in public far more interesting.
- He quotes Alex Hormozi: "Do, then talk about it."

chunks.heading: Content pillars and being polarizing
chunks.text:
Adam recommends one or two pillars, plus building in public.

- Pick topics tangential to the problem you solve, where your prospects share those problems. Choose things you do daily and think about more than most people.
- Example for a CRM aimed at car-dealership sales teams: building in public, how to attract, train and retain salespeople, and the future of dealership sales with AI.
- His own pillars: build in public, the future of BDR/SDR and go-to-market, and bootstrapping versus VC.
- Bland, down-the-middle content gets lost in the noise. He uses Russell Brunson's "polarity" idea: between mainstream and crazy, there is a sweet spot where people on your side love you and the other side hates you.
- His example: around Labor Day 2024 he posted that he got rid of his BDR team and pipeline generation sped up. He argued that the predictable revenue model "was born in 2012 and died in 2023," and that demand is now captured by SDRs, not created by them.
- His alternative was to drive traffic to your site and retarget visitors. He calls it more efficient but less predictable.
- Early on, the goal is a trust-building landing page, not a lead engine. His friend Curtis Matsko (Portland Leather Goods, a $100M/year handbag business) spends 30 minutes a week recording videos. His assistant posts them daily. Engagement is under 10% of Adam's, and he has never tied a purse sale to LinkedIn. But his last three executive hires came from people who watched the videos, and an investment banker now does free finance work for him.

chunks.heading: Profile setup checklist
chunks.text:
Adam says his profile alone drives hundreds of inbound RB2B leads a month. Each fix is small, and together they compound.

- Headshot: professional, looking at the camera, solid background, ideally smiling.
- Banner: branded, with a clear value proposition and a call to action. Use Canva (free tier) or hire someone on Fiverr or Upwork.
- Headline: clear, credible and accurate.
- Link or custom button at the top, pointed at your site or a cold-traffic page with a front-end offer.
- About section: very detailed and specific, with numbers. Put the credibility in the first line, above the fold. Cover what you have done, not who you aspire to be.
- Featured section: direct-response calls to action.
- Roles: detailed descriptions of past and present roles, plus investments, advisory roles and professional networks.
- Education, including advanced degrees and certifications.
- At least 3-4 recommendations, swapping with others if needed.
- With LinkedIn Premium you can see who viewed your profile. He treats those people as warm leads for opening conversations.

chunks.heading: Writing posts that work
chunks.text:
Adam says to write for the audience, not the algorithm, because the algorithm exists to serve the audience. His fix for any algorithm change is to make better content.

**Finding ideas ("idea hunting")**, using cold email as the example niche:
- Study the top creators in the niche. Spend hours on their last 90 days of posts, log the topics in a spreadsheet, and pick the ones where you can take a polarizing view. Don't copy their ideas whole.
- Ask Gemini, which draws on Google Search and YouTube, "What are the most common questions people have about cold email?"
- Mine Reddit threads for the questions people ask.
- He says these three sources give enough ideas for the first 30 days. After that, revisit creators' top posts from a year ago and add your own spin.
- The best posts answer questions people have about your niche.

**Swipe file:** spend two hours collecting the best posts from creators in your space (hooks, templates, closes, calls to action). He looks to Chris Walker for hooks and Nigel Thomas for templates.

**Hooks:** the hook is everything before "see more," and it is the most important part of a post. Write as if no one has heard of you, build credibility fast, and use numbers because "LinkedIn loves numbers." Examples:
- "I spoke to 20 CEOs over the past 30 days."
- "I bootstrapped $20M ARR in three and a half years."
- "I just audited a $50M ARR SaaS with monthly ad spend of X" (a Chris Walker hook).

**Template:** he often uses a list plus two sentences, or bullets. Each post should agitate a specific pain point, offer a solution, and tie it together with a takeaway, like a mini hero's journey. Once you've mastered writing you can drop templates.

**Close:** end with a clever closing line that gives readers a "dopamine hit" and prompts engagement. He says not to write "let's continue the conversation in the comments" or tack on a stupid question.

chunks.heading: Connect campaigns and conversation opening
chunks.text:
Adam's outbound system on LinkedIn:

1. List your 100-250 best prospects.
2. Send 10-20 connection requests per day with no message. Accept rates are high. You can work up to 50 per day, but automation is against LinkedIn terms and risks a ban.
3. When a connected prospect likes or comments on your content, DM them: "Hey [name], thanks for the like/comment. How are things going at [company]?" He says response rates are usually north of 60%.
4. As inbound requests grow, stop outbound and accept only ICP connections. Don't accept people who want to sell to you.
5. After accepting, message "what caught your attention?" and then ask how things are going at their company.
6. Wait 60 days before pitching. Most people wait 48 hours or 5 days. By day 60 you are "famous to them" from your content.

He says to start conversations with anyone who viewed your profile or company page, engaged with a post, or replied to your comment, without pitch-slapping them. His friend Megan Bowen connected with 20 ICP people a day manually for four years, reached thousands of prospects, and now has 30,000 followers and an agency pipeline of leads, partnerships and investment opportunities.

chunks.heading: Community through comments
chunks.text:
- Adam answers every comment on his posts, typically 100 or more per post. He meets many people at in-person events who already know him from the comments.
- Commenters helped fix RB2B's pricing. The company had 3,000 free signups but only 13 paying customers. He posted about it repeatedly, and the feedback led to a pricing change that reached a 10% free-to-paid conversion rate and helped growth from $0 to $3M ARR in 6 months with five people.
- Early on, make a list of influential people in your space and leave at least 100 thoughtful comments a week on their posts. Don't use AI to restate the post and add a question at the end.
- Spend as much time or more commenting each week as you spend writing.
- The audience built around your pillars can eventually move to another platform.

chunks.heading: Video and the 30-day commitment
chunks.text:
**Video:** Adam says getting people to watch and listen to you speak intelligently raises your status in their minds. He copies Chris Walker's format: more polished than a phone in a bedroom, but not heavily produced, with a polarizing view.
- His process: write the post first, then record a free-flowing monologue off the post's bullet points. The video and post end up slightly different.
- Tools: Riverside for recording, and an Upwork editor at about $250 per video.
- Video isn't required. He suggests waiting until you've found your voice and have strong engagement. He also flags LinkedIn's mobile video feed test as something to watch.

**30-day commitment:** he asks people to follow his guidelines for 30 days, about 16 posts and 20 outbound connection requests per day. The expected results are:
- A pull-based recruiting mechanism, because candidates read your posts and are pre-sold before interviewing.
- Inbound partnership approaches from your ecosystem.
- Possibly investor interest, which he says to avoid because he thinks "VC is the enemy of the founder."
- Possibly inbound leads.
- His main reason to stick with it is that you get 30 days closer to finding your voice.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Adam explains how a year of posting on LinkedIn before seeing any direct revenue built a founder brand that became RB2B's sole acquisition channel (about $5M ARR in 13 months). He covers content pillars and content-market fit, hook writing, credibility signals, why video deepens trust, and why he skips AI-written posts and viral-for-followers tactics.

chunks.heading: How Adam started on LinkedIn and why it became his only acquisition channel
chunks.text:
- In January 2022 he began posting on LinkedIn. His first company, Retention.com, was at $13M ARR with six people, and big Shopify stores looked like a dream customer.
- He picked LinkedIn over Twitter because of its creator-to-user dynamic. Many users are on the feed all day for work, and only about 2% post actively.
- The plan was to build 10-20k followers on LinkedIn, then figure out Twitter.
- For about the first year it didn't produce demos. It did make him known in the e-commerce ecosystem, so people approached him at trade shows. It also helped partnerships, credibility and recruiting.
- He says that year he did not know why he was writing what he wrote. He quotes Russell Brunson: posting is "not about engagement and deals and dollars. It's about being one day closer to finding your voice. And then once you have found your voice, you got the keys to the kingdom."
- Today LinkedIn is the only thing he does for RB2B customer acquisition. He says RB2B hit $5M ARR in 13 months with a team of four, "100% a result of this".
- Dave Gerhardt's *Founder Brand* was one seed. Its argument is that most businesses started for a reason, usually a good story, so tell it where your audience lives.

chunks.heading: Content-market fit: why founder content works only when it lines up
chunks.text:
- He says "content market fit" is as real and as hard as product-market fit. You know you lack it when you post into nothingness.
- Three things have to line up: the author, the platform, and an audience that also buys the product. His fit works because LinkedIn's audience are B2B buyers. He says a brilliant TikTok creator wouldn't get the same result.
- He claims personal brand "works a lot faster with a lot less capital" than a company brand. He bought the retention.com domain for $800,000 and says it earns trust, but the personal brand did the awareness work.
- Reasoning: people go on social media to connect with people, so the best brand for a company is a public figure built around a person.
- He expects this to work better each year as more B2B time moves onto LinkedIn.

chunks.heading: Content pillars: build a public figure by repeating one story
chunks.text:
- Posting consistently on LinkedIn means creating a public figure, as a PR agency would have 50 years ago, by telling the same story many different ways.
- A content pillar is just saying the same thing over and over in different ways. Brand marketing is people seeing the same thing repeatedly.
- His pillars: bootstrapped SaaS founder, future of go-to-market, bootstrapping vs VC, and working in public. Ask anyone who he is and they'd say he bootstrapped to $25M ARR, works in public, and talks go-to-market. Hardly anyone knows he has two kids, because he chose not to share it.
- Pick two or three pillars that are authentic, resonate with the market, and are not mainstream.
- Authenticity matters because breakout posts are polarizing. Maybe 10-20% will hate you for what the other 80% love, and you must be able to defend it.
- Status-game noise is what everyone does, so being genuinely human separates you.
- He learned repetition from watching Chris Walker repeat his pillars on a 16-hour drive. The skill is saying it so people don't notice you're repeating.

chunks.heading: Posting tactics: storytelling, listicles, hooks and credibility
chunks.text:
- Reporting what you've done ("do cool stuff and talk about it") is a good start, especially if you're a future version of your audience.
- Deeper storytelling beats reporting. His monthly recap does decently, but a story gets about 100x the engagement. The example: a close friend emailed him that he wasn't ambitious enough after he refused to join a VC-backed startup, and that friend's company wound down the same month his made $1M profit.
- Opinion-only posts underperform posts with a story behind the point.
- Listicles are an easy template: five or six supporting reasons plus a takeaway. They keep people reading.
- Pro tip: find posts of his (or others') with over 1,000 likes and rewrite them with your own facts.
- The hook matters most. Journalists once spent 50% of their time on the headline. Of a mediocre post with a great hook and a great post with a weak hook, the first wins. With his consultant Alec, they won't write a post until the hook exists.
- Hook rules:
  - Use as many numbers as possible: "I've recorded 270 episodes, 10,000 downloads, 17 guests in two years, here are seven things I learned" beats "I recorded a season and here's what I learned".
  - Money, profit and pipeline numbers draw people.
