  - Maximize credibility in every hook. Example: "I've bootstrapped 3 million ARR three times. I've gone twice as fast with half the resources each time."
  - If you lack big wins, broker information: "I spoke to 10 early-stage founders about cold outbound. Here's what's not working and the one thing that is."
- Treat each post as if no one has heard of you. A Peter Confalone analysis found only about 15% audience overlap between his posts, and LinkedIn isn't sequential, so a reader may see a post from six months ago.
- Brainstorm hooks with people (him, Alec, Pete) rather than AI.

chunks.heading: Audience vs. crowd, the gimmicks, and AI
chunks.text:
- His top posts were screenshots of others' tweets with "Founders, do you agree?", from a ghostwriter early on (late 2022 to early 2023), plus engagement circles he no longer uses.
- He now optimizes for trust within his ICP, not follower count. To maximize followers he'd post about work-life balance, HR and posting on LinkedIn.
- The current gimmick is "comment YES for the slides", which draws second- and third-degree commenters. He has heard indirectly that LinkedIn favors those over first-degree comments.
- He doesn't use ChatGPT to write posts. He cites Rick Rubin: what's interesting about art is the artist's perspective, and AI has none. He thinks AI is better at amplifying a person's draft than writing it.
- He says AI SDRs haven't replaced one SDR, though spam filters have made SDRs' work harder.
- He posts about 36 times a month. Replying to comments was an unscalable relationship tactic he still likes but cut back after having a kid in September, partly because of AI comment generators.
- Starter advice: leave meaningful comments on posts by 10 influential people in your ecosystem over several months.

chunks.heading: Video, voice, and the weekly live show
chunks.text:
- LinkedIn is a text platform, so the post's strength determines the video's strength. For a real banger of a text post, they often skip the video.
- Voice is a deeper connection than text, and video deeper again. People came up to him at trade shows without introducing themselves, as if they'd talked the day before.
- He ignores LinkedIn's TikTok-style video feed because it doesn't appear targeted to his ICP.
- Video came unnaturally to him and took a long time. You don't need to be attractive, but you must get comfortable on camera.
- He runs a weekly live webinar rather than a recorded podcast, aiming to be different. He says people want "edutainment", equal parts education and entertainment.
- Segments include the "pitch slap" and "unfuck my startup", where a guest like Sam Parr critiques a viewer's landing page live. He says live media has spontaneous audience interaction that recorded podcasts lack.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Adam Robinson walks through Retention.com's P&L (about 87% gross margin, roughly $6M net income run rate), his failed 2023 push to scale like a funded rival, and how a candid LinkedIn post about a vendor's cease and desist gave RB2B 1,600 pre-launch leads. He also discusses RB2B's credit-based pricing, high free-to-paid conversion, and his open concerns about churn.

chunks.heading: Why Adam went aggressive in 2023, and what he learned
chunks.text:
- Adam shared an office with Dave Rogenmoser and the Jasper AI team. Both companies had been stuck at about $2-3M ARR for two years. Jasper then went from 0 to $50M ARR in 12 months with a tiny team and raised heavily.
- Seeing that, Adam thought "well I can do that too." He took the free cash from retention.com and put it into hiring and trying to build a "unicorn company" around a tighter ICP, hoping to fix churn.
- Churn was not solved. He says he "really lost my religion during this period."
- He was glad he never raised money. Retention.com had been at $12M ARR with six employees (about $2M revenue per employee), and he recommends running that way if you can.
- He calls the pressure to look bigger "everything": "What do you mean you only have six employees?" It takes a lot of ego to resist vanity metrics. He expects he could lose the discipline again.

chunks.heading: Retention.com P&L and margins (January 2024)
chunks.text:
- Run rate of about $6M net income at the time. He says the business is "making a lot of money profit."
- Gross margin was 87%, above the typical 75-80% for SaaS.
- His explanation: it is a data company. You compile a lot of data at SaaS margins, and if you structure it right the data cost becomes fixed, so COGS does not grow with scale.
- G&A was $346K in January, mostly executive salaries (six executives).
- Retention.com made about $1M of profit in the year discussed. It is 85% of revenue and 120% of profit, so RB2B's losses are funded by it.
- Retention.com revenue was flat to slightly declining. Adam says stacking RB2B on top is what shows growth again.
- To keep the team motivated on a flat product, he tells them it is "the fuel behind everything we're doing." Something growing from 0 to 1 feels more exciting than a profitable business that is not growing, "like a baby is more exciting than an 80-year-old."

chunks.heading: Lawsuit marketing: the cease and desist post
chunks.text:
- A vendor Adam used for comparison research, six months before the contract expired, told him it would triple his price. That annoyed him enough to write a LinkedIn post describing what they did.
- They sent a cease and desist. The old playbook is to apologize and delete. Adam saw it as "the single greatest PR opportunity for a company that is 3 weeks old" because it would take him from "LinkedIn guy" to getting every customer of that vendor to learn what RB2B does.
- Risk check: his lawyer said the worst case was a suit costing a few hundred thousand dollars ($300-400K) over about three years. The lawyer said he would never recommend it but understood the logic. Adam judged it worth it.
- Result: about 1,600 likes, 913 comments and several hundred thousand impressions.
- His broader point: founders say they want a founder-led brand, but then everything goes through a PR machine and ends up as fluffy content nobody relates to. Authentic, blunt stories resonate.

chunks.heading: LinkedIn content strategy and pre-launch lead gen
chunks.text:
- Very little of his content is sales content. Roughly one in ten posts gets a hard CTA at the bottom.
- Most of the conversion comes from a "visit my website" link in his profile. People see interesting, transparent posts about the journey and wonder what he does. The algorithm then keeps serving them more of his posts.
- His view: "people don't want to be sold to on social media." Organic content brings people along on a journey, builds community around ideas and builds relationships through comments.
- He admits he cannot fully say why it works so well, but it works well enough that he keeps doing it.
- Pre-launch, the CTA was a free Google Form link dropped into the post. Variants of the post ran three or four times and collected 1,600+ leads. He did not wait for a perfect tech stack or tracking.
- It also produced hundreds of discovery conversations. He and his cofounder were on the phone with about 10 people a day between them for around six months, so they knew what to build at launch. He cites *The Four Steps to the Epiphany*.
- His comparison: instead of a Product Hunt launch, this yielded more leads and more customer conversations.

chunks.heading: RB2B funnel, pricing and conversion numbers
chunks.text:
- RB2B launched March 1, 2024 with no revenue before then. It went from about $5K to about $200K MRR, adding about $60K of new MRR per month on average over the prior three months. About $10K of new MRR came in during the first six days of September.
- Aug 8 to Sep 6: about 3,000 new trials, with almost 10% converting to new customers. Typical free-to-paid is 3-5%.
- He attributes activation and conversion to content that targets a very tight audience of the right people on LinkedIn. Installing the script converts at about 35% of signups, which others call a dream.
- Pricing is credit-based (usage-based, not transactional):
  - Premium: 200 leads/month, delivering LinkedIn URLs into a Slack channel, starting at $99/month (integrations and email included at that tier).
  - About 1,000 leads/month costs roughly $300/month.
  - Average new customer pays about $270/month.
- About 100 expansions in the period, which he describes as "right-sizing" rather than growth.

chunks.heading: Churn problem and plan to fix it
chunks.text:
- Churn is very high, about 10% a month, with a roughly 9-month LTV. An agency cancelled about 80 accounts and consolidated them under one, so it looks even worse than 10%.
- Adam expects churn to be "a disaster" to solve. His cofounder Santos (formerly at Apollo and ZoomInfo) is not worried because the product is so young.
- He cites Nathan Barry's ConvertKit as a benchmark: churn was about 10% at a similar revenue level, then went down over time.
- Adam is unsure he can get there without adding a system-of-record product. The Clearbit Reveal team told him churn was their biggest problem and the only fix was getting other departments using other products.
- Plan: add other products, especially for salespeople (RB2B is currently a marketer's tool), and get more teams using the platform. He prefers building over buying because he is scared of the M&A and integration process.
- He also wants to borrow Russell Brunson's tactics (content, courses, community) to turn free marketing users into paid users and lower churn. He notes Brunson grew ClickFunnels to hundreds of millions after churn stalled at 17%.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Adam Robinson lays out the "sell before you build" framework: pre-sell with a sizzling one-liner and quick pitch, build a manual MVP, find product-market fit through hundreds of calls, and stay tiny. The second half covers getting unstuck from $1M to $10M, hiring almost nobody, inbound-led outbound, and refusing VC money.

chunks.heading: The "elite founder gap" and why order matters
chunks.text:
- Adam says the average founder has under a 10% chance of success, while elite founders succeed over 50% of the time.
- He calls the difference "the elite founder gap". Elite founders take the same steps as average founders but in a different order.
- Average founder: idea, build too much product, then hunt for buyers with one-to-many growth hacking.
- Elite founder: find buyers before building, build almost nothing, skip growth hacking, and do gritty one-to-one work.
- Growth hacking before product market fit (PMF) either fails or "works just enough" to give false hope.
- His own proof: Robly was built for 18 months with zero customer conversations and modeled 800 paying customers at $15/month in month one. It got 10. It survived only because of a lucky growth hack (crawling the web for competitors' signup widgets, then offering "50% more opens for half the price"). It topped out at $3M ARR and shrank about 0.5% per month for years.
- Later, Robly spent over $1M and a year building a Mailchimp-upmarket app without talking to anyone. At a trade show "people's eyes glazed over" because about 10 vendors already filled the gap, and the code was deleted.

chunks.heading: Sell before you build: the Barkbox lesson and RB2B/Retention.com origin
chunks.text:
- Adam learned the approach from Henrik, co-founder of Barkbox. Henrik showed a photoshopped mockup on his iPhone in Washington Square Park and sold about 50 $30 monthly subscriptions via Square, with no website, product, employees or office. Barkbox later had 100,000+ monthly subscribers at $30, versus Robly's 2,500 after three years.
- Three reasons not to build first:
  - Human intuition is a poor indicator of market viability.
  - People are polite and won't be honest. "The single best way to figure out if someone actually likes your idea is get them to hand you money." Even $1 is a strong signal.
  - Software is slow and expensive to build.
- Retention.com origin: after the failed trade show, he told 100 booth visitors "What if I could get you email addresses of people on your website who didn't even fill out a form." All 100 perked up. He took business cards and, for six months, still didn't know how to build the tech.
- 12 months later the product existed. Beta testers came from those cards and Robly's customer base. It reached $1M ARR in 27 weeks and about $22M ARR bootstrapped four years later.

chunks.heading: The four-step 0 to $1M framework and MVP rules
chunks.text:
1. Attention grab and pre-sale.
2. MVP and customer feedback loop.
3. Do things that don't scale.
4. Grow the right way, funded by customers rather than investors.

Early adopter flow:
- Use a sizzling one-liner to get a 15-minute call, then a 5-minute quick pitch, then an offer to get them to pay something.
- If they won't pay, get them to commit to regular feedback in exchange for free access.
- Get 10 to 20 committed users before building.
- Alina Vanderberg (Chili Piper) went to every B2B meetup in NYC, found the most connected people, and showed a notepad drawing asking if they'd buy it and what would have to change.
- Questions to ask:
  - Do you understand the problem?
  - Do you have the problem?
  - How do you solve it today?
  - Would you pay for it as described if I delivered tomorrow?
  - What else would it need to do?
  - Would you pay $100/month?

MVP rules:
- Build as little as possible. Do things manually. RB2B onboarded beta testers by hand for five months before having a website: he emailed a pixel and a daily spreadsheet. The team ran 300+ discovery calls between October 2023 and the March 2024 launch.
- Pick the smallest niche. ConvertKit (about $40M ARR bootstrapped, per Adam) launched for food bloggers, won the top ones, then expanded to all creators.
- Run every onboarding call yourself. Then automate a feedback email sequence: use AI to write 4 to 6 variants of "just checking in, how's it going, are you seeing X value?" and schedule them over 8 to 12 weeks via Boomerang, GMass or a mail merge from Gmail.
- Prioritize features in a Google Sheet every two weeks, with columns for value of the requesting users, request frequency, and estimated build time.
- Watch for "magic moments": overjoyed reactions, people trying to pay for something unfinished, desperation when it goes down. RB2B users said "This feels like I'm cheating."
- Test: "If I took my product away from my users, how upset would they get?"
- Target 25 to 50 paying users in this phase. Get them by referrals (best signal), posting in public, podcasts (matchmaker.fm), commenting on influencers' posts without pitching, LinkedIn advice requests, events, and intros from friends and investors.

chunks.heading: Product market fit rules
chunks.text:
- Do things that don't scale until you have PMF. Before PMF, no ads, SEO, influencers, UGC, partnerships, affiliates, Product Hunt or sponsored newsletters. "Nothing will work if you don't have product market fit. Everything will work if you do."
- Signs of PMF:
  - Strong word of mouth and high retention (exponential organic growth with no effort).
  - Customers who love it despite bad UX (Retention.com began as an identity feature inside Robly; users exported it to Clay and said they couldn't live without it).
  - People prepaying for something that doesn't exist.
  - The market is pulling the product out of you.
  - Customers would be livid if you removed it, and cash is piling up.
- Become ramen profitable so you control your own destiny and don't need investors.
- Be different in a way that matters. "Same but cheaper" gets only 3 to 5% of someone else's business. You need to be 10x better or 10x cheaper, ideally better, cheaper and really different. "Same but free" works only with a premium tier that funds it (his Mailchimp example: a $12B acquisition with no outside funding). Features for a niche that a big incumbent can't copy also work.
- If you already have $250K to $500K ARR but no PMF, restart as if you had zero customers: let prospects, not intuition, define what's valuable, and reintroduce yourself to customers as someone focused on their biggest problems.

chunks.heading: Sizzling one-liner and quick pitch templates
chunks.text:
One-liner: use DigitalMarketer's before-and-after worksheet. Answer what they have, what they feel, what their day looks like, and whether their status changes (e.g. Google certified agency, Inc. 5000, G2 high performer).

- RB2B before: company-level visitor ID ("someone from Microsoft in Atlanta"), reps guessing and cold emailing. After: person-level identification. One-liner: "RB2B: person-level website visitor identity." It opened 300+ discovery calls and is still the site headline.
- Make it clear, concise and differentiated. Never "like competitor X but cheaper."

Quick pitch (four slides, under five minutes):
1. Problem statement, via "It sucks that ___" (e.g. B2B companies can't identify visitors at the person level).
2. Introduction, borrowing the one-liner.
3. The story, one paragraph, memorized, with an image or two instead of words.
4. Solution and offer. Anyone paying before it exists is a strong signal. Offer a huge discount, e.g. RB2B's pitch: pricing starts at $5,000/year, but the first 10 beta testers get unlimited access for $500 for 12 months. Fallback: free for 90 days in exchange for regular, extensive feedback.

More calls make the pitch better and show whether to pursue the idea.

chunks.heading: Finding your first 10 conversations
chunks.text:
Define a tight ICP: "Anybody is the worst answer. Men or women is the second worst. Developers who live in Seattle is a great answer." Outreach works at least 10x better with an intro or an existing relationship (a reason to build a personal brand).

- LinkedIn DMs: ask your network for 15 minutes of feedback on "[one-liner]" built for "[job/industry]". Ask mutual connections for intros. For strangers (director level and below), offer an interview for a paid advisor role. He found his co-founder Diana Ross with that template.
- Cold email (Andy Mewborn's "gift card play"): inbox rotation via Instantly, two emails. Email one asks for feedback and credibility with numbers, with a PS offering a $100 gift card. Email two has a blank subject and says "if you aren't interested, you can tell me to go kick rocks." Reported result: 44 booked demos in 30 days.
- Industry events (the Alina approach), expert networks (Clarity, MentorPass, MentorLoop, around $500+ per call; ask experts for referrals), and professional communities (Facebook, WhatsApp, Slack). Seek feedback, don't sell.

chunks.heading: Growing from $0 to $1M with customer funding and no hires
chunks.text:
- Hot take: hire nobody before $1M ARR. Co-founders only: one builds, one does sales, marketing and success. Examples: Klaviyo's two co-founders hired no one until past $1M ARR (they IPO'd in 2023 at a $9B+ valuation per Adam); Jolie reached a $50M run rate with three employees.
- Recover customer acquisition cost (CAC) fast. Russell Brunson spent $3,000 on webinar traffic and sold six-month ClickFunnels subscriptions bundled with training, reaping about $50,000 upfront per week. Adam ran Facebook ads for Retention.com in 2020: poor long-term customers, but a $5,000/month whale every week or two paid back spend, and the awareness helped cold email and word of mouth.
- Run cheap experiments to find 2 to 3 channels for $1M to $10M, favoring zero or low upfront cash. Double down on the leader.
- Inbound-led outbound: drive traffic, identify visitors with RB2B, filter by ICP, then LinkedIn connect or warm email.
- Talk to every churned customer; require a conversation before cancelling, while making clear cancellation is easy. Adam would not offer an incentive.
- Give early adopters excellent support. If they have large relevant audiences, give them the product free.
- After $1M, hire 1 to 2 people (support, or a sales rep if demos eat your time). Goal: $10M ARR with no more than 10 employees.
- Seven founder mistakes:
  - Overspending on offices, VAs, interns, equipment or a CRM (his team used Google Sheets until $10M ARR).
  - Hiring before $1M.
  - Copying vendors but cheaper.
  - Being an "ideas guy" waiting for an operator.
  - Not doing unscalable things.
  - Not posting daily on organic social (it's to find your voice, not get reach at first).
  - Thinking it's a quick exit.

chunks.heading: Why bootstrap to $10M ARR with six people
chunks.text:
- Adam's thesis: bootstrapping to $10M ARR is the one goal, because afterward you can sell, hire a CEO, or keep paying yourself millions.
- Retention.com went 1 to $10M ARR in 27 months with six people; he says it hit about $12M ARR with six employees (about $2M revenue per employee).
- The mistake: in October 2022 he hired about 50 people in under 60 days, thinking he had a unicorn. Revenue per employee collapsed, the outsourced go-to-market playbook failed, the VP of Sales quit after about six months, 16 of 20 salespeople were let go, and he became "the most hated CEO on Glassdoor." His own conclusion: "Adding more people... does not speed you up."
- He disagrees with Jason Lemkin's benchmark of about 50 employees at $10M ARR; he says 10 max, ideally 6.
- Roger Bannister analogy: once someone proves it's possible, others follow. Let "$10M ARR with six people" be the four-minute mile.
- Founder time: in a six-person team, the week is customers, selling, prioritizing with the CTO, demand creation and some support, all spent improving product and go-to-market (he and Diana went home at 5 p.m. and skipped weekends). At 25 people, a founder loses about 60% of the week to internal meetings, interviews and investors.
- Metrics he tracks: ARR per employee, monthly growth rate, CAC payback (as low as possible, even immediate), churn, profitability.
- Why $10M bootstrapped beats VC:
  - Two co-founders can each clear $1M+ per year.
  - Sale at roughly 4 to 5x revenue ($40 to $50M) to many buyers.
  - Option to hire a CEO.
  - Option to keep working.
  - Option to raise later with more leverage and less dilution.
  - Option to reach $25M ARR with 25 people and pay yourself $10 to $15M a year.
- His case against VC: "imaginary wealth effect" valuations, go-to-market "help" that burns cash, and "VCs are not your friend." He argues growth is worth 3 to 10x profitability only if you reach an exit, so discount that multiple by 80 to 90%. His advice: talk to no investors until $10M ARR.

chunks.heading: Inbound-led outbound: replacing SDR-led pipeline
chunks.text:
- Outbound is "dead" because buyer demand for subscription software is cyclically low, more sellers chase the same prospects, and AI-volume outbound is countered by spam filters.
- At Retention.com, going from 1 to 5 SDRs still booked one meeting a week. His lesson: "These SDRs didn't create demand. They were only capturing demand created elsewhere."
- Four steps:
  1. Drive traffic through LinkedIn and social, podcasts, partnerships, events, SEO, or wherever buyers are.
  2. Identify website visitors at the person level with RB2B.
  3. Retarget first-time and repeat visitors by email, LinkedIn and phone.
  4. Focus sales (about 90% fewer resources) on bottom-of-funnel buyers.
- Claimed results: ultra-low CAC, 50% higher close rates, two-thirds shorter sales cycles, and more deals closed by 10 to 20% of reps.
- Key principle: scale unmeasurable original demand sources (podcast guest spots, events, organic social posts, others posting about you) even though you can't attribute them. Don't scale only what you can measure, as he did with BDRs.
- Demand-creation tactics: organic LinkedIn posting/connecting/commenting; thought-leader ads behind best posts; matchmaker.fm podcast spots; incentivized UGC; influencer campaigns coming to B2B; newsletters and joint-venture webinars; weekly live events (he reports 600 to 1,000 signups and 200 to 350 attendees, with 66% repeat visitors); partnerships; and a LinkedIn Live event titled with the buyer's pain with $10/day ads, then Phantom Buster to pull attendee contacts.
- Pick 2 to 3 channels and go all-in.

chunks.heading: Getting unstuck between $1M and $10M ARR
chunks.text:
- Stuck means a PMF problem. Fix: stay or become very lean, iterate fast, and stay close to customers. Don't raise money to get unstuck. If you're already too big, cut the team to the necessary functions.
- Strategy 1, go all-in on your lowest-churn segment: segment customers by persona, find the lowest-churn group, define it as the new ICP, and stop giving demos to anyone else. Turn down off-ICP revenue and product requests. This "took retention.com from 12 million to 23 million ARR"; the segment was Shopify Plus stores.
- Strategy 2, solve broad churn (when top-of-funnel and close rates are fine but churn is bad):
  - Talk to every churned customer personally. Alina Vanderberg (Chili Piper) emails each: "I would really, really, really love to know what you hate about our product and why you churned."
  - Questions: why did you churn, how did you use it, did you replace it or just stop, would cheaper keep you, which features would keep you, how often did you use it.
  - Explore adjacent features. Clearbit told him a three-feature customer churned 75% less than a one-feature customer.
  - Move upmarket to larger deals, which churn less.
- Strategy 3, run bold, low-long-term-cost experiments on pricing, features or new segments (e.g. the rebrand to Retention.com and adding features for Shopify Plus that upmarket vendors already had).

chunks.heading: Hiring principles for a team under 10
chunks.text:
- Co-founder split: the business co-founder owns product plus sales or marketing until $10M; the technical co-founder builds and talks to customers. If you lack a technical co-founder, hire one engineer.
- Principles:
  1. Hire people, not teams. A management layer cuts velocity by up to 75%.
  2. Hire experienced individual contributors (5+ years) in areas to offload. Look overseas (Eastern Europe, Brazil, Colombia, Argentina; Canada is about 30% cheaper). Wellfound is a source.
  3. Hire with LinkedIn job ads, not expensive recruiters. Post about hiring in organic content and put a hiring link in the email footer.
  4. Use contractors and agencies for non-core work.
  5. "Hire unreasonably slow, fire unreasonably fast." Hire only when it hurts; fire once you're sure. Be definitive, take the blame for the mishire, be kind, and try to find them another role.
- Support: hire a support or success rep to answer tickets and improve self-serve docs. A salesperson with a sales assistant for admin and follow-up is more productive.
- Retention.com's $12M ARR org: Adam, Diana Ross (sales) with a sales assistant, Clint (onboarding), Tate (built everything), and Anne (support and product direction input).

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Adam walks through reaching $1M ARR with Robly (17 months), Retention.com (27 weeks) and RB2B (16 weeks). Each used a distribution channel with little competition, and RB2B was built audience-first via founder-led LinkedIn content. He is candid about the failures, high churn and layoffs behind the wins.

chunks.heading: Bootstrapping three SaaS companies to $1M ARR
chunks.text:
Adam co-founded Robly (email marketing) and Retention.com (originally Get Emails), then started RB2B. He got to $1M ARR faster each time: about 17 months, then 27 weeks, then 16 weeks.

- **Robly:** launched Jan 1, 2014. It stalled at a mid single-digit ARR and then shrank. He sold it to private equity in 2021 for an eight-figure exit, and the founders owned 100% (no outside funding).
- **Retention.com:** founded Nov 2019. It is at $21.8M ARR and targets e-commerce brands.
- **RB2B:** started March 2024, aimed at SaaS companies with sales teams. It went from $1M to $2M ARR in six weeks.
- **Starting capital:** he says you need some money to start, even if tiny (about $50-100K). It can come from a day job, an agency, info products, or friends and family. He had saved from 10 years as a trader at Lehman Brothers and lived frugally.

chunks.heading: Robly: a channel with no competition makes customers cheap
chunks.text:
- **Core belief:** "What makes acquiring customers expensive is competition." If you have a channel nobody else works and a good offer, acquisition is cheap.
- **The list:**
  - Adam's team crawled websites for Constant Contact signup widgets. That was a list of paying customers.
  - About 250,000 domains were enriched into phone numbers by a team in Pakistan.
  - A call center then pitched "50% more opens for half the price", and about 5,000 customers switched.
  - Nobody else was calling this list, so human sales worked on $15-50 a month subscriptions.
- **Onboarding:** the magic moment was a customer hitting send on their first campaign. Customers who did stuck 100% of the time, but busy small-business owners wouldn't get there alone. The team first hand-built templates for each customer, then ran one-to-many onboarding calls. Those had a better show rate, and a $25 incentive got people to show up.
- **Why it stalled:** once the list was burned through, the product wasn't competitive. Mailchimp had a better product and a free tier, and Robly wasn't cheaper.
- **Layoffs:** a second Constant Contact-style list failed when nobody picked up. He had scaled sales around it and had to cut from 38 to 6 people.
- **Hindsight:** "I wouldn't start it." Email marketing is a brutal space, and he copied UI as a first-time founder.
- **Why it still mattered:** its cash flow funded the experiments that led to everything after.

chunks.heading: Retention.com: fast payback ads, then cold email to a better customer
chunks.text:
- **Origin:**
  - He spent about a year and a half learning how to identify anonymous website visitors by email.
  - It started as a feature inside Robly. Users kept downloading the file and putting it in the email app.
  - He spun it out as Get Emails.
- **Before it:**
  - A Constant Contact "authorized local expert" reseller model failed. He wasted money and got sued over a non-compete.
  - A build aimed just above Mailchimp's buyer failed because he built before selling. About ten others were already doing it.
  - He then spent two years and hundreds of thousands of dollars on things that didn't work before landing on Get Emails.
- **Selling first:** he asked people at a conference, "What if I could get you the email address of people on your website who don't fill out a form?" Every one of them wanted it.
- **Facebook ads:**
  - He and his wife made weekly one-minute videos that were inflammatory about privacy and also answered sales questions. The goal was to have people anticipate the next ad.
  - Targeting was by interest (Shopify, entrepreneur, Ezra Firestone, Klaviyo, Mailchimp).
  - Ads paid back fast. A self-serve $5,000 a month plan sold about once every two weeks and covered the prior ads.
  - He kept pouring money back in. After eight weeks with no big customer, he had spent about $100K.
  - The customers were poor: high-churn wannabes, around 15% monthly churn.
- **The pivot:** he stopped ads and built features for high-value users. His co-founder Diana prospected Shopify and Klaviyo lists by cold email. MRR went from about $200K to $600K over the next year.
- **Cold email:** it worked in 2020-2021 with five people in the Philippines, half the day on list building and half sending manually from Gmail inboxes. He says it would not work the same way today.
- **Churn:** he calls it a high-churn category with a high-churn buyer. He says you are always trying to outpace churn. The next step is larger deals with omnichannel retailers, because the Shopify audience has topped out.
- **Market shift:** he says the addressable market went from about 50,000 stores to about 1,400, with more competitors. A third layoff was planned. In his words, no founder has regretted making that move.
- **Mindset:** after hitting $3M ARR twice and stalling, he wondered if he was "just a 3 million ARR guy."

chunks.heading: Building a LinkedIn audience from zero
chunks.text:
- **Starting point:** zero followers in Sept 2022; over 92,000 at this interview.
- **Year one:**
  - He posted daily video and general business thoughts to sell Retention.com to Shopify owners. It didn't work.
  - He kept going because he believed deeply in social media's power. He cites the Kardashians as an example.
- **Work in public:**
  - His angle was sharing financials and failures.
  - When his 2023 sales scale-up failed and he cut the team by about 75%, that post exploded.
- **The pivot:** around Labor Day 2023, his LinkedIn consultant Alec told him B2B content would "absolutely crush." He wrote hot takes aimed at SaaS revenue leaders, including that BDR teams don't work anymore.
  - A typical post got 30-50 likes. The first of these got 3,300 likes in 24 hours.
  - He then dropped three more. They got about 2M impressions and his follower slope changed for good.
- **What those posts had:**
  - He talked about his own failures to peers.
  - He said what leaders only say to their spouse.
  - It was "my first feel of what a hot take was."
- **His rules:**
  - Be as transparent and human as possible.
  - Talk about how go-to-market is changing and how to build SaaS in 2024.
  - Be "a dealer of hope" and show you can bootstrap to $10M ARR.
  - Don't be boring or neutral.
- **Lesson:** he says he is in the "edutainment business" with a SaaS at the end of the funnel. If you do organic content well and large competitors can't, you have about 100x more efficient awareness generation.
- **Thought leadership ads:** boost a post that already crushed organically. Clicks are cheap because LinkedIn already rewarded the post.
- **Haters:** LinkedIn is politer than other platforms. The hardest hate came from outbound agencies when he said "outbound's dead." The Facebook-ad era, where he insulted commenters from the brand account, was bad for his mental state.
- **Book:** he recommends Russell Brunson's *Expert Secrets* for why organic social works.

chunks.heading: RB2B: audience first, then a free product
chunks.text:
- **What it does:** a script on your site matches anonymous visitors to LinkedIn profiles and pushes them into Slack with a business email, free.
- **Pricing:**
  - Up to 200 leads is free, and 85% of signups stay on it.
  - Paid is $99 a month, or about $750 a month for a mid-market SaaS.
  - The idea was "take pricing off the table." It is zero-touch PLG.
- **How he got there:**
  - He deliberately chose the opposite of cold email, which he sees getting worse.
  - It is founder-led content plus a free, punchy value proposition. He did about 10 podcast spots a week.
  - He thinks enterprise software growth may now depend on this kind of distribution.
- **Launch prep:**
  - He and COO Santosh held about 300 discovery calls between October and March 1.
  - Thousands of people were on a waiting list.
  - Beta testers gave feedback on a rough version.
  - The audience was warmed up for about six months beforehand.
- **Order of operations:** audience first, product second. He names Greg Isenberg as an example of building this way. He compares it to DTC brands that start with influencers and then distribute product to the audience.
- **Free users:** he says free users may be more important than paid ones. He criticizes a competitor for dismissing them.

chunks.heading: Principles and quotes
chunks.text:
- **Sell before you build:** he now advocates validating with buyers first, because he failed by building without it.
- **Channel fit:** "product and distribution and what is available at the time determines what grows."
- **Product-market fit:** businesses can go in and out of it. A company's size can be set for a market that no longer exists.
- **Layoffs:** he used the EOS framework to focus people on what moves the needle. He found he could do the same with half the team.
- **Best advice received:** "Do not take institutional capital."
- **Trait of successful founders:** focus.
- **Productivity:** a checklist.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Adam Robinson breaks down his LinkedIn playbook: define a clear, consistent character, take polarizing and vulnerable positions, optimize your profile, write hook-driven posts, run patient connect campaigns, and build community through comments. He credits it with 140k followers in 2 years and RB2B reaching $4M ARR from LinkedIn alone.

chunks.heading: Building a LinkedIn personal brand: the story and the prolific zone
chunks.text:
Adam says a personal brand on LinkedIn is "the fastest, most efficient, and highest leverage way to grow a startup that has ever existed." He went from 0 to 140,000 followers in 2 years. Over 18 months he grew RB2B from 0 to $6M ARR with no funding, and reached $4M ARR using LinkedIn alone.

**Your story is a character you create in your market's mind. It rests on three C's:**
- **Clear:** be unambiguous about who you are. The market knows him as "a bootstrapped SaaS founder who builds in public with radical transparency."
- **Consistent:** he does not talk about his personal life or hobbies, only that one identity.
- **Constantly reinforced:** repeated brand impressions across more channels build trust, and trust leads to purchases.

**Find your prolific zone:**
- Mainstream takes are noise because everyone is already saying them.
- Take positions far enough out that, say, 80% of one side loves you and 20% of the other side hates you. Too far out and you are treated as a lunatic.
- Polarizing takes inside that zone are what cut through.

chunks.heading: Vulnerability as an unfair advantage on LinkedIn
chunks.text:
- Big companies have to talk like big companies, and small players are afraid to share their biggest mistakes. LinkedIn is a professional network where people try to impress, so almost nobody admits real work problems. Doing so puts you in the under-1% of creators.
- Example: Adam posted about a layoff. His executive team told him not to and begged him to soften it. They wanted him to cut the parts saying the company had fallen out of product-market fit and had been unable to fix its churn problem for the prior 18 months. He refused.
- His reasoning: the brutal honesty is why his content resonates, and employees understanding the real situation leads to better long-term decisions.
- He calls this an extreme example. With investors or a co-founder you probably can't write this way.
- Rule of thumb: "If you can say things on LinkedIn that you might only say to your spouse behind closed doors, it will do better than anything any larger company could ever post."
- Tip from Devon Reed: people behave on LinkedIn like they behave at work, so being a bit inappropriate stands out.

chunks.heading: Optimizing your LinkedIn profile to convert
chunks.text:
Adam's profile alone drives hundreds of inbound RB2B leads every month. Each change is small but the cumulative effect is large.

- **Headshot:** professional, looking straight at the camera, solid background, smiling.
- **Banner:** branded, with a clear value proposition, an offer and a call to action. Canva's free version works.
- **Headline:** clearly states what you do and who you help, maximizing professional credibility.
- **Link:** in the top section, via a link or custom button to your website. A page built to convert cold traffic into a front-end offer is better.
- **About section:** very detailed. Be clear about who you help and how. Cite specific accomplishments with numbers. Put maximum credibility in the first line, above the fold. Don't be vague or talk about who you aspire to be.
- **Featured section:** direct-response calls to action (website, newsletter, podcast). Don't feature your best-performing post. Send people somewhere that moves them closer to converting.
- **Roles, education, recommendations:** detail every role, including adviser and investor roles. List education, degrees and certifications, which still matter for entrepreneurs. Get 3-4 recommendations, using swaps if necessary.
- **Warm leads:** with LinkedIn Premium you can see who viewed your profile. Opening conversations with them is much easier than with cold contacts.

chunks.heading: Finding post ideas
chunks.text:
Mindset: write for your audience, not the algorithm. The algorithm is designed to serve the audience, and the only answer to any change is better content. The best posts answer questions people have about your niche.

His process, using cold email as the example:
1. Study the top creators in the niche. Spend several hours finding their best posts of the last 90 days, bookmark the ones with far more likes than usual, and log their topics in a spreadsheet.
2. Pick topics where you can offer a prolific, polarizing take. Never copy their ideas; write your own version.
3. Ask Gemini (powered by Google and YouTube search): "What are the most common questions people have about cold emails?"
4. Search Reddit threads on the niche and read what people ask.
5. Between these sources you have enough ideas for your first 30 days.

chunks.heading: Writing posts: swipe file, hook, template and close
chunks.text:
**Swipe file:** spend 2 hours straight on the best LinkedIn posts from influencers in your space. Look at anything with over 1,000 likes and apply your own facts to the template. Save favorite hooks, templates, closers and calls to action in one place.

**Hook:**
- The hook is everything before the "see more" button, and it is the most important part of the post. Its only goal is to get the click.
- Write as if no one has heard of you, and build maximum credibility with something bold enough to keep people reading.
- He uses numbers heavily because "LinkedIn loves numbers."
- Examples he uses: "I spoke to 20 CEOs over the past 30 days" (brokering information reads as credible) and "I bootstrapped 20 million ARR in 3.5 years."

**Template:**
- His common format is a list of bullet points with about two sentences of explanation under each. Sometimes he uses sub-bullets or numbered lists.
- Lean on templates until you master posting. Put your story on top of a template that works for others.
- Every time: (1) agitate a specific pain point, (2) offer a solution, (3) tie it together with a strong takeaway. This is a mini hero's journey in one post.

**Close:**
- End with something clever and cozy that gives a "dopamine hit" after the pain and the solution.
- Tip: write the post, paste it into Claude, and ask it for five cozy closes that give the reader a dopamine hit. Pick the one that fits your tone.
- His example close: "Here's a few lessons for my fellow bootstrappers… Keep building."
- Never close with "let's continue the conversation in the comments" or a generic question.
- Experiment, but stick with one approach for a while to build consistency before mixing things up.

chunks.heading: Connect campaigns and the 60-day rule
chunks.text:
1. **Build a prospect list** of 100 to 250 of your best prospects.
2. **Connect** starting at 10-20 per day, with no message. Accept rates are very high and rise as you grow your audience. You can work up to 50 per day, but automation technically violates LinkedIn's terms and risks a ban.
3. **RB2B tie-in:** installing RB2B on your website sends the LinkedIn profiles of visitors to Slack so you can connect with them. He calls these practically the warmest leads you'll have.
4. **Wait before messaging.** After a connection is accepted, they start seeing your content. He waits about 60 days before messaging. By then they think you're a celebrity, and he reports an 80% reply rate. He says this makes LinkedIn "the most effective conversation opening vehicle in the entire world."
5. **Be patient.** People who wait 48 hours or 5 days still count as impatient. Don't pitch right after a connection. The wait builds a parasocial relationship and trust.

**Inbound once you've grown:**
- Accept only ideal-customer-profile requests, and decline people trying to sell to you, so your audience concentrates in your ICP.
- After accepting, message: "Hey, first name, what caught your attention?" then follow up with "How are things going at [company]?"

**Consistency example:** his friend Megan Bowen has manually connected with 20 ICP people a day for four years, reaching virtually all her prospects (thousands). Combined with strong content driving inbound requests, she has over 36,000 followers and a trust machine producing leads, partnerships and investment opportunities for her agency.

chunks.heading: Building community through comments
chunks.text:
- The ideas you post about become the shared values that bring people together in your comments. This works on any platform, and you can later move the community elsewhere.
- Adam answers every comment on his posts, typically 100 or more per post. At live events he meets many people he already knows online.
- **Pricing example:** RB2B had 3,000 free signups and only 13 paying customers. He posted about the problem non-stop and commenters helped him fix the pricing. The result was a 12.5% touchless free-to-paid conversion rate, and growth from $0 to $6M ARR in 18 months with just three people.
- **When you're starting out:**
  - List influential people in your space and comment on their posts for 15 minutes a day.
  - Don't use AI to write comments that regurgitate the post and end with a question. He hates it and so will they.
  - Thoughtful, consistent comments get you remembered by the creator and attract their audience.
  - Spend as much or more time commenting each week as you spend writing.
- Also connect with 10-20 ICP people every day, no matter what.

chunks.heading: Adding video to LinkedIn posts
chunks.text:
- Video isn't required to start, but LinkedIn keeps pushing video and it may become necessary. Getting people to watch and listen to you say something intelligent raises your status in their minds.
- His process:
  1. Write the post first, which gets the topic in his head.
  2. Record a free-flowing monologue, looking at the post's bullet points and elaborating on whichever are most interesting.
  3. The video and post end up slightly different, which he considers a net positive.
- He recommends holding off on video until you've found your voice and get strong engagement on text posts, because video adds a lot of extra work.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Adam Robinson explains why founder-brand content on LinkedIn replaced outbound for RB2B. He covers the sales motion around it, how to write hooks, handling backlash, using paid thought-leadership ads, and why AI should not write your posts.

chunks.heading: Why Adam says founder-led LinkedIn content is no longer optional
chunks.text:
- He argues outbound as it was a few years ago is dying: response rates are collapsing, spam filters keep tightening, and personalization only works if a human actually reads the message.
- Predictable-revenue style sales (target lists, Lakers-game dinners) will still exist, but it is not efficient. It is not what the last decade's startups grew on.
- His stance: "I don't think it's an option anymore." You either build a founder brand around yourself (his preferred route) or harness organic social the way Clay does, by aligning incentives with a tight group of users who post about the product.
- People are on social media to connect with people, not companies. You can build affinity around a person in about 1/100th of the time and money it takes to build it around a brand (his example: what Drift spent in 2017 to make a word and a robot matter).
- He would pick "the ability to be great at creating organic social content over any other marketing strategy by far," and for B2B that means LinkedIn.
- He expects products to change to fit the distribution available: founder-led, free, a point solution you can understand in one second, which spreads on its own as outreach gets harder.

chunks.heading: How he sells to mid-market and enterprise with it, and how long it takes
chunks.text:
- His motion, learned from Alec Paul (who runs this for his clients' CEOs):
  1. Early on: outbound connection campaign to your ICP, they accept, you post great content, wait about 60 days, then ask for a demo. He claims about 80% conversion on those demos because prospects see you as a celebrity.
  2. Once big enough: inbound connection requests, accept ICP visitors, ask what caught their attention, post for 60 days, go in for a demo.
- Connecting with about 10 ICP people a day for a year to a year and a half gets you connected to most of the people you want. You do not need 100,000 followers; a slow, steady inbound flow compounds.
- Timing: it took him about a year. The click came around Labor Day 2023, when he understood hot takes, sharing weakness, and naming things people fear to say (for example, "it's okay to admit that outbound is dead, it's not your fault").
- Niche fit: he says two non-martech CEOs on a Dave Gerhardt panel (a parental-leave SaaS and Bridge, an online/offline data company) got about 80% of lead flow from founder-brand LinkedIn content. He concedes it likely works better today for sales/marketing tech, but more industries are arriving on the platform.
- Even if it does not book demos at first, he says committing to posting until you find your voice "will open up doors," because you are building a character people care about, not hitting content pillars nobody cares about.
- Why VC-backed companies struggle: it is not repeatable on a timeline, so investors would say hire a VP of Sales instead. He sees that as the opportunity for bootstrapped founders willing to commit.
- Founders need founder-market fit.

chunks.heading: Building the audience: connections, followers, and the early stage
chunks.text:
- Follower-boosting tricks (e.g. "comment interested and I'll send the top 15,000 ads"): helpful early because follower count signals credibility, less important later when you care about who the ICP is.
- Over time, prune off-ICP connections (for example engineers if you now sell to sales), but not at the very start. Better: run an outbound connection campaign to the ICP and trim the lowest-quality connections as people accept.
- He used LinkedHelper for outbound connection campaigns once; now Alec Paul and Kyle Williams handle triage of inbound, and they no longer run outbound.
- Engagement pods: he used one at the start (he had under 1,000 followers in September 2022) and thinks it helped a bit, but the durable answer is "write a great hook, write a great body, write a great close, and drop it."
- First fans: connect with and comment on influencers in your space, 10 connections a day, write thoughtful comments, and answer every comment on your own posts. He dislikes AI-generated comments that just summarize his post and ask a question.
- "The best time to plant a tree was 20 years ago, the second best time is today."

chunks.heading: Format and cadence choices
chunks.text:
- Format: he is a video guy. It has less reach but a deeper connection.
- Cadence: once a day, five days a week is right when starting. He had dropped to three a week and is trying to post more to lift organic impressions. He notes Andy Mowat posts twice a day, but Adam still favors quality over quantity.
- Timing: Alec posts his content around 3-4 pm Eastern, weekday or weekend; Adam does not challenge it.
- Channel choice: if he had to pick one channel for life it would be LinkedIn for B2B, because it builds an audience and community around him. Email can't create that kind of connection.
- UGC (the Clay model) is one layer more complex than founder content because you are wrangling people you do not control, and it only works if the product fits their workflow. He says it works for RB2B for similar reasons.
- Repurposing one idea into text, image and carousel versions can work, but he thinks the real driver is consistently reinforcing one identity in the market. He points to Chris Walker, who has talked about attribution for five years in ways that never read as repetitive.
- Switching audiences means starting over. He cites Devin Reed moving from writing for sales to writing for marketing.

chunks.heading: How he writes hooks and chooses what to say
chunks.text:
- His best-performing generic business posts (10,000+ likes, for example on not micromanaging employees) did nothing for RB2B. He compares followers earned that way to "being rich with Monopoly money." He chose niche value over reach, citing Sam Jacobs's feel as what he wanted his brand to be.
- Hooks are the most important part. In his weekly 45-minute Monday idea session with Alec, they discuss post ideas and hooks first; ideas with weak hooks do not get written.
- Hook rules he gives:
  - Treat the reader as if they have never heard of you and build as much credibility as possible in the hook (for example "I bootstrapped...").
  - Cite conversations with important people, even anonymous ones ("I spoke to a CTO who has to cut his dev staff by 80%..."). Anonymous can feel more mysterious than naming someone, unless they are famous.
  - Voice what people say privately but are afraid to say publicly.
  - Stack numbers (time period, dollar amount, customer count, days) in one hook.
  - Be definitive: "the golden era of SaaS is over," or "99% of startups think they should focus on reducing churn, they're wrong."
  - He reads Chris Walker's posts before writing his own, such as "X in 60 seconds" style hooks.
- Weekly planning covers: what worked or didn't last week, conversations he's had, work-in-public updates, and which of his three audiences (marketers, sales, founders) he has not hit lately.
- Polarizing views work only if you actually believe them. He holds that falling response rates mean software floors rise (for example from 25k to 50k ACV and beyond), so outbound-heavy models break. He says LinkedIn comments are mostly respectful, so backlash is manageable.

chunks.heading: Work in public and AI
chunks.text:
- Until RB2B, his work-in-public was about one monthly update; the rest was market takes and conversations. A report he was shown said founders care about work-in-public, while sales and marketing audiences prefer predictable-revenue style content.
- He writes about milestones the day they happen: the idea, the launch, $1M ARR at 16 weeks, and $2M. He calls it "good journalism." Typical work-in-public posts do worse than a strong bootstrap vs VC or "predictable revenue is dead" post.
- He is adding SEO, a UGC motion, ads, and a Russell Brunson-style one-to-many "how to bootstrap to $10M, plus RB2B" motion, which gives him more to write about.
- On AI: he writes all his own posts. "Art is interesting because of the perspective of the artist," and ChatGPT has no perspective. He wants typos, emotion, and original experience, and thinks AI is better for repetitive mechanical jobs like customer support.

chunks.heading: LinkedIn thought leadership ads: spend logic and numbers
chunks.text:
- Approach: post organically, see what crushes, then put money only behind posts the platform already likes. He suspects better ad fit lowers bid costs.
- Test: spent $10,000 in the first month.
- Numbers he gave: click-through to free signup costs about $70, with a 10% conversion rate, so roughly $700 per paying customer. Average subscription is $275 and conservative LTV is about $2,700 (customers stay about 10 months). He notes this metric is the worst one, since the program isn't optimized for it.
- He argues the ads also boost brand impressions and trust beyond signups, amplifying a program already working.
- Plan: double spend each month until the signup cost metric "shits the bed" (he'd back off if it rose to around $150 per signup) rather than fixating on a signup target. LinkedIn ad contacts told him $10K is low.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Adam Robinson explains why he treats his company as an "edutainment" media brand with software at the bottom of the funnel. He covers writing for people with his own pain, saying the uncomfortable truth, building a warm audience above sales, using LinkedIn comments for networking, and bootstrapping to $10MM ARR.

chunks.heading: RB2B's growth model: one-to-many "edutainment" instead of a sales team
chunks.text:
- Adam says he sells through a one-to-many awareness engine: 80% of his time goes to LinkedIn posting (about four days a week) plus roughly 10 podcast guest slots a week.
- He says he'll do any show that isn't a first episode, because it is "the most effective awareness you could get today."
- He calls this the future of B2B selling: "very long sort of like influencer, thought leadership that just slowly brings people down the funnel" and builds an audience you can do a lot with.
- RB2B went from $1MM to $2MM ARR in six weeks. He says it is the first time that has happened to him.
- He believes CEOs are about 10 years away from accepting this is how they should spend their time. His line: "business is doing what no one else is doing."
- He says there is "a tremendous arbitrage" in organic social, because it delivers an unbelievable amount of one-to-many selling.
- Organic social is already proven in direct-to-consumer (he cites the Kardashians) but hasn't reached software yet. B2B has less margin, so it has to be more efficient.
- His view of the platforms: they are built for people to absorb entertainment, so you are a media brand and must choose which one.
- He cannot measure his own performance in this job and says the individual pieces are not measurable. He spends on expensive consultants and a docu series without knowing what the series does, and treats it as the way the future plays out.

chunks.heading: How Adam found his voice: pivoting content from Shopify owners to SaaS founders
chunks.text:
- His first company stalled at $3MM ARR. Retention.com started as a feature of it, because people used the feature and ignored the rest of the email platform.
- Retention.com bootstrapped to roughly $22MM ARR with six people, but with high churn.
- After narrowing to one ideal customer profile, he treated low penetration as an awareness problem. He chose a personal LinkedIn profile as the cheapest route to awareness, even though it overlapped imperfectly with Shopify store owners. LinkedIn had a better competitive dynamic for a content creator than Twitter, which he called harder.
- After nine months the content stopped winning e-commerce deals.
- Over Labor Day weekend (2023) he switched to writing for people like himself: SaaS founders feeling the outbound pain everyone had that year.
- His typical post got about 50 likes. The BDR posts, about getting rid of BDRs, VP Sales quitting and saying what nobody would say in public, got about 3,000 likes each.
- He then built a product (RB2B) for revenue teams, since the audience mechanism was so strong.
- Lesson he draws: write to people who are basically you and feel your pain at the same time you do.

chunks.heading: Content strategy: edutainment, vulnerability and saying what others won't
chunks.text:
- He says he is in the "edutainment business" and happens to sell SaaS at the bottom of the funnel. He competes with rivals on edutainment, not features.
- Competitors copy "working in public" and fail. He says they tell stories poorly and aren't as credible as someone who bootstrapped to $22MM ARR in four years, then launched a new company and put a live metrics dashboard in public.
- Great content, in his view, is saying what people feel but won't admit to themselves.
- He posts about laying off 40% of the staff of one business. His chief of staff said it would make the managers' jobs impossible. His position is that it's an opportunity: with no product-market fit, "you have to get as small as possible and find a new one."
- He argues the team should know the true market characteristics (low deal sizes), so they stop asking for features and spend appropriately.
- He expects pushback on this from clients' CEOs and says almost none will do it.
- Being honest about errors builds a tribe, and he says people will love you more when things work again.
- He says it is hard to teach: you will be "bruised and beaten for a very long time," and it feels irrational to commit that time.
- Most people quit after seven engagements per post. He compares finding content-market fit to finding product-market fit; it takes a long time.

chunks.heading: Product as marketing: freemium and the "perception of free"
chunks.text:
- He says every big product is both a killer product and killer marketing.
- Last year's outbound pain led him to ask: "what if response rates were zero, how would you sell software?"
- His answer was an influencer edutainment channel, plus a big freemium offer so getting started has zero friction.
- The aim is to create a market perception that the product is free, so it distributes on its own and doesn't need to be sold.
- Admitted weaknesses: it is a point solution in a high-churn category with a high-churn buyer persona. He says it could top out around $15MM ARR but would be very lean.
- RB2B has a PLG motion, so the website captures demand and no people are needed for that.

chunks.heading: Why Adam thinks the sales-team model is breaking
chunks.text:
- He contrasts the venture model (hire a bunch of people, build features, charge more, churn) with a lean alternative he thinks works now.
- He argues "the VC way has become a whole lot less effective." Exits are low probability and founders end up as "underpaid salaried" workers.
- Many SaaS companies have fallen out of product-market fit. They can't switch to efficiency mode because their valuations require growth.
- On outbound: scaling reps and messages without scaling "the warming machine above it" fails. He cites a Rippling BDR leader (125 BDRs) who agrees with that view.
- His example: one outbound rep booking five demos a week doesn't mean five reps book 25. The rep is only capturing the warmth that content created above.
- He says you can't hire your way into this: "it's impossible to give a bad business good advice." If people don't want the product, no lead source fixes it.
- His mission is to evangelize bootstrapping. His plan: run profitable businesses, aim at $2-3MM ARR first, then aim a little higher with the next one, and hold on to roughly $10MM ARR. He compares it to the four-minute mile.

chunks.heading: Using RB2B for lead generation: his advice to customers
chunks.text:
- He says you first need to be able to list your ideal customers, and have a sales motion that converts qualified leads. Otherwise that is the problem, not lead volume.
- Treat your go-to-market as a "tumbler" (a term he credits to someone else): email, LinkedIn connects and DMs, ads, content, thought leadership. You can't measure each piece alone, but the whole works.
- His instruction: filter identified visitors to your ICP, throw away the rest, and drop them into the existing cadences.
- Enrich to a phone number and call them if you still use phones; he calls them "super high intent."
- Expect higher response rates and better funnel conversion than from an Apollo-style list.
- He prefers not to mention you saw them on the website. He says there's no need to tell them, and that it sidesteps the "creep factor."
- Run channels together as fast as possible after intent: a message a day across two channels, two to five touches.
- GDPR question: he says the tool is US only, so no GDPR governance applies.
- Roadmap (from Oct 2023 to March 2024 discovery with demand-gen marketers): a traffic-insights product by ICP, department, industry, company size and UTM. It would show which campaigns and SEO drive ICP traffic, which Google Analytics can't. He hoped to ship by the end of the next quarter.
- Agencies are a big channel, and churn drops when customers actually use the product, which agencies help with. An agency page was being redone.

chunks.heading: Using LinkedIn for networking and comments
chunks.text:
- He says LinkedIn is the most powerful networking tool in the world. His account has about 100,000 followers, but he says people with far smaller, more targeted followings use the tool better than he does.
- For referral- or partnership-led businesses: connect with everyone you want as partners, then post good content so they feel they know you over time. Then reach out.
- Trust builds passively, even when posts get only about 10 likes. He says knowing people is "a secret to business."
- Sequencing: design the go-to-market after your content is already performing. Until then, use LinkedIn as a networking tool, and content makes networking work better.
- Comments: he answers almost all of the 50-100 comments on each post, and thanks people who mention RB2B.
- He comments heavily on posts mentioning RB2B because people borrow his reputation for reach, and he wants to train the algorithm to see that as good.
- When starting out, comment in other people's feeds; he says comments are how you enter their feeds. That is harder than replying to your own, since you must read the post and write something meaningful.
- Pick a few people you want to get close to and engage with all of their content. Block half an hour a day for it.
- He avoids AI-generated comments and says he can usually tell.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Adam Robinson explains how RB2B started as a pivot from LinkedIn content, how a crude Slack mockup proved demand, and how he built a founder brand by repeating a few ideas. He also covers the risk of depending on one channel and the churn ceiling that pushes him to widen the product.

chunks.heading: RB2B origin: from Retention.com feature to a B2B visitor-ID product
chunks.text:
- Adam's first startup, Robbley (a newsletter app), had a feature that became Retention.com. Nobody wanted Robbley, everybody wanted the feature, so he spun it out. Retention.com reached about $20M ARR five years later.
- RB2B began the same way. His B2B data partner Santosh argued there was no person-level website visitor identity for B2B. Adam first resisted ("focus, focus, focus").
- He was posting founder-brand content to promote Retention.com to Shopify stores. About 25% of it was SaaS content on his own journey, and that content drew a different audience with roughly 10x the engagement.
- He followed that signal and built the B2B product. RB2B hit about $6.7M ARR in under two years, bootstrapped, with 3 full-time staff (4 once a designer joins).
- His view of the "1,000 true fans" playbook (build the audience, then the product): it rarely happens that way. More often one thing works okay, and you stumble onto a better thing and go all in on it.
- Retention.com resolves visitors to a deliverable personal email (ecom). RB2B resolves to a LinkedIn profile plus B2B enrichment, so it has a separate site, go-to-market and brand.

chunks.heading: Validating with a crude product: the Slack feed was the unlock
chunks.text:
- His rule: ship something crude and see if people pay. If they won't use or pay for it, "you have the wrong product" and need to address a bigger pain.
- Version 1 was a daily spreadsheet of visitors' personal emails. Enthusiasm was about 2 out of 10.
- Version 2 was a spreadsheet of business emails. Slightly better, but a spreadsheet is a headache to read.
- Version 3: his CTO Tate built a fake Slack channel showing visitors with headshot and LinkedIn profile. Adam showed it on his phone to people. Enthusiasm jumped to about 11 out of 10, with reactions like "is that out yet? What's the URL?"
- The data was identical. The presentation changed. The headshot and LinkedIn URL made visitors feel like real people ("a line of data in a spreadsheet is kind of just like, well, you could be making that up").
- The Slack idea came partly from a conversation with Brendan Short, who wanted lead gen to feel like a dating app: people are fed to you and you say yes or no.
- Adam likes premium (free tier plus paid) models, modeled on how Mailchimp took on Constant Contact. The team considered keeping the in-app view free and charging for Slack.

chunks.heading: Why LinkedIn worked: leverage, timing and transparency
chunks.text:
- He had about 20,000 followers, then grew to 40,000 in 30 days and 80,000 in the next 90 days after posting about B2B visitor identity. That showed him he had unusual leverage: "if this is even an okay product, it should be a pretty good business." It proved true.
- Launch benefit: the audience gave him a big waitlist and a large amount of Zoom discovery calls. Reaction split into a privacy camp (it's wrong) and an aggressive-marketer camp (it's transformational).
- Why it broke through, in his view:
  - First mover on radical transparency while building in public at a growth-stage SaaS (over $20M ARR; almost no one else was doing it).
  - He shared unique numbers, including "we just laid off 40% of our staff."
  - He argued that putting a 20-year-old in front of Outreach.io to click through sequences no longer works.
  - Bootstrapped vs VC became a core pillar. VC suits outliers (his examples: Elon Musk sending people to Mars, OpenAI), but the YC/VC pipeline pulls in many businesses, by his estimate about 80%, that would have been better off bootstrapped.
- He says a year of obsessive effort preceded the breakout, and that "if you can't get very obsessive about things, you should probably find another job."
- He expects imitators to dilute it. The Gamma CEO now builds in public at about $100M ARR, which he welcomes.
- Because AI-written posts now copy his style, he is looking for a style that is the opposite of the noise.

chunks.heading: Content playbook borrowed from Chris Walker
chunks.text:
- Adam says he "completely ripped off his playbook." What he took from Walker:
  - Video: he believes the parasocial relationship from video goes beyond what engagement metrics show, and he used a lot of it.
  - A funnel from big LinkedIn post to "listen to the pod."
  - Strong, hard-held beliefs stated with authority.
- His key insight, from listening to Walker's podcast for hours on a 15.5-hour drive home from Aspen: Walker says the same four or five things over and over from different angles. You don't notice until you're deep in. "You say the same couple things over and over again in a thousand different ways on every single possible channel, and then you're the guy that is that."
- He built a spreadsheet of Walker's content: main point, sub-points, and enemies. Then he wrote his own version: his points, his enemies, mapped to his own positioning.
- His positioning is a bootstrapped founder who builds in public and is wildly transparent, a few other small themes rotate on and off. Anyone who reads him would say that, which was intentional.
- Post architecture: go through your own and others' real bangers (over 1,000 likes, not "comment X for Y" posts). Line them up and study the structure. Putting your story on a proven structure has far better odds than starting from scratch. LinkedIn "likes the bones of that post."
- Learning it is like learning French: it takes sustained commitment. Storytelling improves as you absorb great content and emulate it.
- Organic social is "the cheapest awareness you could ever get," because people come to you and sit through the content.

chunks.heading: Channel concentration risk: the LinkedIn shadowban
chunks.text:
- His account appears to have been shadowbanned since August 27 after an automation flag, though he says he doesn't use automation. A human was sending DMs for a "comment this for that" campaign. Reach has dropped by about 80%.
- Evidence it's the platform, not the content: his 2026 predictions post, which peers (his LinkedIn consultant Alec, Brendan Short, the SaaS Club chat) called his best in six months, got about 13,000 impressions, versus roughly 150,000 to 250,000 normally.
- Lesson he draws: he is "totally beholden to this machine" and needs other ways to market besides the founder brand. Heavy dependence on one channel is a risk.
- Diversification moves: YouTube, a live show, a Twitter/X specialist, LinkedIn ads, SEO and AI search (done with an agency). He weekly spends about one Tuesday on content: one YouTube video, one live show, three or four LinkedIn posts.
- He had always been bothered that only LinkedIn worked for him. YouTube videos got about 100 views against hundreds of thousands of LinkedIn impressions for similar content. He thinks each channel needs someone familiar with it to adapt content.

chunks.heading: Churn ceiling and the plan beyond RB2B
chunks.text:
- RB2B's buyer is a US-based marketer at a 5-20 person SaaS, but his founder brand reaches a wider set (very early-stage, international founders). A narrower paying audience caps the top of funnel.
- Churn problem: visitor ID doesn't magically book demos. Buyers who haven't done outbound before ask why it doesn't work. His answer is that they need to know what to say to whom and combine it with other signals. He sees this as roughly a 25% ceiling for the business as it is.
- Fix: widen the top of funnel and build more into the product so it gets stickier. He has talked to ex-founders of Clearbit and Leadfeeder: you can beg people not to cancel and win maybe 10%, but building other features makes it stickier.
- Idea he is exploring: a simple, premium all-in-one outbound platform (contact database plus visitor ID, e.g. RB2B plus a database) using other vendors' APIs, run with AI. Likely buyers are early-stage founders who wouldn't pay for RB2B alone.
- Market read: tools like Instantly and Smartlead are in a feature arms race with products far beyond what's needed for cold email. Flodesk reached about $30M ARR bootstrapped in four years in the newsletter space with a narrow, cheap, dead-simple product and inbound funnel.
- Growth logic: "if you're not growing you're dying." He expects to hit $10M just continuing as-is within about 18 months, then slide without expansion. He projects roughly a $29M run rate across RB2B and Retention.com by year end. He calls $10M ARR "FU money."
- He is not yet convinced of the final feature set. He wants to build with AI and test whether a year-long project can ship in a quarter.

chunks.heading: Reflections
chunks.text:
- He doesn't think much about doing things differently. Whatever he did at launch, the five competitors who later entered visitor ID would have positioned against RB2B anyway, so a different offer would have drawn a different response.
- He believes every lesson took the time it needed, and the AI support system he refined is now something he can copy to other products.
- He says the drive to keep growing is a net positive if it's driven by interest in the problems, not by a goalpost that never arrives. He is moving full-time to Aspen, Colorado, as an extreme version of the lifestyle-business idea.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Adam Robinson walks through Robly, retention.com and rB2B: validating go-to-market before building, why word of mouth makes every channel work, and why churn and buyer persona decide a SaaS. He also covers keeping teams lean, a layoff, and using a public founder brand as the main acquisition channel.

chunks.heading: Starting with a niche email tool, then finding a product-led wedge
chunks.text:
Adam's first startup was Robly, an email newsletter app he began around 2012 after leaving a credit-default-swap trading career. He wanted a small lifestyle business, inspired by Tim Ferriss and 37signals.

- **Go-to-market came before the product.** He scraped small business websites to find Constant Contact customers (flower shops, churches, 1-3 person businesses), then called them pretending to be Constant Contact to validate they were customers. He pitched "50% more opens for half the price" at about $50/month and got roughly 5,000 of their 300,000 customers to switch.
- **That channel was exclusive.** The product was uncompetitive everywhere else (MailChimp had freemium and a better product), but nobody else was calling Constant Contact's list. When the list ran out, growth stalled.
- **Robly hit about $3M ARR and stayed there for roughly three years.** It was profitable with about six people.
- **What he would change:** He wouldn't have started in the small-business email newsletter market, where "it's so hard to pay salaries on a $30 a month SaaS" and churn is highest. He would also have niched down much harder, as Nathan Barry did with ConvertKit by targeting food bloggers first.
- **He recommends "The Four Steps to the Epiphany."** Develop customers in parallel with the product. If people pay for something that doesn't exist yet and the TAM is big enough, "you will almost surely succeed to some extent."

chunks.heading: Spinning out a feature that outperformed the main product
chunks.text:
Adam's breakout came from a feature inside Robly, not from Robly itself.

- **The feature:** It identified anonymous website visitors and added them to email lists. He positioned it as "everyone's trying to grow their list. What if you could get emails of people that didn't fill out a form but hit your website."
- **The signal:** Customers downloaded the file into Klaviyo and gave it a 10 out of 10 NPS without using the rest of Robly. He realized Robly's ESP was too far behind to compete with Klaviyo.
- **The spin-out (Nov 2019):** He built a standalone product with basic integrations to three or four ESPs. He wrote a sales letter from the DigitalMarketer course and paid a freelancer on Upwork to make a 2.5-minute animated video. The first $5,000 of Facebook ads produced $10K MRR with a self-serve PLG flow. "If I spent $5,000 on Facebook for Robly I wouldn't have gotten $50 of MRR."
- **The wide price range:** Warby Parker signed in the first month at $20,000/month, while the plan started at $9. He says they didn't land a customer like that again for about four years.
- **Exit:** He sold Robly for about $10M (he recalls roughly 7x EBIT) to a customer that was rolling up small ESPs.

chunks.heading: Choosing ICP and why churn followed
chunks.text:
The product grew to about $25M ARR (the transcript has him giving "25 million" as the peak figure) as Adam narrowed to Shopify ecommerce brands.

- **Early stall:** It went 0 to $3M quickly, then sat at $3M for 9 months. At month 18 he wondered if he was "just a 3 million ARR guy." Diana started prospecting ecommerce more heavily at month 18, and the company went ecommerce-only at month 36 (roughly $8-9M ARR).
- **Why ecommerce worked:** Big Shopify stores told friends they loved it, rarely churned, and had lists large enough to layer in these emails.
- **Second product:** Abandoned-cart and abandoned-product flows for the shoppers Klaviyo can't reach because they aren't logged in.
- **Team size:** About 6 people at $10M ARR, with growth from cold email and inbound. He says "product actually enables go to market": outbound only converts if prospects are also hearing about you elsewhere.
- **What he got wrong:** He assumed churn would look like Klaviyo's. It didn't, and the categories differ:
  - Email is a system of record, and list growth outpaces cancellations.
  - Leads and intent data are high-churn: when results disappoint, the only thing that changes is losing the leads.
  - Because it's a pixel, builtwith.com shows every customer, so five competitors pitched "better and cheaper" within 18 months.
  - His $5,000/month unlimited plan for large brands, meant to expand later, ended in contraction when competitors offered $2,000.
- **Average customer life** is about 18-24 months, so the book has to be replaced every 18-24 months.
