- **Current strategy:** Move upmarket to mid-market and enterprise for stickier revenue, add cost-per-lead deals, and explore publishers. His stated 2025 goal is revenue quality over growth. He also says that getting multiple departments on the product reduced churn at Clearbit.

chunks.heading: Buying a premium domain and an affiliate-driven sales motion
chunks.text:
- **The domain:** He bought retention.com for $800,000 (a broker negotiated; the seller had held it about 29 years and had earlier backed out of a similar deal). He treats it as a "$300K tax" over what patient negotiation might have cost, justified by the $20K/month lease-equivalent math and having the cash. When he bought it the company had eight people.
- **Why it paid off:** The name signals a big business ("you just assume it's a big business"). He compares it to cart.com spending $5M on its domain. He cautions against buying a huge domain at the start because it can give false positive signals, and says a weaker name early forces the product to be great.
- **Affiliate motion:** He paid 20% of cash collected for introductions to ecommerce brands. Deals were roughly $30K at the time, closing around 80% of people who showed up in 7 days, and the sellers were young DTC operators motivated by about $5K per intro. Affiliates only work if the incentive is large enough that they "drop everything" for you, and the deal size and velocity must match who the connectors are. Billionaire VCs won't care about 20%.
- **Today:** Sales is largely in-person and enterprise-style, such as getting a Foot Locker CMO to a Taylor Swift box and then running a nine-month process.

chunks.heading: Layoffs and running lean
chunks.text:
- **Overbuilt for a unicorn that wasn't coming.** At the end of 2022 he assumed the company would reach $100M+ ARR, and he hired accordingly, including a COO (Santos), eight VPs in one day in Feb 2023, and a 20-person sales team.
- **Team size follows throughput.** He says headcount should track the number of deals you sell and service, not revenue. Deal volume fell to about a fifth of early 2023 levels even as revenue doubled.
- **The cut:** In 2024 he cut from about 50 to 30 people, mostly in go-to-market and customer success, keeping engineers. The business had about $8M annual free cash flow. His rule: "the smallest possible version of what you can be at that time."
- **Cuts mean less work, not more.** He told staff the remaining team should do less activity, only the activity that matters.
- **Customer success was oversized.** At $1,500/month, customers see the product as self-serve and want fast, thorough answers when something breaks, not quarterly business reviews. A main churn reason is something going wrong in implementation.
- **Outcome:** Profit rose after the layoff. He says profit is now about $1M/month and he owns a little under half the company. Revenue run rate is about $12M, and he targets about $30M across product lines with no added headcount.
- **EOS:** He adopted the Entrepreneurial Operating System with an executive coach for planning, focus and accountability, calling it "not the answer" but a useful shared framework.
- **Santos's value** was in the 10-to-100 stage; he transitioned out as processes matured.
- **His lean-company thesis:** Getting to $10M ARR with two co-founders and very productive individual contributors is "the promised land," since you can then raise, sell, or take distributions. The risk is accepting $8M of investor money at $4M ARR that you don't yet know how to spend. "If you don't take money you can only spend what you have."

chunks.heading: Building RB2B and its early go-to-market
chunks.text:
- **Origin:** His COO Santos pushed for person-level B2B identification. A half-hearted attempt in late 2022 failed.
- **The trigger (Sept 2023):** He posted about shrinking the sales team and why BDR headcount doesn't scale linearly. It drew about 3,000 likes in 24 hours. His point was that a BDR now mostly captures demand from other marketing rather than creating it, and that hiring 10 BDRs requires 10x'ing the surrounding marketing. A consultant (Alec Paul) told him a LinkedIn-led motion would "crush" for a B2B product. He decided to go all-in on B2B content.
- **Method:** He batch-wrote posts, found the ones that resonated, and kept writing. Offers at the bottom of posts led to calls with him and Santos for qualified people, with others placed on a waitlist, which generated lots of customer discovery before launch.
- **Result:** Launched in March 2024, reached $4M ARR in about 9 months, mostly from his and Santos's posts. Cold email was a supplement. Impressions were about 500K/week at peak and about 150K/week when recorded.
- **Content cost:** He did 9-10 podcasts a week plus 3-4 LinkedIn posts during launch and says he wouldn't repeat that. He now plans content a month ahead and holds a weekly one-hour idea call, with a goal of writing a month of posts in one day.

chunks.heading: RB2B churn and the shift from "leads" to signals
chunks.text:
- **The problem:** Churn hit 11-12% per month in Oct-Dec. Adam says his Clay-driven user-generated content (UGC) pushed an inaccurate use case, "LinkedIn profiles into Slack, put a human in front of a Slack channel," which fails for ordinary B2B companies with noisy traffic. Customers also get discouraged when the visitor list shows low ICP traffic.
- **New thesis:** A website visitor is "not a lead, it is a signal." He contrasts a signal-led use (feeding a lead score, for sophisticated PLG teams) with a TAM-first use: filter signal through the company's target accounts.
- **Implementation:** Send signal into HubSpot or Salesforce. If the visitor is a named account, alert the rep or start a sequence, and ignore the rest. He wants every rep to get "a win a day," meaning an insight, not necessarily a booked demo. This cut churn by about two-thirds while sign-ups slowed.
- **Roadmap:** Salesforce integration, reverse-IP company-level lookup (to replace tools like 6sense or Clearbit), and later extra signals such as job changes. He doubts customers want another outbound "platform."
- **Also:** He stopped cold email and ads for now and is monetizing his founder community with courses and help, around $1,000-2,000, focused on customer discovery and clear messaging.

chunks.heading: Building in public, SaaS lean teams and AI
chunks.text:
- **Why he builds in public:** He started in 2022 as the best way to build awareness among Shopify brands. He says he wouldn't have reached $4M ARR on RB2B without it. His angle is credibility: "a guy who's at 25 million ARR who's working in public. There's no one else." He shares what's going wrong too, including the layoffs and a pricing change that didn't work, and was writing for who he was five years ago when stuck at $3M.
- **Channel reasoning:** LinkedIn's creator-to-consumer dynamic is more favorable than Twitter's, so the plan was 10-20K followers there first.
- **Founder-brand caveat:** Brand marketing is hard to tie to dollars for a bootstrapped company, so benefits are mostly unquantifiable. He says copying Jason Fried's style would not work for him because each founder has to find their own angle.
- **AI view:** He is a late adopter. AI helps a tiny team, and his customer support (Intercom) handles many tickets with two people. But he thinks it increases competition, since more people can build SaaS quickly, and sees enterprise sales as the hard part to defend. His advice: ask "what is hard in a world where building is easy?" He doubts that agents will replace SaaS soon, guessing five years or more.
- **Related example:** He notes the builtwith founder ran to the high-teens millions ARR before hiring anyone.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Adam Robinson explains how organic LinkedIn video built an audience that shaped RB2B's go-to-market: a massive free offer, paid features added over time, and patience on revenue. He also covers why churn depends on product category and why free users are worth keeping.

chunks.heading: Why Adam chose LinkedIn and video as his distribution engine
chunks.text:
- Adam started posting on social about a year and a half before this 2024 conversation, while selling retention.com (a roughly $22M ARR bootstrapped company) to big Shopify stores.
- He wanted the fastest way to spread awareness of a product he believed worked for everyone with no real competitor.
- He read Gerhart's "Founder Brand" and heard "just tweet every day" advice, but refused to tweet into the void without knowing how the game works. He compares himself to someone who is "LeBron James" at a few things and "just lost" on social media.
- Instead he sought out a vendor selling to the same people that had reached about $10M ARR using only social. He offered to teach them his cold email motion if they taught him social.
- Their head of social said Twitter had worked for them, but LinkedIn was the ripe opportunity now. That led to LinkedIn, with an agency writing for him at first.
- He added video on purpose. His reasoning comes from his experience of watching ten courses by a business-coach founder over about two weeks. After about 100 hours he felt the guy was his best friend, while the guy treated him like a stranger. Adam wanted to turn that one-sided affinity into an advantage.
- Video builds affinity "in a way that nothing else can" because people observe your mannerisms, phrasing and voice.
- The result: strangers now walk up and ask "are you Adam Robinson?" A founder told him he put the B2B product on his site and his BDR booked five demos in a day.

chunks.heading: What made LinkedIn click after 9 to 12 months
chunks.text:
- LinkedIn didn't work for roughly 9 to 12 months. Something clicked when he replaced a ghostwriter with a consultant, because he wanted to understand the machine himself.
- He also changed the subject. He pivoted from talking to Shopify founders to talking to SaaS revenue leaders, about the unpleasant experience of trying to scale his own company: sales, marketing and people problems.
- He started addressing SaaS revenue leaders around Labor Day 2023 and launched the B2B product on March 1 (2024). By launch he had about six to seven months of audience-building behind him.
- He notes that the distribution informed the go-to-market decision, not the other way around. The LinkedIn response was so strong that he decided to launch with a massive free offer, a Mailchimp-style go-to-market, because the free thing "is going to work way better for me with this megaphone than anybody else who didn't have it."

chunks.heading: Reading business context before copying a playbook: his churn lesson
chunks.text:
- He says context matters: what he's doing may be wrong for others. He is bootstrapped, profitable, expecting high single-digit millions of free cash flow, has no investors and no time horizon.
- Retention.com economics: a paid-trial close is about an 18-month LTV at roughly $1,200 a month, so a mid-$20Ks customer. It is mostly inbound with little spend and generates about $7M of free cash this year, but churn is so high that growth is hard (he hopes to reach 30% in a couple of years).
- Why: in martech the lowest-churn products are systems of record (CRM, email platforms). Mission-critical workflows come next. The worst category is selling leads and intent data, and the buyer was an SMB e-commerce store, a high-churn persona.
- Comparison: Klaviyo has roughly 120% net revenue expansion, while his gross churn is about 60%. With Klaviyo-like SaaS metrics he says he'd be a unicorn.
- His early read (huge TAM, fast closes, churn would fade) was wrong because they were overselling, and the TAM was smaller and deals slower than expected.
- Lesson on funding: raising money on a plan to grow from $15M to $50M would have made his life miserable, because the actual problem was revenue contraction. He enjoys being able to run without "walking the plank."
- Fixes he names: point sales above the SMB buyer persona, improve operational efficiency (such as detecting when competitors put scripts on a site), and tighten positioning.

chunks.heading: The free-offer strategy for the B2B product
chunks.text:
- The product: anonymous website visitors are identified at person level and the leads are pushed to Slack for free. He compares the model to Mailchimp, which was about $2M ARR when Constant Contact went public, then launched a huge free tier and bootstrapped to a roughly $12B exit.
- 22 days after launch: about 2,500 signups. 75% self-served installing the JavaScript, and activation doubled in the following week and a half. About 100 new signups show up on a normal day, with 70 of them installing the script.
- His thesis: be incredibly patient on revenue, on a scale of years. Give away what others charge $50K to $100K a year for, and become synonymous with person-level website visitor identity "synonymous with my face," so no competitor can match it. His data cost is low enough that a new entrant would have to pay unit costs he doesn't.
- The free offer spreads on its own. An agency owner told him he was "literally selling your tech" repackaged for a $5,000 setup fee and $3 per ICP lead while paying Adam nothing. Adam's reaction was "great, I hope you make a lot of money." Another user said he can't stop talking about it because it feels like getting away with something.
- On pricing, his stance is: keep adding value to the paid plan until conversion is decent, rather than taking value away from the free one. He is building goodwill with the audience by keeping it free.
- His planned paid hooks (about $495 a month): an ICP filter (once volume passes roughly 50 to 75 leads a day, traffic is mostly noise and the higher the traffic the more noise), plus a two-way HubSpot and Salesforce integration. Free users don't get repeat-visitor info or page-view history. He says today's paid features are not yet enough for 5% conversion; a $99 plan with the same features would not convert at 5% either.
- He gives full-featured 30-day trials, and wants the paid workflow to be a lower-churn use case than the lead data itself.

chunks.heading: Turning free users into value: reviews and the chatbot question
chunks.text:
- A friend, Stuart, runs Shopify apps (e.g. email newsletter capture) and holds that "no user is a free user": you get something from everyone. Segment early, and send users who won't pay down a funnel that earns something else, such as reviews.
- Stuart's review machine: the onboarding creates any excuse to start a live chat. He hires about 40 "highly charismatic women in their 20s" with one bubbly profile, who "nice them to death" through onboarding. About 30% of those conversations convert to a review, and he gets a hundred times more reviews than competitors. Reviews often praise the person, not the product.
- Adam's contrast: he has nine G2 reviews after 22 days and a self-serve, no-human app, like Mailchimp's free tier, where you couldn't reach a human if you tried.
- Open questions he plans to test this quarter: can he and a colleague personally reach free users to get reviews at Stuart's rate? Can that be scripted for a team? And the "holy grail": can an LLM chatbot create the interpersonal obligation? He thinks that is probably a couple of years away.
- He doesn't favor gaming reviews.

chunks.heading: Staying engaged in public and building community
chunks.text:
- Reply to comments on every post. He answers comments more than DMs on purpose, since public answers build community. He frames free users and commenters as "giving something back."
- He builds in public with real numbers and failures (including a mean-tweets style video of reading his Glassdoor reviews for the first time after a layoff), not vulnerability for show.
- He mentions that a coworker told him to say "we" more than "I." His LinkedIn headline approach doesn't work with "we."

chunks.heading: Why small teams, AI and underpriced SaaS are an opening
chunks.text:
- He's excited by AI letting a very small group do what a large one used to. Example: one support person processing 2,000 tickets a week.
- Combining AI with an "influencer-type founder" distribution can create a playbook for bootstrapped startups at scale, with highly skilled staff using AI tools.
- On Clearbit (told to him by its former CEO): they reached $8M ARR in about 18 months with two reps and three other people, underpriced relative to value, which built great brand and goodwill. After raising venture money, boards pushed for fair-value pricing (e.g. "you charge GitHub $40K, how do we make it $500K?"), and that hurt the brand over eight years. Clearbit also could not compete with a free data company.
- His broader read on SaaS: it is bloated with bundles. Zoom Info and Apollo each have one product everyone wants (contact data) and several others that about 90% of users don't use. A self-serve point solution with a massive free offer and a tiny team could undercut them, and the incumbents' only lever is raising prices.
- His light, self-serve identity app is partly a stepping stone toward a contact-data app with a similar UI.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Adam walks through his actual weekly calendar, showing most of a CEO's week going to content and podcasts. He explains why organic founder content beats paid ads, how to start (ghostwriter, study creators, comment thoughtfully), why he runs on gut over metrics, and how to follow up with website visitors.

chunks.heading: Adam's content schedule and time allocation for founder-led LinkedIn
chunks.text:
- Adam is CEO of two tech companies (retention.com and RB2B), and still spends most of his working time on content. He calls a calendar with a lot of content slots a "light week".
- He aims for 3-4 LinkedIn posts a week. Hooks for those posts are meant to be nailed in a weekly 1-hour idea session with his LinkedIn coach (Alec). They review last week's posts, what worked and what didn't, and what's happening in his work life.
- Monday is internal meetings for the other company, plus the coaching session. Tuesday is his content day. He fills open slots with other people's podcasts and webinars.
- He keeps Wednesday mornings free until 11:00 for his two-year-old daughter.
- He hands off everything he can. The retention.com business (50 people) is run by his co-founder, so he can spend most of his time on content and on RB2B marketing and product.
- His rule for gaps: "whenever I don't have a meeting I'm trying to crank out a LinkedIn post."
- Content ideas come from repeated questions. He heard "isn't inbound-led outbound just marketing?" about five times in a week and turned it into a post, with the hook "says every Revenue leader in SaaS, here's why they're wrong".
- He runs a weekly inbound-led-outbound workshop with his co-founder Santos. It's 20-30 minutes of talk, then Q&A. The first one drew about 1,300 on LinkedIn Live, and later ones draw 100-300 on Zoom. Topics included "how I bootstrapped $22M ARR" and how he grew his LinkedIn following.
- He uses the workshop and weekly calls to gather material for the next season of his docuseries. He invited Aaron Ross (author of Predictable Revenue) to debate it, because Adam says "predictable revenue is dead".

chunks.heading: Why Adam believes organic founder content beats paid ads in B2B
chunks.text:
- He argues organic content is now worth "1,000 times more" than paid ads for B2B SaaS.
- He says that if he had $100 million but could not post on his own profile, he could not have built the awareness and trust he has. He began writing for B2B in September, and says the awareness is higher than any ad campaign or sponsorship would have produced.
- Reach compounds through collaboration. He uses other people's podcasts, webinars and co-created content to get in front of their audiences.
- He calls the efficiency of spreading awareness this way "dumbfounding".
- Scale result: RB2B launched its website about 13 weeks before this recording, and he says "basically everybody in B2B knows what RB2B is".
- He credits Chris Walker's playbook for the video approach.

chunks.heading: Overcoming the "I don't know what to write about" objection
chunks.text:
- Adam says the muscle is hard to build. Ideas and writing are difficult at first, and it takes a long time to find what resonates and where you can offer real insight. "Everything is working against you in the beginning", like any startup.
- His recommendation: start with a ghostwriter and watch them write for a few months. They can show you what you might write about.
- He later switched from a ghostwriter to a LinkedIn consultant, Alec, who insisted he write himself. Alec's view: it only works if you actually write it, it will suck at first, then it becomes natural. Adam says he pays Alec more than he paid the ghostwriter.
- Sanity check first: is your audience on LinkedIn? Adam sells to salespeople, marketers and founders, who spend lots of time there. If you sell to hospitals, you probably can't systematically book demos through a LinkedIn profile, so find another way to use organic social.
- Even where LinkedIn doesn't drive demos, a CEO profile helps recruiting, partner and agency relationships, and anyone vetting the company. It is less likely to drive business outcomes.
- If you get "the content bug" (it's doing something even if you can't say what), then work on making it your own.

chunks.heading: What good LinkedIn content looks like and how to study it
chunks.text:
- Adam rejects the view that LinkedIn content is dumb or all selfies. He says your feed is not indicative of great content. LinkedIn is where the deepest thought leadership goes because the audience is professional and the platform is still long-form and text-based.
- Seek out the best creators in your space or adjacent spaces, not the accounts with the most followers. Big-follower creators often aggregate audiences that let them sell ghostwriting, courses or coaching. He says that audience is not valuable to a business.
- He studies Chris Walker's feed to work out why one post got 600 likes and another 150: the hook, the topic, or the template.
- Walker "only talks about like five things" and has for seven years, but makes each post feel new. Recurring topics include multi-touch attribution, the dark funnel and "why paid ads don't work".
- Walker's loop: the topics hit, super-fans form around those ideas, he brings them to a weekly event where they ask deeper questions about the same ideas, and that reinforces the loop.
- Adam's own content is more diverse and more ambitious, because he uses a consultant.
- For LinkedIn, he says to treat every post as brand new because the platform is not sequential. The hook has to be a strong credibility-building statement that makes people read more.

chunks.heading: Measurement, authenticity and "make them feel like they know me"
chunks.text:
- Adam admits he doesn't really measure content. He keeps a loose scorecard of signups and impressions, and notes that the week of a particularly well-fitted post had far more impressions and signups than a later week with similar impressions but worse audience fit.
- His core principle: make people feel like they know him as a friend. He engineers content to do this by telling stories, bringing people along on the journey and showing his face.
- His reasoning: software is getting commoditized. He compares it to the Kardashians selling lipstick: hundreds of millions of people feel like they're friends with them.
- He says that if he optimized only for what can be measured, his content would drift toward Justin Welsh-style content, he'd avoid video because it lowers reach, and he wouldn't make a docuseries or start a YouTube channel.
- He is wary of running everything on metrics: "the most important things cannot be measured", and measurable things crowd them out. At an early stage, running largely on gut is not crazy; he says he'd be criticized for it at a $100M ARR company.
- He cites Elon Musk as an example of valuing unmeasurable things (energizing executives with big-picture talks, unfiltered authenticity on Twitter) and says Jeff Bezos doesn't get this.

chunks.heading: Prioritizing content as a founder with limited time
chunks.text:
- Adam's position: product-market fit is the thing that matters first. Once you have it, audience-building skill amplifies it dramatically. He had a product with fit and was already good at content when RB2B launched, so he commits fully.
- For an early-stage founder, he advises documenting the journey and writing about the problems you're solving. If the problems are real and you write well, you can build an audience on some network (LinkedIn, Twitter or elsewhere). Level up once the product has traction.
- Example: Triple Whale reached about $20-25M ARR in under two years on founder-led social, in coordination with other Twitter accounts. Their founders had around 23,000 followers, "the perfect followers", highly influential people in the Shopify ecosystem.
- Make yourself a presence in whatever ecosystem you operate in.

chunks.heading: A starter routine and engagement tactics
chunks.text:
- If starting with limited time, he would write on two days a week (e.g. Monday and Thursday) and spend the other days commenting.
- Make a list of about 10 influential people in your ecosystem and thoughtfully comment on their posts, not with AI-generated comments. Commenting can lead them to comment on yours, and you build karma in the ecosystem.
- He dislikes AI-generated comments (for example, summaries of his post followed by a generic question).
- He tries to reply to every comment on his own posts, with a reply about as thoughtful as the comment.
- His connection-request and inbox handling is semi-automated by his coach's team, depending on the goal at the time (for example, booking discovery calls with VP-level marketers at Series B startups).

chunks.heading: Getting the team to post and the shared-brand approach
chunks.text:
- Adam says more people posting widens the "attack surface": every employee's profile links to the website, which is RB2B's only traffic source.
- His co-founder Santos is heavily courted by recruiters but stays because he finds the work interesting. Adam is not worried about poaching.
- He encourages new hires to build an audience. His pitch: joining him means that in two or three years they're likely to get a much better job, because content is "a forever skill".
- Building a personal profile is about 10 times easier than building a company profile, because people go to social networks to connect with people, not companies.
- Posting is a strong recommendation rather than a requirement. If a role truly required it, he wouldn't hire someone who refused. Otherwise it's their loss.
- He also credits the co-founder pairing: they support and shout out each other on posts.

chunks.heading: Turning website visitors into outbound, and where outbound is heading
chunks.text:
- RB2B puts a pixel on your site and resolves anonymous visitors (who didn't fill out a form) to a LinkedIn profile and business email, pushed to Slack. It is free and unlimited for the first month, then capped: about 85-90% of users stay free and the top ~10% pay.
- Follow-up timing: reach out within single-digit hours. Immediately, they'll connect it to your site; after two hours they may forget; after a day they may have forgotten the brand; after a week they have never heard of you.
- Use the same playbook as for outbound demos (phone, LinkedIn connect and message, cold email sequence). He says RB2B won't help if you can't book outbound demos; it gives you the best leads and makes your traffic channels more efficient.
- He had sold similar tech to the ecommerce space for five years and says being contacted after visiting a site is not infuriating in 2024, since people are used to retargeting.
- GDPR: RB2B doesn't identify EU traffic and only has US data subjects on US soil. He argues a European company using it for US traffic is not out of GDPR compliance, because the EU isn't seeking to regulate US tech on US soil. Compare CAN-SPAM, which is opt-out, not opt-in, a similar widespread misunderstanding.
- Outlook: he believes outbound response rates trend toward zero because of automation volume and blocking. Some of it goes back to field sales (target account lists, events, meetups through mutual contacts). His inbound-led outbound thesis survives this: people who engage with a founder's content will still answer a message from him.
- A message from his profile to book a call with a teammate (Pete) has a 100% book rate and 100% show rate in his experience, so the profile scales beyond his own hours.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Adam Robinson explains how he built an audience on LinkedIn first and then built RB2B for it, using organic founder content, radical transparency and podcast cross-pollination as a low-cost, bootstrapped demand engine. He also shares stories of starting from zero three times, why VC doesn't accelerate sub-$10M ARR companies, and why a clear one-liner can launch a product.

chunks.heading: Why audience-first beats product-first for startup go-to-market
chunks.text:
- Adam argues you can now build demand first and the product second. Building an audience of buyers while building the product is, in his words, "four steps to the Epiphany" turbocharged.
- He had not decided to build RB2B until he saw how effective his LinkedIn content was. The opposite of "build a product, then search for demand."
- During the roughly five months of developing RB2B he did 300 discovery calls. Many came from people commenting on his posts, whom he could reply to with "by the way, we're thinking about building this thing, would you talk to us about it?" Every one said yes.
- His rule: if you have access to a voice that can create organic social content for a group of target prospects who truly want it, create a product for that audience. He compares it to why the Kardashians or billionaires sell so efficiently in B2C.
- He frames it as "a brand new path" to bootstrapping. What used to need a 25-person sales and marketing team (and about $5M raised) is done by his LinkedIn brand plus two contractors.
- Product still matters equally. He says RB2B was disruptive in its pricing, and "magic lightning in a bottle happens when those two interact with each other."

chunks.heading: Why LinkedIn content worked for Adam: skill, fit and radical transparency
chunks.text:
- He wrote about this topic for a year before it really worked, and stuck with it. He started writing in September of the prior year. A glimpse of what might work came in July, then a Labor Day experiment produced four absolute bangers in a row.
- The shift: he stopped aggregating an audience of Shopify stores and wrote directly at SaaS revenue leaders about a problem they all shared but nobody acknowledged. Big BDR teams might not work anymore; "you could probably reduce the head count by 90% and get the same amount of book demos," because power shifted back to marketing.
- He identifies a "perfect author to content to platform fit."
- Positioning rule: be different from everyone else, but in a way that is "not quite crazy but definitely not mainstream," and related to what you do. Down the middle doesn't work.
- Being bootstrapped lets him do things VC-backed founders can't. He shows financials and monthly recurring numbers, and he publishes a live SaaS metrics dashboard for RB2B in his newsletter every week, including bad churn.
- Why he shares it: when he was stuck at $3M ARR for four years, he reached for anything written by someone further along. He knows how novel that transparency is.
- Advice: don't copy someone's tactics; understand the thought process behind why they made a decision.

chunks.heading: Turning controversy into free PR: the cease-and-desist post
chunks.text:
- He attacked a larger incumbent and got a cease and desist. He believed there was a good chance he would be sued, but posted the letter on LinkedIn and rewrote what they had sent him.
- He calls it a pivotal moment in his career. It moved him from being vaguely known as "a LinkedIn guy" to being understood by all of that incumbent's customers, who he expects will become RB2B customers as it drifts upmarket.
- He describes it as "millions of dollars of free PR" and says it could not have happened any other way.
- He says it was not malicious: it was a plain account of what was happening, which is where the authenticity comes from.

chunks.heading: Using organic social and podcasts as demand creation (not just lead gen)
chunks.text:
- He considers himself "in the edutainment business" and happens to have a SaaS at the end of the funnel.
- Cold email and LinkedIn outreach to launch a startup (the predictable-revenue playbook) was "a hack" and "shouldn't have been that easy." He argues it was really a demand-creation mechanism, and that those days are gone or on the way out; founders should plan for a future where it's impossible.
- His current approach: cross-pollinate audiences with people who have audiences made up of your prospects. Once your audience is bigger than the host's, they want you on their show and distribute it for you.
- He does about 10 guest podcast slots a week related to go-to-market. A year and a half earlier he paid Lemon Pie to book them; now it is inbound. He has told the market he'll come on any show that invites him.
- Why he likes it: it's a "prospect dinner" he didn't have to attend. Talking to one person about what he's doing is easy for him, and he doesn't drink.
- Even if only 10 people listen and half check out RB2B, that counts.
- Downside: it can't be measured. When signups dip by 100 in a week he has no idea why, and he can't attribute signups to specific activities.
- He argues a VC-backed founder couldn't easily pitch investors on "spend four days a week creating founder brand content and I'm not sure when it will start working."
- The compounding value: that audience also helps in recruiting, partnerships and investor relations, even where customers aren't on LinkedIn (his example of agriculture tech or insurance).

chunks.heading: Building the habit, ghostwriters and getting through the zero-follower stage
chunks.text:
- Posting is work for him. He treats it as a muscle, like going to the gym, and says every habit he has built got easier with time.
- He ran a ghostwriter for nine months, and recommends starting with a ghostwriter for about 90 days to learn how writing on LinkedIn works. You can see the benefits (inbound from investors, recruiting) without committing heavily.
- He later switched to a more expensive coach (Alec) who doesn't write for him. His view: you writing it yourself is the more valuable skill, and "there's no way a ghostwriter could write as profoundly as you."
- His own barrier was that he wouldn't post without understanding the game, since he is now "playing in the pros" at product and marketing and wasn't going to "start tweeting against LeBron James." Learning why things work solved that.
- The start is "brutal": a first post can get about four engagements while he gets 1,600. "At some point everyone had zero subscribers, zero followers, zero revenue." He cites "the best time to plant a tree was 20 years ago, the second best time is today," and says it is only just beginning.
- Content as beacons: every piece is a little beacon, and if it's true to you, interesting people and problems gather around it. Old posts keep pulling people in years later.
- He treats being a founder as finding the point of maximum leverage and going as hard as possible until you max out. For him, LinkedIn is "100 times more leverage than anything else" in either company.

chunks.heading: The long game: attention arbitrage and a voice that outlives the company
chunks.text:
- His thesis: if you build an organic social voice and know what good content is, you can carry it to any niche. He thinks he could make good content for another audience, such as agencies instead of SaaS, though less prolifically.
- Quoting Russell Brunson as his source: once people will pay you for advice, "you are one of the most powerful people in the world."
- Benefits beyond revenue: he can message anyone who spends time on LinkedIn and get a 30-minute chat, including CEOs. He says this is a bigger superpower than the money he has made.
- Founders resist this because they are entirely focused on the current business. He says he used to think "I don't care about that," and now definitely does.

chunks.heading: Finding product-market fit through a one-liner: the Get Emails / Retention.com story
chunks.text:
- His earlier email marketing platform (a V2 aimed at a segment he thought a competitor was leaving) took six engineers and a year. At a trade show people's eyes glazed over; they already had the problem solved. He describes that night as rock bottom: "no one cares."
- Having heard it was possible to resolve an anonymous site visitor to a deliverable email address, he started asking on day two of the show: "What if I could give you email addresses of people who were on your site but didn't fill out a form?" The reaction was immediate: "where do I buy that?"
- He had no idea how to build it technically. The signal was strong enough to send him digging until he found the few people who understood that part of the internet. They white-labeled a provider and then made it their own; that became Retention.com.
- The product launched as Get Emails. In the first month he spent $5,000 on Facebook ads and reached $10K MRR. It had very high churn, but a high-ticket PLG dynamic: "we get 100 bad customers and some whale would come in and pay five grand and pay the ads back."
- His takeaway: it started with a searingly clear one-liner and watching people's faces react, before he even had the product.
- RB2B followed a similar pattern. When he described person-level website visitor identity, people first said they already had it (meaning company-level tools like Clearbit), then asked where to buy the person-level version.
- He is betting against sweeping regulation of tracking and retargeting, calling it a fundamental underpinning of the internet's economic engine. He notes that third-party cookie removal was predicted "in 12 months" every year for about five years and then did not happen. He says the product works only in the US.

chunks.heading: Views on venture capital and what actually accelerates growth
chunks.text:
- Widely held belief he rejects: that venture capital under $10M ARR will accelerate your growth. He says what accelerates growth is making your customers happier.
- He thinks VC often slows you down early by adding people and management layers when you don't yet know what you're doing. "When we were seven people and not 22... we were iterating so fast."
- He says capital is never the answer to hitting a wall. He believes it can help speed things up later, but not before roughly $10M ARR.
- He argues for efficient, bootstrapped paths. Funds like Sent invest only in founder-owned, profitable, growing businesses past $15-20M ARR, and he believes that model is better for founders than the VC odds.
- Current working tactic outside LinkedIn: a UGC motion where lead-gen agencies post on LinkedIn to grow their own businesses, using RB2B and the content Adam gives them. He calls it working "incredibly well" and a green field for B2B companies.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Adam Robinson recounts taking Retention.com from zero to $22M ARR with a tiny team, using outrageous Facebook ads, cold email and word of mouth. He covers the stalls, the failed 2023 scale-up, and the pivot to B2B, where LinkedIn content let him build a waitlist of ideal buyers before the product shipped.

chunks.heading: Why Adam says he pivoted from e-commerce to B2B
chunks.text:
- Adam's co-founder Santosh, who built Apollo and ZoomInfo, kept telling him to sell the product (resolving anonymous site visitors to deliverable emails) to B2B teams. His argument was that the leads and person-level data are worth more to B2B sellers than to stores selling "a $100 pair of shoes".
- Adam's LinkedIn content aimed at e-commerce stores gave him visibility, partnerships, agency credibility, recruiting help and investor interest. It did not book demos with e-com store owners.
- His LinkedIn coach Alec told him that if he wrote about B2B he could "book demos with literally anyone". Adam made the content pivot in September, before the B2B product existed.
- The first B2B post got about 100 times the engagement of anything else he had written. He wrote three more and all of them did well.
- He puts the fit down to "author to platform to audience fit": he is his own ICP (a SaaS founder and revenue leader) and that ICP lives on LinkedIn.
- He had about 15,000 followers in the e-com space the previous July. He says he would not be where he is without the B2B shift.

chunks.heading: Co-creating the product with his LinkedIn audience
chunks.text:
- Adam recommends *Four Steps to the Epiphany* (Steve Blank) and the Lean Startup method to every startup founder. His reading of them: your intuition is a poor indicator of market viability, so build the buyers at the same time as the product.
- Doing that de-risks the launch two ways. Initial buyers are already waiting when you launch. If nobody wants it, you can stop building and start over.
- While Tate built the product, Adam and Santosh took 5 to 7 calls a day with perfect-ICP people who responded to his posts.
- His posts argued things like "outbound is dead" and "third-party intent data sucks, here's what I learned from talking to 6sense customers".
- He used very soft CTAs. DM responders above a certain threshold got a phone call (Calendly link). Those below went onto a waiting list.
- The waiting list had 2,000 people before the product started.
- The content built enough trust that he planned to sell mid-market and run a free offer instead of a sales-led motion. He argues a free offer helps someone with a big megaphone far more than someone without one.

chunks.heading: Finding content-market fit on LinkedIn
chunks.text:
- Adam took 12 months to find content-market fit (a Devin Reed term). He says others with it also took 12 months or a little longer.
- The unlock was writing about his own hard B2B journey: expanding a sales force too hard, then contracting it, and being down four months in a row. "No one else is sitting there saying that they're down 4 months in a row", though many people are.
- He says to articulate a very specific pain "incredibly clearly", something you can only do if you are one of them.
- Alec's view, which Adam now agrees with, is that you work out your content pillars as you go. A Justin Welsh-style content-pillar spreadsheet doesn't tell you in advance.
- Alec's formula: write the best hook you can, the best body you can, and a "killer close" that gives a dopamine hit and provokes engagement.
- Adam does not use engagement circles or ask big accounts to comment, though he did when he started.
- He studies people winning the game, such as Chris Walker, and asks why they win. He likes Nigel Thomas's list-format templates.
- The weekly "killer close" he showed was a simple soft CTA reused across several related posts.

chunks.heading: Why founder brand beats a good offer alone
chunks.text:
- A listener said the offer (free visitor identification pushed to Slack) was good enough that he would have said yes to a cold email. Adam agreed it is a great offer, but said fewer people would say yes if they didn't know who he was.
- He cites Dave Cancel (Drift): HubSpot had a business-model innovation (a free CRM), but by the time Drift started there were 600 chatbot apps. Drift treated brand as the opportunity.
- Adam calls his LinkedIn effort "today's Drift". Competitors can copy the product, but the trust built through a founder-led LinkedIn presence is hard to emulate.
- The advantage is partly that he and Santosh have the experience and willingness to share, and partly that a cash-flowing other business funds the time. In effect he can give the product away and build "a bulletproof megaphone".
- He says the biggest determinant of a cold email's open rate is who sends it, more than the subject line.
- He does not measure the brand work by demos booked. "It is how we are going to win in the long run", and it is non-linear and makes everything else work better.
- Founder-profile calls still convert when someone else takes them. In the PLG funnel, if a valuable signup doesn't install the script, they get routed to Pete, Sean (enterprise) or Santosh. People show up equally for calls booked through Adam's profile whether or not he takes them.
- Caveat: it works for him because his audience (B2B revenue people) is on LinkedIn and he is that ICP. Not everyone will get the same result.

chunks.heading: Zero to $1M ARR: Facebook ads and an offer that wowed
chunks.text:
- Adam's rule: with decent product-market fit and strong word of mouth, there are many ways to accelerate it. Without word of mouth, nothing you do will work.
- Zero to $1M in 28 weeks came from a Facebook ad campaign. He spent $5,000 on ads the first month and got $10K MRR. It was very high-churn MRR, but a strong early signal of product-market fit.
- Format: 60-second ads, inspired by the arrival of Snap and Instagram Stories, with a different background each time. They answered the sales questions and were designed to be anticipated.
- Tone: deliberately inflammatory toward privacy-minded people. He insulted commenters from the brand account to draw out more long replies, and the negative energy made the ads perform better.
- His takeaways: the offer matters most, and you can do aggressive, outrageous things in the first months because there is "no brand to destroy".
- The ads also made cold email work better through awareness, even when people didn't click.
- He suggests Facebook or Twitter ads as a way to get early awareness if starting from zero, and says to run tight, cheap experiments with defined time limits.
- Before $1M, he says the race is for feedback: "not a race to a million, it's a race to as much feedback as humanly possible".

chunks.heading: One to $10M ARR with six people
chunks.text:
- The team was six people: one salesperson with a sales assistant, and three people in the Philippines. Those three did lead gen half the day and sent outbound email from individual Gmail inboxes the other half.
- The motion was inbound, a 15-minute demo and a one-call close, on a simple product, plus word of mouth. It reached about $12M ARR with six people.
- Adam's point is that the right product and one or two channels plus word of mouth go further than you'd expect with far fewer people, if you have the discipline. He says to get as far as humanly possible with as few people as you can.
- The cost: you need unusually productive individual contributors, and when it is time to grow nobody knows how to manage or has processes.
- The Philippines team: his co-founder Diana used one trusted contact (Jim) who could follow instructions, and Jim's cousins joined. People found alternate emails not in Apollo or ZoomInfo, and sent manually from Gmail rather than with Outreach or Salesloft.
- He treats this work as very mechanical, with no room for independent interpretation. With hindsight he would look for people who add more value than ticking off checkboxes.
- A friend, Stuart Chaney (Shopify app), advised building the playbook in the US first, then finding one person who fits the profile to work alongside you, then slowly building the team. Stuart finds people on onlinejobs.ph.

chunks.heading: Mistakes in the 2023 expansion and churn benchmarks
chunks.text:
- Adam publicly forecast going from $13M to $50M ARR in 2023 (he made a docu-series) and missed by over 50%.
- Reasons he gives:
  - He believed narrowing to the ICP who loved the product would fix churn. It helped only a little.
  - He now thinks there are high-churn product categories and high-churn buyer personas, and some categories will never be low churn.
  - The market got competitive as others began solving the same problem.
  - Processes were missing. He now has an executive coach working with eight executives and is rolling out the Entrepreneurial Operating System (EOS).
  - Senior hires brought their own ways of doing things on top of no company way.
  - Biggest mistake: he lost his bootstrapper's discipline with money, started behaving like a venture-backed CEO, and a highly profitable company stopped being profitable.
- Revenue stalled around $3M ARR for four years at Robly. At retention.com, quarterly revenue was flat to down for nine months (Q2 2020 to Q1 2021), and it shrank four months in a row (about 2.3% in the fourth). He still throws off roughly $400-500K a month.
- Churn benchmarks he gave:
  - Klaviyo's gross revenue retention is about 88% (usually about 70 for SMB), with about 120 net revenue expansion.
  - Retention.com's SMB lead product churns about 5-6% a month with the paid trial included and about 4% without it.
  - Enterprise logo churn is about 2% a year, with 130-140 net revenue expansion (great companies about 180). Mid-market sits halfway.
- Why leads-as-SaaS churns: many reasons to stop have nothing to do with the vendor, such as a new employee who doesn't know the tool or a lack of ROI.

chunks.heading: Staying small, bootstrapping and reviews
chunks.text:
- Adam says bootstrapping caps the downside. A venture-backed company in the same bind would be in a "huge pickle", while a profitable bootstrapped one can only get so bad.
- His lesson from Jasper's founders, who were stuck at $2.5M ARR, out of money and ready to sell, is "keep building new baskets to put your eggs in because you just never know". Watching peers like that made a big outcome feel possible for him.
- On raising money or venture debt: "I would rather shrink my team than take someone else's money." Fundraising sells expectations rosier than reality, and he calls venture debt terms "a deal with the devil". His instinct is to get smaller and more efficient.
- On G2 reviews: he sees them as a legitimacy threshold (a good-not-great website, reviews across the internet), not a source of leads, and says leads he bought from G2 were terrible.
- Santosh's addition: reviews get gamed, and content like Adam's builds more trust than chasing reviews.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Adam Robinson explains why brand and community are the real moats in SaaS without network effects. He covers how he built a LinkedIn audience by working in public, and why he pairs a big free offer with a paid upsell. He also gives his view on churn, premium media content and creator-led distribution.

chunks.heading: Work in public as the foundation for a LinkedIn audience
chunks.text:
- Adam started writing on LinkedIn about a year and a half before this recording. Tommy from Triple Whale offered to ghostwrite for him through a side agency.
- He started when the business was at $12 million ARR with six employees. He knew that combination would shock people, because most founders have less revenue and more staff.
- His point: working in public only works if the numbers are impressive. A founder under $1M saying "I'm working in public" is not interesting. A founder with $12M and six people sharing everything makes people listen.
- The first plan was 60% email content and 40% work in public. He hated the email content ("I don't care about email marketing, I've never sent a DTC email") and it felt inauthentic, so it moved to all work in public.
- Even though it did not generate hard DTC leads, the LinkedIn presence raised the brand's profile among DTC agencies and vendor employees, and made hiring easier.

chunks.heading: Finding the format: twelve months of bad posts before a hit
chunks.text:
- His early videos (about September of the prior year) were rambling. He says they looked like a person who did not know what he was doing.
- A video producer pointed him to a YouTube format: hook, story, three lessons, soft CTA. He bought whiteboards and tried to post one video a day, writing and recording them all in one session.
- Posts got about 22 likes. People at trade shows said "I watch every one of your videos," but he knew the audience was tiny.
- He bounced between topics (work-life balance, spirituality, firing people, hiring A players) with no focus.
- He then worked with Alec Paul, a coach and consultant who is not a ghostwriter. Alec is strategic and acts as an editor: he sharpens headlines, knows how the LinkedIn machine works, and shows templates that hit. They talk about what happened in Adam's life that week and decide what to write.
- Adam's average post got about 30 likes; a great one got about 100.

chunks.heading: The B2B pivot that made posts hit
chunks.text:
- Adam felt it was inauthentic to write about ecommerce because he had never run a store. Alec told him: "If you actually sell something to that audience... we have a machine that systematically generates inbound leads. It will work, I promise."
- Around mid-August he started writing to salespeople, marketers and founders. The breakout post was about speaking to 30 BDR leaders and the eight pains they share: a pipeline crisis, being told not to buy, outbound emails that no longer work.
- He then sat down one night, wrote three posts, and decided that if they hit, he would know what "great" is. They hit. His reasoning: once you know what great looks like, you can keep the machine going indefinitely.
- It took about 12 months to reach that point, and he says people could probably get there faster by being more direct about audience.
- Over the next three months the audience grew so quickly that it shaped the product decision (below).

chunks.heading: LinkedIn audience shaped the product and go-to-market
chunks.text:
- Adam says the LinkedIn presence was "informing the product" and the whole go-to-market.
- Original plan for the B2B product: skip small customers (they churn) and go straight to mid-market at 30 to 50K ACV.
- Because the posts hit so hard, he switched to a big free product with an upsell, gating integrations. He reasoned a big premium offer helps disproportionately someone who already has a megaphone.
- Pricing logic: sell the idea "if you want to save time with integrations, pay $500; if you don't, knock yourself out with the free app forever." Anyone who wants to save time has already found value in the free product, and $500 a month is "a drop in the bucket."
- The free product sends LinkedIn profiles of site visitors to Slack. His goal is 250,000 people using it.
- Ambition: move upmarket later, once the privacy question for larger buyers (who have a CISO) becomes relevant.

chunks.heading: Brand and community as the only moats
chunks.text:
- Adam says that in SaaS without network effects, "brand and community are the only moats." Retention.com has no network effects, so his moat is his brand.
- The community is built around problems and ideas tangential to the technology, not the product itself. He calls it extremely difficult and very long game.
- His advice on where to start community: begin on a social network where your audience is. For his audience that was Twitter or LinkedIn.
- He chose LinkedIn because only 1 to 2% of LinkedIn users create content versus a much more crowded Twitter, so there is more reach for the effort.

chunks.heading: Premium media: the docuseries and what it cost
chunks.text:
- A producer, Christie, made a reality-style series about Adam. A cameraman, John, traveled with him to about five or six work trips over a year, plus a weekly one-hour interview. Episodes were pieced together out of sequence.
- It cost over $10K per episode (he had budgeted $5K) across 18 episodes, around $250K total. His view: it makes the viewer feel connected to everything he does, and people say "I've watched every single episode."
- Distribution caveat: the premium content did not perform on YouTube or LinkedIn. A polished eight-minute episode got 5,000 to 6,000 view minutes at best, while a hot-take video of him talking to a laptop got about 40,000. LinkedIn rewards talking-head takes over Netflix-style production. He did nothing to promote the series.
- He hired Christie full time. Current shows: "Events That Don't Suck" (partner Kyle building an event motion people want), and "The Art of Excellence" on the DTC side, profiling revered founders like Curtis from Portland Leather Goods and Ben from True Classic. These are brand stories, not case studies, and do not mention the product.

chunks.heading: Building in public weekly and getting the team to create content
chunks.text:
- LinkedIn lacks a timeline, so episodic series do not work there; it serves old and new posts together. To give people a more immersive view, Adam records his hour-long Monday B2B strategy and tactics call, posts the Notion board with key metrics and a TL;DR, and plans to do it every week for a year.
- His reasoning: he would have "died to know" week by week what 0-to-1 and 1-to-10 companies focused on.
- Getting the team to create content: Alec's advice is that when others see you doing it regularly, especially if it works, they follow. Santos and Kyle have joined; Diana is harder due to her workload.
- Stunt example: he plans to make ChatGPT the entire support org for the B2B business and hire a person to be a chatbot influencer. He says he would sacrifice sales and support quality because the "no people using OpenAI" story should create more virality than it costs.

chunks.heading: UGC and influencer-led PLG plan for B2B
chunks.text:
- Adam believes hiring 20 SDRs will not work; one talented growth marketer can do more. The best motion looks like what Jolie Skin did: a tiny team plus a huge UGC machine.
- Idea: a premium PLG product where users post, in detail, how they booked their first demo, like 20 LinkedIn posts a day of "this is how I booked a demo with Retention.com." He says he has not seen anyone try this in B2B.
- He is working with Morgan Ingram on a six-month deal: 10 sales influencers (not micro, not big), flown to Atlanta two per month, filmed using the product. Each produces three to five pieces of content, and they agree to put "Retention.com" in their LinkedIn title.
- The content is then amplified with inexpensive thought leadership ads. Goal: create the perception that Retention.com is everywhere.

chunks.heading: Early marketing, churn, and lessons from Robly
chunks.text:
- Early Retention (Get Emails) marketing in late 2019 to early 2020: about six months of Facebook ads, one 160-second selfie-style video ad per week answering sales questions with his wife. COVID made ad inventory cheap, so ads paid back in a day.
- Lesson: "If you want to go fast you care about time to payback; if you want to grow big you need low churn." Facebook-acquired customers churned around 20% per month, so he stopped.
- Churn: he expected a lower end-state churn than reality. Systems of record are the lowest-churn category; selling leads or intent data to small businesses is inherently high churn. Mid-market customers are stickier than SMB by orders of magnitude.
- Approach: sell upmarket, ensure correct onboarding, and make sure the customer understands what the product does. The product works better for bigger stores because it amplifies throughput. Pricing is not linear, so bigger stores get more value.
- Robly (email marketing) reached about $3M ARR then stalled. Mailchimp's free offer beat them: nothing Robly could say that someone who knew Mailchimp would not choose Mailchimp. Mailchimp went freemium at $2M ARR while Constant Contact at $100M ARR could not follow because it could not take the revenue hit.
- Lesson: a premium offer or a free offer can be the thing that beats an incumbent. Get Emails started as a Robly feature that people used without the rest of the app, so he spun it out. His model: run positive cash flow businesses that fund experiments on other ideas.

chunks.heading: Privacy and role
chunks.text:
- Privacy view: after hundreds of hours with privacy attorneys he believes laws are tightening but will not hurt this business. Outcomes will mostly be more cookie banners and disclosure. CCPA does not apply to businesses under $25M in revenue. There is no private right of action, so enforcement would target large companies first, and he argues the fear is greater than the reality.
- B2B vs DTC: business contact data is mostly untouched except by CPR, and B2B companies care about privacy only once they hire a CISO.
- His role: he handed the Shopify business to co-founder Diana Ross and spends about one hour in an executive meeting plus one-on-ones on it. He is now founder-CEO of a zero-to-one, very public experiment on the B2B side, acting as the entire marketing engine and much of big-picture product. He is building the brand from zero, before the product existed.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Adam Robinson explains how cheap thought-leadership awareness plus near-zero marginal fulfillment cost let RB2B price below rivals' CAC and unit costs, freezing the product at a simple $79 offer. He also covers skipping VC for lean sub-VC-scale businesses and his plan to build Moltsets, a contact-data brand for Claude Code users, on top of existing content and data assets.

chunks.heading: Why RB2B's price undercuts competitors' acquisition cost
chunks.text:
- Adam launched RB2B (person-level website visitor identification) with the explicit goal of building "the leanest system possible" where AI could amplify human labor "by a thousand X."
- That goal forced a freemium, PLG, SMB-funnel model. He accepted a cap on revenue in exchange for an operation that eventually runs with almost no human input.
- The risk of that model is a direct competitor starting a feature war, which makes the product complicated again.
- Competitors copied RB2B after a supplier publicized how much money it was making. Two advantages let Adam price below what a rival spends to acquire a customer:
  - **Near-zero acquisition cost:** his LinkedIn thought leadership gave him very cheap awareness.
  - **Near-zero fulfillment cost:** RB2B was already a data company with two other product lines and data scientists. It layered "a few hundred thousand dollars of B2B data" and other signal onto an existing data asset, so it had "no marginal cost of fulfilling a contact."
- Warmly, by contrast, was paying a data vendor (he names Apollo.io) about 7 cents per email. Its unit economics of fulfilling a contact were "literally higher" than RB2B's subscription price, so it could not match the price.
- He also argues RB2B's mechanism for identifying people was better than rivals', though it took the market a while to notice.

chunks.heading: Competitors forced upmarket, leaving the cheap simple product alone
chunks.text:
- Because rivals could not compete on channel cost or price, they built extra features and moved to roughly $30K per year contracts. Their investors also wanted guaranteed new recurring subscription revenue.
- Adam's read of the last vendor to do this: the competitor had "the perfect product," then built everything else. The remaining position was "put the pixel on your site and we'll resolve the contact and push it somewhere else."
- His framing of the offer: if you want anything else, go pay someone else $20,000; if you want to get started in 60 seconds for $79, RB2B is "the only game in town."
- Result: with no direct competitors left at that price point, he chose to leave the product "frozen in time."

chunks.heading: The lean-operation outcome
chunks.text:
- Approaching $9M ARR ("going to hit it any day now") with a very small time cost:
  - His developer (Tate) has not touched the code in 6 weeks.
  - The support lead (Rob) spends about 15 minutes a day on ticket escalations.
  - Adam posts about three times a week on LinkedIn, and not about RB2B.
- The wider company has about 30 full-time employees and a 5-person executive team. Two executives run the other two product lines, and one handles finance, legal and HR.
- He notes the lightning-in-a-bottle element: "so much of business is… an incredible multivariate equation," and parts of this he could not have planned.
- He says a business at this scale needing 15 minutes a day is "the dream" and that he would like "a hundred of those."

chunks.heading: Sub-VC-scale businesses as an advantage
chunks.text:
- He values a business that is too small for venture capital, because VC-backed rivals cannot afford to chase it. He frames the opportunity as having no heavily funded competitors going after your market share.
- He accepts that RB2B's churn is bad and that it will top out. Even so, a portfolio of lean $10M ARR businesses, some growing and some shrinking slightly, is an appealing goal to him.

chunks.heading: When to raise venture capital (and when not to)
chunks.text:
- Capital is necessary for some businesses, such as OpenAI's data centers, space travel, or lending businesses that need money to lend out.
- For software, he argues money does not buy product-market pull. Spending before you have pull is "a big waste." Create the pull first, then spend on channels to speed it up.
- Seed money can come from outside the VC industry, for example friends of your parents who think you are smart, as with a restaurant.
- Raising can make sense when the metrics are exceptional. He cites Fixer, a UK email company with 155% net revenue retention, a working Meta funnel, strong CAC/LTV and a very large TAM.
- The danger he describes: venture investors hold a portfolio and care about it, not about you. They expect you to "grow forever" until someone acquires you at roughly 3x or more.
- Many founders who raise do not have Fixer-like metrics. He says a hyper-efficient company without that capital has a better quality of life and a higher chance of success, with a harder start and a much less stressful later stage.
- His Klaviyo example (from a conversation with its founder): the success depended on factors the founders could not have foreseen. They tied themselves to Shopify when it was a $50M valuation (now $150B), picked the SMB space with real net revenue retention (e-commerce email priced on list size), and benefited from a Mailchimp opt-out controversy. He says most peers who raised at that time failed.

chunks.heading: Keeping the team lean
chunks.text:
- He advertises clearly that the company is "highly profitable, super capital efficient." That attracts scrappy, lean people.
- Some founders are wired the opposite way. He mentions his mentor Brett Hurt, who would scale an ice cream stand globally. He notes that approach worked for Hurt but that Hurt began his career when what Adam does was not possible.

chunks.heading: Pricing and positioning for his new product (Moltsets)
chunks.text:
- The product is a contact database positioned for autonomous agents and Claude Code users, who might otherwise use Clay only to build lists and enrich emails and phone numbers.
- Planned pricing: fully unlimited tiers at $19, $199 and $999, with API rate limits as the only difference. He hopes to get "5,000 people pay me 200 bucks a month."
- The offer is meant to be disruptive on price because his marketing leverage keeps customer acquisition cost low. As with RB2B, his database is already paid for, so there is "no incremental cost of fulfilling" a subscription.
- Go-to-market plan:
  - UGC and influencer content with creators in the same ecosystem.
  - A weekly workshop called "Claude did what? B2B experts share Claude skills that you can deploy today," which does not need to involve his product. The aim is to aggregate attention around the Claude Code for go-to-market mechanism and become the "make my face equivalent to Claude skills for go-to-market."
  - His recent Claude Code show drew about 900 live attendees, which he reads as strong demand.
- He admits low conviction on this one ("the least conviction I've had since I knew what I was doing"), but sees idea-to-launch in about 5 weeks and extra upside: LinkedIn content helps all his products at once, and success would also help RB2B.

chunks.heading: Content as the distribution engine
chunks.text:
- It took about a year to find his voice. He tried Shopify-store content with a ghostwriter, then worked with a LinkedIn consultant (Alec) and switched to writing exclusively about B2B SaaS, with unusual transparency.
- Routine: Tuesdays are for content, about 4 hours a week on LinkedIn (about a day including other channels). An hour-long strategy call produces five post ideas with hooks and main points, then he writes them in a block of roughly 90 minutes later in the week.
- Channel roles: LinkedIn and Twitter for awareness, newsletter for trust. He estimates about 90% of the value comes from LinkedIn. He admits he is weak at capturing audience into the newsletter.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Adam argues that a lean, profitable bootstrapped business beats the VC treadmill, and explains how a founder-led LinkedIn brand plus a novel product took RB2B to about $5M ARR with a handful of people. He also says SDR-style outbound has lost its arbitrage while thought leadership and real-world events gain power.

chunks.heading: Why Adam argues bootstrapping beats the VC treadmill
chunks.text:
- Adam says he knows many founders who raised VC, few who exited, fewer who took large secondary rounds, and a handful who took small ones. Those small-secondary founders "have great businesses" but have pulled out only a few million dollars.
- His view: "if you have a great business, you should make millions of dollars every year. In every other market in the world, you do."
- He describes a middle path between the tiny lifestyle business (uninspiring) and the IPO dream (statistically hard outside killer enterprise SaaS): a lean company that stalls at a ceiling but throws off cash.
- The idea came in 2017, when his company was stuck at $3M. He heard about a sole founder in the email newsletter space who grew to $30M ARR, stalled, and was "banking $20 million every year." To Adam that seemed easier than building something that grows indefinitely and IPOs.
- He says none of his businesses have had net revenue expansion. Natural churn stalls them at a certain size, so he sizes the goal around that ceiling.
- Cash flow means no pressure to sell. He pays off his mortgage and sets his family up financially without selling anything, and "it's better if I don't."
- Even on the venture track, he says, the path "is probably taking you a decade anyway and it's probably not going to work out for you."
- His pitch to founders at $3M ARR facing an $8M offer: taking it likely ends any future as a profitable dividend-paying company. If you hold out a couple of years, the outcome he is living may be available instead.
- When people say he isn't a "real" bootstrapper, he answers: "I have 30 million AR company that has 40 people. I'm a bootstrapper."

chunks.heading: The word-of-mouth rule and how Adam gets air cover on top of it
chunks.text:
- Core belief: "without word of mouth, nothing else that you do will work. With word of mouth, there's a million things you can do to speed it up."
- Both Retention.com (formerly Get Emails) and RB2B launched with a novel product. In the Retention.com market, nobody had heard you could get an email from a website visitor who didn't fill out a form.
- RB2B's pricing was novel too: the product was free at launch.
- He treats marketing as "air cover" that accelerates word of mouth:
  - For Retention.com it was funny ~60-second Facebook ads with Adam and his wife. They answered the sales objection, and viewers looked forward to the next one. "If they were looking forward to your ads, you won the game."
  - For RB2B it is his LinkedIn founder brand.
- He says he will try anything, and "the crazier it is the better." He stops when something stops working, and says he doesn't know if the Facebook approach would work again.

chunks.heading: The Facebook ad experiment for Retention.com
chunks.text:
- Facebook B2B normally brings bad customers: would-be entrepreneurs with about 20% monthly churn.
- Adam's product-led setup let customers click their way to a $5,000/month plan. Roughly once every week or two, a "whale" bought a $5,000 plan without talking to sales, and that paid for the prior weeks of ads.
- It worked for about 6 months. As he scaled spend it got less effective.
- Eight weeks passed, about $40K of spend, and no big customers, only the high-churn small ones. He stopped.
- Even so, the ads made his cold email work better. Signups would say "I saw the ads" whether or not they clicked, and without them growth would have been much slower.

chunks.heading: Why founder-led LinkedIn is brand marketing that works at zero revenue
chunks.text:
- Adam says the only brand marketing that works for a zero-revenue startup is the thought-leadership type he does on LinkedIn.
- Conventional brand marketing, like trade show spend, is expensive and reinforces a brand already in people's minds. He says a $1M trade show spend a year ago would not have left anyone remembering RB2B.
- The same applies to DTC: category thought leadership from an influencer-style individual works there too.
- Trust built this way is much deeper than paid ads: "if you've read like 50 of my posts and you're just like man this guy's got it figured out."
- It can't be tied to metrics short term. He can't say whether December's program beat November's or trace it to trial signups, but over 12 months "it's been epic."
- Audience came before product at RB2B. After a big July B2B post about downsizing his sales force, he asked his LinkedIn consultant Alec whether he should spend a month writing about the BDR problem and other sales issues SaaS companies had in 2023.
  - He wrote three posts on a Friday and they got about 100x the engagement of his Shopify-store content.
  - Only then did he decide to build a product for those readers.
- He steers who reads a post by topic: ABM draws VPs of marketing, zero-to-one and bootstrapping draws early-stage founders, and he knows what draws salespeople.
- He predicts more B2B startups will use thought leadership in 5 years, rising at the same rate as email sends.
- Product-led growth plus an influencer profile may not reach $100M ARR, but "it is a super efficient way to create a very nice business." At the time RB2B was nearly $5M ARR without five people working on it.
- Top creators don't take attention from each other. The best "push the average people down" and authentic voices can't be copied: "you couldn't copy my stuff. It wouldn't work for you."

chunks.heading: Choosing an ICP and writing for it: write to your earlier self
chunks.text:
- Easiest starting point: write to yourself from five years ago. He was stuck for 3 years before Retention.com, "I just know the pain," and says that version of him "would have killed for" content like his, since few people at his stage were writing it.
- He tried writing for Shopify store owners for about 12 months and never resolved why they'd read him over someone who builds landing pages for ecom brands daily. When he switched to B2B go-to-market, it "just exploded."
- Reason: he is a go-to-market leader who runs marketing daily and "got kicked in the nuts like everyone did in 2023," so he speaks from lived experience. He didn't feel that with ecom owners complaining about Meta flagging unsubstantiated claims.
- Lessons he cites from that period:
  - Hiring more BDRs when growth is slow doesn't fix it.
  - "You got to grow the brand first, then the marketing machine, then you can start adding BDRs" to capture the demand.
- If you are your own ICP, start by writing to an earlier version of yourself. That also helps with imposter syndrome.
- He thinks a follower copying his build-in-public approach is still worth doing, since a body of work over a long journey becomes valuable, but at 12 months it is less magnetic because the journey is shorter. His own count: about 50,000 followers a year earlier, 120,000 now.
- Storytelling beats detail: "If I stopped entertaining, zero. If I stopped teaching, zero. It's like 50/50."

chunks.heading: How Adam writes a LinkedIn post
chunks.text:
- A writer's goal: write a sentence so the reader feels exactly what the writer felt writing it.
- Hook: written so the reader has to click "see more."
- Structure: a mini hero's journey. Articulate the pain, agitate it, then give a takeaway that resolves it.
- Ending: a "koi little play on words" or something pithy for a dopamine hit. Example from a post about Clay: "unicorns are built one call at a time."
- On AI: he's open to testing it, but says his lived perspective is what makes the content valuable and AI can't replicate it. It helps the best builders move faster, but the average engineer just ships crap faster.
- On a book: he won't write one until he can commit the energy, citing how much work Alex Hormozi puts into his.

chunks.heading: Why outbound and the "predictable revenue" model stopped working
chunks.text:
- He calls it the predictable revenue model: put university grads in seats typing keys and clicking a mouse to create demos. "When there were 10 and 100 companies doing that, it worked beautifully. When there was 100,000 companies doing that same thing, that's just not the arbitrage anymore."
- Supply and demand flipped. More email will be sent in 2026 than in 2025, and AI SDR tools like 11x and Artisan are "just spam cannons." "The world doesn't want a robot to spam."
- The usual response to lower effectiveness is higher volume, which makes the problem worse.
- Deliverability: five years ago he used the primary domain with five people in the Philippines doing manual lead gen half the day and manual sends from five inboxes the other half. "You can't do that now... your domain will get torched." Getting cold email delivered is 100 steps now and may be a thousand next year. Those who master it still win.
- SDR/BDR headcount grew exponentially over the last decade and is now shrinking.
- What he is constructive on: owned events and real-world experiences.
  - Retention.com's only outreach is a target list of about 1,000 brands. They find people who know those contacts and build an experience good enough that the targets attend.
  - Example: a box at a Taylor Swift concert, so good that the Foot Locker CMO didn't believe the invite was real until Diana messaged her from LinkedIn.
  - Trade shows still thrive for the same reason.
- If your motion is a million-dollar deal after a sports game, it works. But the question is how you reach that person, and his answer is usually through someone you both know.

chunks.heading: The lean-team philosophy: spend only when it's clearly working
chunks.text:
- He attributes running a $30M-ARR company with 40 people to a bootstrapper's attitude about spending: scale something up only once you're sure it works, versus the venture approach of "run 10 large experiments this quarter."
- Example: he and a Clay founder both use an SEO agency. Clay's founder isn't sure it's working but, after raising $90M, paying $20K a month "is totally fine." Adam paid $10K a month and says he needs to know it's working in a real way.
- Exception he makes for LinkedIn brand: he accepts it's only visible as working over long periods, and still funds it.
- Leverage framework: Clay might get 90% of growth from one high-leverage channel and layer 15 others for the last 10%, which can be worth it for them.
