A bootstrapper only does things where 80/20 is in their favor, "where we have not seen the diminishing returns yet," and would "rather sacrifice growth than see diminishing returns."
- Culture: his team all think and act this way, and are proud of it.
- Benchmark he showed at a team offsite in Mexico: companies at $1M ARR with as many people as his, then companies at $30M ARR, where the smallest team was about 140 people. Hardly anyone keeps $750K to $1M of revenue per head as they scale, though they're doing it the venture way, so it's not a fair comparison.
- He says few bootstrapped companies reach $25M-$30M because investors get in early and put founders on a track many shouldn't be on.

chunks.heading: RB2B funnel: product-led to sales-assisted, and the plan for outbound
chunks.text:
- Year one (RB2B turned a year old in 11 days from the interview): customers signed up and used it on their own. The workflow they pushed, "put a human being in front of this noisy Slack channel," wasn't great.
- They also told people to use the leads to book demos, which he no longer believes is the value of the signal.
- Current hypothesis: run the signal through the CRM and alert reps via CRM workflows:
  - add it to lead score;
  - send it to a Slack channel for a target account;
  - start automated outreach from the CRM.
- That fits customers with reps, a CRM and a target account list, so it needs human onboarding. He has one salesperson now and will probably add another, calling it sales-assisted PLG.
- Next step: outbound off his LinkedIn profile to sell a 30K-50K a year improved suite to a defined buyer persona, starting with frequent content engagers. Those lists can be pulled with tools.
- He thinks the same signal motion works for a sales-led business as for PLG.

chunks.heading: Courses, community and education as a funnel
chunks.text:
- Last year he got excited by Russell Brunson, who bundled education on growing an internet business with the ClickFunnels platform fee. He tried a webinar-style sale.
- The problem was ICP mismatch: his paying software customers are marketers at roughly $10M ARR and above, while his content audience is zero-to-three-stage SaaS founders. Russell's overlap was about 100%; his is partial.
- Marketers either like or hate his content; founders mostly see him as who they want to be in five years.
- Belief from that experience: startup content makes founders do things before product-market fit that they shouldn't (cold email, ads). Unless you get word of mouth, "the only way to get to word of mouth is to get in a proper customer discovery loop and it's super manual."
- So he is starting a community and premium funnel around the message that you're wasting time and money on anything other than talking to prospects and customers until you have word of mouth, plus a network for lonely founders.
- It's a separate product line, a "sideshow" not directly feeding the SaaS, and he put his head of growth, Pete, in charge.
- Closing line: "edutainment is the secret weapon for growing a B2B company. There's no doubt."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Adam Robinson, who has scaled three SaaS companies to 35M combined ARR, walks through eight marketing strategies he uses at RB2B: founder brand, inbound-led outbound, cold email, LinkedIn DMs, paid ads as an accelerator, UGC, and word of mouth. His core argument is that product-market fit and word of mouth come first, and every other tactic only works well once you have them.

chunks.heading: Founder brand content as a distribution engine
chunks.text:
Adam says a founder who isn't building a personal brand is "leaving millions on the table". His LinkedIn audience helped scale RB2B from zero to $1M ARR in six weeks.

- **Common mistakes:** sounding like a big professional company, sharing only wins, and avoiding vulnerability out of fear of competitors.
- **What he does instead:**
  - Be clear about who you are. His identity is "a bootstrapped SaaS founder who builds in public".
  - Stay consistent on that identity across every piece of content.
  - Be vulnerable and authentic in ways big companies can't. He calls that the competitive advantage.
- **His breakthrough came from a public failure.** In 2023 he predicted on LinkedIn that retention.com would triple revenue from $15M to $45M ARR. It grew only about 40%, and he had to fire his entire BDR team after outbound crashed. He shared all of it. Other founders were going through the same struggle but nobody was talking about it, which gave him his most engaged audience.
- **Leverage:** each post reaches at least 50,000 people, sometimes 100,000 or more, and his videos get thousands of views. This drives thousands of inbound leads a month to RB2B at no cost except his time.

chunks.heading: Inbound-led outbound: following up with website visitors
chunks.text:
Adam says this hybrid took RB2B from zero to $1M ARR in six weeks. Traditional cold outreach gets less effective every day, so he combines inbound and outbound.

1. Drive traffic to your site through content, podcasts and partnerships.
2. Use RB2B to identify which visitors fit your ideal customer profile.
3. Follow up with them the way you would with cold prospects. They aren't cold anymore, because they've already shown intent by visiting.

He reports conversion rates 10 times higher than traditional cold outreach, and time spent on high-intent prospects instead of a wide net.

**Cold email workflow for these visitors:**
1. Install RB2B to identify anonymous visitors.
2. Connect RB2B to Clay to enrich and process the data.
3. Use Clay's AI to write a personalized email for each visitor.
4. Push everything to Instantly or Smartlead and send with domain rotation.

He says campaigns like this convert at over 10%. The same list also works for LinkedIn connection requests, where acceptance and response rates are "through the roof" because people just visited your site.

chunks.heading: Cold email at scale: lists, verification, domains and copy
chunks.text:
Adam says outbound still works if you have the right list. RB2B sends over 200,000 cold emails a month.

**List building**
- Pull from five or six data providers, not one, because coverage differs and you want to cover your total addressable market.
- B2B leads: Apollo, Instantly, Clearbit-style tools such as ZoomInfo, ListKit, Seamless AI, LinkedIn Sales Navigator, UpLead, Wiza, Lead411.
- Vertical-specific B2B: Ocean.io and Adapt.
- Venture: Crunchbase and PitchBook.
- E-commerce: StoreLeads and Weo.
- Local businesses: D7, Leadfinder, Lead Scrape.
- Always validate emails with NeverBounce or LeadMagic. Invalid emails "will absolutely destroy" deliverability, and he calls this non-negotiable.

**Sending infrastructure**
- Tools: Instantly and Smartlead. Both work, and the team switches depending on the moment.
- Inbox rotation across hundreds of domains.
- Don't send from the main domain. Use variants like try-, the-real-, get- prefixes on rb2b.com. Buy the domains through Instantly or Smartlead.
- Create two inboxes per domain and send 2 to 10 emails a day from each. He says this gets past Gmail and Outlook spam filters.
- Keep volume high but list quality high, with multiple verification steps on every email.

**Messaging**
- Short and punchy, no corporate speak, direct benefit in the first line, one simple call to action.
- One of his best performers: "We launched a tool that lets you know when individuals, not companies, visit your site. We send you their LinkedIn profile in Slack, and we don't charge you a dime. Respond back with yes if you'd like me to send you a link to sign up."

chunks.heading: LinkedIn outbound: connect, value, follow-up
chunks.text:
Adam calls LinkedIn outbound one of the most underutilized strategies. Connection requests with no message get high acceptance rates, and once accepted the person starts seeing your content in their feed.

- **Automation:** HeyReach or La Growth Machine.
- **Volume:** 10 to 20 connection requests a day to people in your ICP. More than that risks a LinkedIn ban.
- **Sequence:** connect, then value, then follow-up.

**Step 1: connection request.** One relevant sentence, no pitch, no links. The goal is the connection, not a meeting. Example: "I saw you're hiring two SDRs. I work on making new reps' first 30 days easier. I'm happy to share what's working."

**Step 2: value message after acceptance.** Something simple they can act on today. Example: "Thanks for connecting. If you want to close the loop on ABM, try identifying site visitors at the person level rather than the company level. I can show you how to set it up if it's helpful."

**Step 3: follow-up drip using the rule of three.** Send three messages, then stop.
- Message 1: a quick reminder.
- Message 2: a concrete offer, such as a template, the copy he used, and the signup link.
- Message 3: the final ask or close, such as "Do you want person level ID or should I close this thread?"

He says it works because there are no attachments, no walls of text and no fake urgency.

chunks.heading: Paid ads as an accelerator, with the creative formula
chunks.text:
Adam says paid ads "still work, but they're not a growth machine anymore". They are an accelerator, not the foundation, and other channels must be working first.

**How he uses them**
- Retargeting on LinkedIn, Meta, Google and Twitter. Install each platform's retargeting pixel and stay in front of people who already engaged.
- Matched-audience ads to ABM lists: upload the list built from Apollo or ZoomInfo and run ads directly to decision makers at target accounts. Works on LinkedIn, Meta, Google and Twitter.
- Lookalike audiences from your paying customer list, uploaded to Meta and Google.

**Creative script:** Russell Brunson's who, what, why, how.
- Who: "Hi, I'm Adam Robinson, the founder of RB2B."
- What: "We identify your anonymous website visitors at the person level, free forever."
- Why: "You're spending money on ads, content, and outbound to drive traffic to your site. But 97% of visitors leave without taking action. You have no way to follow up with them."
- How: "Click the link below and start identifying your website visitors for free today."

**Production:** the best-performing content is authentic. He takes selfie videos on his phone, with no fancy production, actors or agencies, talking into the camera about a real problem and how the product solves it.

chunks.heading: User-generated content and creator communities
chunks.text:
Adam calls UGC "the current superpower in marketing". It is authentic, free or very cheap, builds trust branded content can't, scales beyond paid marketing, and the best pieces can become ads.

- **B2C:** focus on volume, with thousands of pieces.
- **B2B:** focus on community, with deep relationships with fewer creators.

**RB2B's B2B program**
- They work closely with Clay agencies that use the product.
- It is run by one person on the team, who tracks mentions and stays in touch with creators.
- Incentives:
  - Recognition as market leaders. These are usually agencies growing their own business, so visibility matters to them.
  - Access to other business owners and the internal team. Their network strength equals their business strength.
  - Revenue through the partner program, which pays 20% commission for life on anyone they send.
  - Physical perks like custom figurines with their face on them. He says Clay is the best in the world at sending gifts that make people feel special.

**Key lesson:** people don't create content because they care about your company, they do it to grow their own business. Align incentives with theirs: "Help them make more money and they'll create content for you forever."

**Growth loop:** users post about RB2B on LinkedIn, the content drives traffic, RB2B identifies those visitors and converts them to customers, and the new customers create more content.

If the product doesn't naturally generate content, build content creation into the product or offer something free that people want to share. Make it "stupid simple" to create and share.

chunks.heading: Word of mouth and product-market fit come first
chunks.text:
Adam says word of mouth is the hardest channel to get but "the only thing that actually matters". With it, everything else works. Without it, "nothing you do will work". It can't be bought, faked or forced. It comes only from product-market fit.

- **Definition:** the perfect product for the perfect group of buyers at the perfect time. Strong fit builds a massive company. Weak fit means a decades-long grind.
- **Common mistake:** adding paying customers and starting to growth hack with ads, SEO, influencers and newsletter sponsorships. None of it works without word of mouth.
- **His rule:** do things that don't scale. Until you have verifiable product-market fit, skip ads, SEO, influencers and partnership programs. Talk to users one-on-one yourself and build fast feedback loops that iterate on the product.

**Signs you have product-market fit**
- Very strong word of mouth and high retention.
- Doing nothing would still produce exponential organic growth.
- People will prepay even though the product isn't built yet.
- It feels like the market is pulling the product out of you.
- Customers would be livid if you took it away, and cash is piling up in the bank.

He says it takes longer than you think. Getting impatient and growth hacking too early "dooms" you to a mediocre business, and once you have fit, the other marketing strategies work much better.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Adam breaks down the lean outbound machine behind $13M ARR with six employees: a $3k/month Philippines team manually building target lists, a four-email sequence, a three-step LinkedIn flow, and ads to the same list. He also says what he would change today (multiple domains, sequencers, LinkedIn content) and why the 2020-21 conditions mattered.

chunks.heading: Manual list building beat database platforms at Get Emails
chunks.text:
Adam scaled his SaaS Get Emails (retention.com) from zero to $13M ARR in 36 months with six employees. He did it with a lean, manual list-building operation run by five people in the Philippines for less than $3,000 a month.

- His co-founder Diana saw that most companies bought Apollo or ZoomInfo and blasted automated emails.
- Everyone else uses the same databases and the same addresses, so "those email addresses get absolutely smashed." Open and reply rates are poor because you compete with every company hitting the same prospects.
- Manually researched contacts were fresh and not hammered daily. Adam says this produced meetings at about 10x the conversion rate.
- This worked in 2020 and 2021.

chunks.heading: The four-step manual list-building process
chunks.text:
1. **Pick target companies.** Use BuiltWith to find companies running complementary or competitor software. For Get Emails that meant Shopify stores using Klaviyo for email or Attentive for SMS. Verify traffic with SimilarWeb. The sweet spot was Shopify Plus customers with over 10,000 monthly unique visitors.
2. **Find 3-5 people per company.** Use LinkedIn Sales Navigator. Always include the CEO, plus the VP Marketing, head of e-commerce, email marketing manager and director of growth. Copy all of them on the same email to raise the chance of an open.
3. **Find emails manually.** Find the person on LinkedIn first, then look up the address in Scrap.io, then Hunter.io if Scrap has nothing. If neither has it, move on. Adam says this two-tool check gave much better deliverability than Apollo alone.
4. **Send manually.** Every email in 2020-2021 was sent one by one from individual Gmail accounts, by humans, under several sender names (for example the head of sales and a sales assistant) with multiple address variations. "Our emails looked completely human because they were completely human."

chunks.heading: The 4-email sequence
chunks.text:
- **Email 1, direct value prop.** First name, then the product line: Get Emails identifies up to 35% of anonymous site visitors and gives you their email addresses. Cite customer results ("Vital Proteins sees a 9.25x+ ROI") with a case study link, and a calendar link for a 10-minute intro.
- **Email 2, gentle reminder.** Bump the first email, ask for a short intro, and mention capturing more first-party data. Calendar link again.
- **Email 3, problem agitator.** Shoppers show purchase intent and leave without identifying themselves. With recent Apple updates "you may never get them back." Repeat the 35% claim, note it is CAN-SPAM and CCPA compliant, and repeat the case study.
- **Email 4, final summary.** Recap who it helps (Shopify Plus customers), say the addresses are verified as engaged and deliverable with open rates matching the in-house list, and offer a trial discussion.
- **Timing:** first email, follow up 3-5 days later, then a third email a week after that.

chunks.heading: Team structure and management philosophy
chunks.text:
- Five people in the Philippines: a team leader (Jim) at $1,000/month and four team members at $500/month each. Total about $3,000/month.
- Jim hired his wife, his friends and his friends' cousins.
- Shifts: 8pm-midnight Eastern for lead generation, 8am-noon Eastern for prospecting.
- A US BDR at the time cost $50-70K a year plus benefits. Adam spent about $36,000 a year for what would have cost around $300,000 in the US.
- Philosophy: "We loaded them up with activity, not problems to solve." No complex decisions, and the process was fully repeatable (find companies in BuiltWith, identify 3-5 people on LinkedIn, find emails with Scrap and Hunter, send email 1, follow up, send email 3). They worked from home and set their own hours within the shift windows.

chunks.heading: LinkedIn outreach: connect, value, follow-up
chunks.text:
The same list was worked on LinkedIn at the same time as email, so prospects got both together. Connection requests without a message got very high acceptance rates, and once accepted, prospects start seeing your content in their feed.

1. **Connection request:** one sentence about something relevant, no pitch, no links. Example: "saw you're using Klaviyo for email capture. You want to collect 10 times more emails from your site visitors." The goal is the connection, not a meeting.
2. **Value message after acceptance:** something simple they can act on today. Example: offer to get email addresses of anonymous website visitors who don't fill out a form.
3. **Follow-up drip using the "rule of three":** three messages, then stop.
   - Message 1: a quick reminder.
   - Message 2: a concrete offer, such as sending the template and copy.
   - Message 3: a final ask or close ("This is the last note from me").

Why it works: no attachments, no walls of text, no fake urgency.

chunks.heading: ABM ads layered on top of outreach
chunks.text:
- Upload the target list to Facebook and Google so prospects see ads while also getting email and LinkedIn messages. This created the impression that Get Emails was "absolutely everywhere."
- Also ran ads to lookalike audiences of the core list, and retargeting ads to all site visitors.
- Also emailed those site visitors using addresses captured by the Get Emails product itself.
- **Ad script:** Russell Brunson's Who, What, Why, How. Who you are ("I'm Adam Robinson, founder of Get Emails"), what you have (identify 35% of anonymous visitors), why they need it (97% of visitors leave without filling out a form), how to get it (click the link).
- **Creative style:** authentic. Adam took selfie videos on his phone, talking to the camera about a real problem and how the product solves it. No actors, no agencies, no production.

chunks.heading: Why it worked in 2020-21, and what he'd change today
chunks.text:
Conditions that made it work:
- Strong product-market fit. "If you don't have word of mouth... this will not save you," but with PMF, high-volume outbound can speed you up significantly.
- Shopify Plus buyers were responsive to cold email in 2021-2022. Response rates are much lower now, so the strategy would be harder.
- Senior employees wore multiple hats. His head of sales managed the Philippines team, closed deals and refined messaging.

What he'd do differently today:
- Still build lists manually, because database platforms are even more saturated now.
- Don't send from the primary domain. They never had major deliverability problems sending from getemails.com, but he calls that luck. Use multiple sending domains to protect the brand domain.
- Use Instantly or Smartlead instead of manual sending. Tech has improved enough to automate while keeping a human feel, and "the edge you're going to get from using humans to send is just not there today."
- Create organic LinkedIn content. A personal brand multiplies every other channel: prospects see your content, your ad, your email and your DM.
- Install RB2B on the website to identify visitors from your ICP and push their LinkedIn profiles to Slack, then add them to outreach immediately. Adam calls these the warmest leads because they are already researching and visited the site.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Adam tells the years-long backstory behind RB2B: a stuck email app, a feature customers loved, and a pivot found through LinkedIn posts. He covers validating demand with 300 discovery calls, a free Slack integration, pricing mistakes, founder-brand distribution, radical transparency, and keeping the team tiny.

chunks.heading: Retention.com: from a stuck newsletter app to 13M ARR with six people
chunks.text:
- Adam's first startup, Robbley Email Marketing, stalled at $3M ARR in a space Mailchimp dominated.
- He cites the "22 Immutable Laws of Marketing" idea that a player with over 60% share must be outspent about 3 to 1. His read: if 7 of 10 people in a room use a product, you use it too.
- He then spent about two years on catastrophic bets:
  - Rebuilding an entirely new product in a market with 10 vendors, without proper customer discovery. It cost a year and $1M, and he deleted the code.
  - Taking over an "authorized local expert" program from Constant Contact. The unit economics didn't work for a small startup, he shut it off, and Constant Contact sued him.
- The pivot came from a feature. He learned it was possible to identify an anonymous website visitor and tie them to a deliverable email, and white-labeled it inside the newsletter app.
- Customers loved the identity feature but wouldn't use the newsletter app. They downloaded the file and loaded it into Klaviyo. That was his product-market-fit signal.
- He spun the feature out as Get Emails (now Retention.com). On Nov 9, 2019 he launched with a Word Art video made on Upwork using DigitalMarketer's video-sales-letter template, recorded on an iPhone. He put $5,000 of ad spend behind it and reached $10K MRR in three weeks.
- Facebook ads gave "air cover": cold email replies said "I've seen the Facebook ads, I'll do a demo." The ads stopped working after about 6 months.
- Retention.com launched with 6 people and had the same 6 at $13M ARR:
  - Adam on marketing, plus a product and support pod with Tate (CTO) and a support/product teammate.
  - Diana on sales, with a sales assistant on every call and an onboarding person.

chunks.heading: The ICP, churn and defensibility mistakes before RB2B
chunks.text:
- Get Emails was a high-churn PLG product. Adam didn't find an ICP until about 3.5 years in, and didn't realize ecommerce was the best fit until about 2 years in.
- The signal: big Shopify merchants kept sending friends, never asked to be paid, and never cancelled. So the team gave demos only to big Shopify merchants.
- His plan was to add features, get Klaviyo-like stickiness and expand revenue.
- Context: he had watched Jasper go from stuck to unicorn while renting a desk in their office, and thought he could do the same.
- He hired heavily, and every week his expectations rose.
- He misjudged the market. In Dec 2022 he thought there were 50,000 stores to sell a $50K deal in 7 days at an 80% close rate. In reality there were about 1,500 stores for a $20K deal in 30 days, at a still-high 60 to 70% close rate.
- Churn never got solved.
- Pricing mistake: he put customers paying $10K to $20K per month on $5K, planning to raise it to $10K the next year. By then six competitors were offering $2K deals, even though customer ROI was around 50x.
- Defensibility lesson: there was no network effect, and he oversold those customers.

chunks.heading: How LinkedIn content turned into the RB2B opportunity
chunks.text:
- In July 2023 the VP of Sales quit. Adam cut the team from 20 reps to 4 and didn't replace the VP, believing outbound no longer worked and the brand was what pulled in demand.
- He wrote a post about it that got about 30x his normal engagement. People then asked "how's it going?" and he said it was "moving faster."
- A follow-up post on BDRs got hundreds of times more engagement, with thousands of likes.
- He took this to his co-founder and pitched pivoting his content brand from Shopify merchants to B2B SaaS, splitting 50/50. He kept tweeting for Shopify and wrote for LinkedIn on B2B.
- Test of the hypothesis: he wrote three more posts for B2B revenue leaders on three different topics. Each got 2,500 to 3,000 likes within 24 hours. Had they flopped, he would have concluded he didn't understand LinkedIn.
- Santosh, a B2B veteran (Apollo, ZoomInfo), had pushed him for a long time to build a B2B product. The first attempt in 2022 had failed. It was personal emails for business use, and Adam removed it from the site.
- Adam started posting about account-based marketing (ABM), 6sense and demand-based marketing, with a footer line along the lines of "DM me if you want to close the loop on ABM and get website identity at the person level." Hundreds of people wrote in.
- Between Oct 2023 and Mar 2024 (launch), he and Santosh ran about 300 discovery calls. They built a 2,000 to 3,000 person waitlist.
- He calls this "the most unfair marketing advantage you could possibly have." The reach was bigger than the unicorns in the space, and it was exactly the people they wanted to sell to, before there was a product.

chunks.heading: Discovery and validating RB2B before and while building
chunks.text:
- Discovery was aimed at ABM practitioners, mostly senior marketers. The questions were about the existing workflow:
  - How are you using website identity right now?
  - How does that information get to your reps?
  - What do they complain about?
- Every time, people said they wanted to know who the person was. He treats the complaints about the current process as the validation, not "do you like this product."
- Early test: they mailed spreadsheets of data and tried to charge $495 a month. Nobody bought it, though a couple of people said they'd pay $99.
- They then pushed the data into Slack. Adding an actual headshot and LinkedIn URL created a "magic moment." Adam would pull out his phone at parties and say "these people are on my website right now."
- He had planned to charge for integrations. His CTO Tate, normally the one who wants to charge for everything, argued the Slack integration should be free if he wanted it to go viral, because that was the magic moment.
- Takeaway: free doesn't mean giving away everything. Give away the part that makes people feel the value.
- V1 was a Slack integration, a PLG signup flow that worked end to end, and a basic dashboard. He knew it was differentiated because it was first to market.

chunks.heading: RB2B pricing: what failed and what worked
chunks.text:
- Inspiration: Built With, which he calls the coolest product pricing (about one person to roughly $20M ARR). His first idea was free unlimited, then $495 with integrations.
- It confused buyers (why pay $495 if $295 works?), and the jump was too big. People could also back-door the contacts through Zapier or just parse the Slack block, so they didn't need the paid integrations.
- Adam posted about his pricing struggles publicly. That made buyers wait for the price to drop. It still dragged on for about 6 weeks.
- What worked: a $99 entry point, credit-based. The final shape:
  - Free tier with the Slack integration.
  - Contacts capped at 150 before paying.
- Free-to-paid conversion has been about 10 to 12% ever since.
- He dislikes credit-based pricing but doesn't know how to do value-based pricing here. The product is most valuable for companies with high-value deals, who generally have low traffic. A company selling a $19 product with huge traffic pays a lot and gets less value. Someone with 100 uniques a month selling $10M deals pays little and gets enormous value.
- Lesson: if the jump from free to paid is too big, few people jump. If there's no usage limit or key feature that makes them want to, it's hard to pull off.

chunks.heading: Channels, transparency and moats
chunks.text:
- Channels at RB2B: LinkedIn organic (his estimate is about 95% of the result), cold email ("pirate" style, multiple domains), LinkedIn ads promoting thought-leadership posts, and a UGC program.
- His view on the extras: he couldn't tell whether cold email mattered, and the ads were not clearly better than organic. He cut them at the end of 2024.
- UGC program:
  - Pete cultivated a community of Clay agency people who posted regularly.
  - They benefited from the exposure.
  - Adam would feature one of their posts in his own feed.
- He added his co-founder Santosh as a character in the content, and planned to add Diana (sales co-founder, the only rep on two $0 to $10M journeys) for the sales-facing V2.
- Pause on growth: he stopped growth spending at RB2B until the product is fixed. He says he sees deep flaws, such as an expected 10-month LTV, and doesn't want to burn leads. He says he can afford that clarity because the company is profitable. A venture-backed company would be told to 10x and ignore churn.
- Why he builds in public:
  - The product category triggers red flags (how is that legal?), so total transparency builds trust.
  - He would have wanted this information himself when stuck at $3M.
  - Money details spread on social media.
- RB2B metrics are public at rb2b.bearmetrics.com.
- Downside: competitors. One person copied his content playbook and added AI, aggregating identity tools into an AI SDR. Adam says it won't work. He thinks competitors will exist regardless, and a copycat only takes a small share from the trusted, best-known brand.
- Moats he lists:
  - Founder brand.
  - Distribution.
  - Data. The plan is a premium product that sits on top of a salesperson's inbox, with hundreds of thousands of users opting into a data co-op. Examples: "did this contact sit in a sales demo in the last 7 days" (5 out of 5), "responds to email at this address" (3 out of 5), unknown (1 out of 5).
- Honest take: if the next version has no network effects, RB2B might add roughly another $5M ARR. If it's stickier, maybe $10M to $15M.
- If RB2B reaches $20M ARR with his lean approach, he calls that doing great.

chunks.heading: Staying small and removing sales friction
chunks.text:
- Adam's rule: don't hire until the company is above 10 people. He wants to reach $10M ARR on the current team (RB2B reached $5M ARR with five people).
- Small teams force focus. People wear many hats, and there's no one inventing goals.
- Owner-operator reality: he says it isn't realistic to be the owner who lets operators run everything. He enjoys doing a lot himself, like rewriting all the website copy in a day rather than coordinating five team members.
- Sales and onboarding friction:
  - RB2B: free trial, no credit card, no payment. The trial started as free forever, then 30 days, then 7 days. People get the full value first, and calls happen only when they have questions. He is still unsure where sales fits.
  - Get Emails: 25 emails for free. Higher-traffic accounts were locked until they took a roughly 5-minute call with Diana, who answered the same questions every customer asked. She then put them on a 60-day paid trial at a smaller volume than they needed, and they either cancelled or upgraded. She could do about 15 of these a day.
- Reference point he mentions: UserFlow with three people sold for $60M, so a small team doesn't hurt exit potential.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Adam describes his journey from failed email products to a free, plg tool (RB2B), and why personal-brand distribution beats outbound. He covers category creation, a weekly LinkedIn/Zoom event as a feedback loop, word of mouth as a prerequisite, and why outbound response rates are collapsing.

chunks.heading: Positioning and category creation for a bootstrapped SaaS
chunks.text:
- Adam says a founder must be able to fill in a statement of value card: "Company X helps group Y do Z." He learned this from Ryan Deiss's DigitalMarketer course around 2015-16.
- In his first email product he could not explain why customers should pay $45 a month instead of using MailChimp, which was free. That started a multi-year search for what MailChimp wasn't doing.
- He says it helps to coin a category even if it isn't fully real. For RB2B he coined "inbound-led outbound", meaning you bring visitors back to your site and use retargeting, with RB2B as the novel retargeting method.
- His first workshop was titled "What is inbound-led outbound", inspired by Chris Walker.
- He thinks the right move is to join a new workflow people aren't yet doing rather than compete in an existing one.

chunks.heading: Why Adam gave RB2B away free
chunks.text:
- Adam credits MailChimp's free offer, and the 18,000 sign-ups a day it produced, as his inspiration. A dominant brand that is free for 90% of people makes "more free than MailChimp" impossible to beat.
- He considered a $30-50K ACV mid-market sales motion but rejected it. His reasoning: a mid-market sales operation doesn't benefit from scale advantages, while a free offer benefits a lot from a huge megaphone.
- The goal is to turn free users into the distribution engine. He wants free users to create UGC, so more free users produce more UGC, which becomes the moat. He cites Ryan Bzibzi's Jolie showerheads, which reached a $50M run rate in 18 months with a co-founder and one full-time employee. They got roughly 20,000 pieces of UGC from medium-sized influencers.
- He accepts earning less revenue than a future acquirer could: "How can I run this in the way I want to run it."
- RB2B is positioned as person-level website visitor identity, free, pushed to Slack with LinkedIn profiles of people on your website.

chunks.heading: What failed: the first free/paid split
chunks.text:
- Adam's hypothesis was that people would see leads in Slack and upgrade for $450 a month. About 6,000 sign-ups produced zero self-serve upgrades.
- The "Magic Moment" is seeing leads in Slack, so he gave it away free. The planned paid hook was charging for integrations, but anyone can parse the Slack block with Zapier or no-code tools.
- On discovery calls, willingness to pay was very high before people saw the free version. Afterwards they said they'd stick with the free plan.
- The fix he arrived at: give the free tier to about 85-90% of people but gate the contact and account data. He expects high churn but accepts it because there is zero CAC.
- He also found some Enterprise leads come inbound (roughly two or three a week, from companies of around 5,000 employees such as Rippling and MongoDB), though he says closing them is hard given the nature of the product.

chunks.heading: Using LinkedIn as a real-time product feedback loop
chunks.text:
- Adam posts detailed monthly updates, including monthly recurring revenue and P&L, and publicly shares hypotheses, including ones that don't work out. Hundreds of commenters give deep feedback and frameworks. He says this told him exactly what to change about the free/paid split.
- He used the content and inbound connection requests to run about 500 discovery calls while building the app, with one person building and the other on the phone with VP Marketing types about ABM and outbound.
- He cites the book The Four Steps to the Epiphany and the Lean Startup idea: build your buyers while building the product, because software is hard to get right. If you find out early that what you're building sucks, you quit while stakes are low.
- He says LinkedIn lets him do that at a scale the book's example (10 cold calls a day for a week yielding 5 conversations) couldn't match: about 10 conversations a day for three months, with ideal people who came to him after a soft CTA to DM.
- He values the quick feedback loop on posts. A bad post is forgotten within about three weeks.

chunks.heading: Weekly webinar as a distribution and market-research engine
chunks.text:
- Chris Walker advised Adam to create a recurring Zoom meeting scheduled through the end of the year so sign-ups land in people's calendars. Walker reportedly gets 50-200 attendees each week, does a 10-30 minute monologue, then takes questions. Adam says it helps with narrative, market temperature and finding where the pain is.
- Adam promoted his first event a couple of times and in one LinkedIn post. He had about 120 registrations and expected around 30 attendees (using a 20% show rate rule of thumb).
- About 1,300 people attended. Roughly 200 were on Zoom and about 1,100 came through LinkedIn Live, streamed via Restream, with around 200 comments.
- He credits the personal brand (his face on the promotion) rather than the company brand. A G2 VP Marketing told him their best event ever drew 200 people.
- His view: a personal brand may be 10x on any individual action, and because the effects compound, "in a year it's 10,000x."

chunks.heading: Founder-led sales and the path to distribution
chunks.text:
- Adam started as a credit default swap trader (about 10 years), then founded an email product that poached Constant Contact customers using a "BuiltWith"-style technology lookup.
- His first sales lesson: direct mail converted around 0.2% on a finite list, while cold calling a list nobody else was calling converted about 5-7%. That was roughly 40x better than direct mail, so he built a phone-sales engine.
- Once he burned through the list, he realized he needed marketing, not just sales.
- He made two big pivots that failed in consecutive years before landing on the product that became RB2B (originally called "get emails"). It began as a feature in the newsletter app. People downloaded the file and used it in Clay or MailChimp, so he spun it out and connected it to everything else.
- He says advisers split into two camps: grow the $3M ARR business that throws off about $1.5M to two co-founders, or start something new because the product isn't good enough. He ultimately thinks the second is right but landed in between.
- His rule on word of mouth: "If you don't have Word of Mouth, nothing works." Everything else amplifies it. If you have it, everything works.

chunks.heading: Outbound is declining and what to do about it
chunks.text:
- Adam scaled outbound from two BDRs to about eight and booked the same number of demos. He says that worked when money was free. After shrinking the sales squad, the culture improved and things sped up.
- His core argument: response rates are getting crushed because the world will send more email each year. He'd bet "everything I have" that 2025 sends more emails than 2024. Even the best personalization fails if the channel is annihilated.
- He argues the economics: outbound only works at higher ACV as response rates fall. If rates halve, $20K ACV needs to be about $50K, then $100K, then $200K, "and then no one's got a job."
- He uses a mall analogy: a friend (a former Goldman Sachs investor) bought a mall and mall equities around 2017-18 on the thesis that Amazon fears were overdone. They went bankrupt because the mega-trend was still worsening.
- He expects the SDR/BDR role to wind down. He thinks a rep's best hedge is to build an audience organically on social media and become "a trusted source of knowledge," which gets you pushed higher as more people enter the space.
- He expects the future workflow to run on intent signals: create desire so people come to your site, capture that signal, and then move them down the funnel any way possible, with a human on the last mile.

chunks.heading: When to pick fights and how he handled the Six Sense post
chunks.text:
- Adam wrote a satirical post about Six Sense after an account exec there allegedly tried to triple his pricing, and said he wondered if they had created an RB2B account themselves.
- He based it on what he'd learned about their financials: roughly, that if they stop growing they may have to lay off a large share of staff. The draft was more inflammatory, and some friends advised him to stay with facts and drop the humor. He did, and says that removed the bite.
- About 850 comments came in, roughly 80% positive. About 20% called him "thirsty," which he agrees with, especially since he also posted his P&L alongside it.
- His conclusion: "I'll never do anything like that again." He says people don't want that from him.
- His wife also told him he was "above that now" and asked what example he sets for their daughter. His earlier controversial Facebook ads for "get emails" worked because privacy-minded commenters wrote hate that made the ads perform better; he then made new videos from the comments.
- He says about 95% of what he posts is positive and inspiring. He sees removing the filter, and being open about how hard things have been, as what makes people reach out and say they thought they were the only ones struggling.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Adam Robinson explains how cold email drives about a third of RB2B's $6M+ ARR. Most founders fail by ignoring infrastructure, emailing only truly cold lists, and quitting early. RB2B ran three strategies: waitlist launch emails, pure cold outbound, and AI-personalized retargeting of site visitors, which converted best.

chunks.heading: How Adam diagnoses why cold email fails
chunks.text:
Adam scaled RB2B, his SaaS, past $6M ARR (the video later cites $6.3M). He says 32% of revenue ($1.9M) comes from cold email alone, about $160k/mo at the time. He says the way most people do cold email is dead, and he names three mistakes:

- **Message before infrastructure.** "Your perfect email means nothing if it lands in a spam folder." Many senders never realize their emails aren't being delivered. Build bulletproof infrastructure before writing a word.
- **Only emailing totally cold audiences.** Random lists with no prior touchpoint or reason to care become noise in a crowded inbox.
- **Quitting after a week or two.** People send five emails, get three replies, see no sales, and conclude cold email doesn't work. They never test different messages or audiences.

His fix has four parts:
- Build awareness on LinkedIn first.
- Email people already showing interest, plus cold contacts in the same ecosystem.
- Use an AI system to tailor each email, even at millions of sends.
- Commit to a 4-month testing window.

chunks.heading: Prime the audience before sending: 3 months of LinkedIn first
chunks.text:
- Adam spent about 3 months posting on LinkedIn before sending a single email. He built in public, covering the problems RB2B would solve, the journey, the struggles and the early wins.
- The cold contacts he emailed were B2B SaaS people, likely to have already seen his content. He may even have connected with some of them on LinkedIn.
- He says this "warm outreach disguised as cold email" is the framework behind 20% of all signups, 30% positive reply rates, and one campaign converting at 12.7% (one signup per ~8 emails).
- His three strategies together produced 42% of total revenue.

chunks.heading: Strategy 1: Waitlist campaigns (about 6% of revenue)
chunks.text:
- He captured a waitlist with a simple CTA at the bottom of LinkedIn posts: "If you want LinkedIn URLs of your website visitors pushed to Slack, DM me... and it's 100% free."
- By launch day, 3,000 people were waiting to sign up.
- The launch email was deliberately plain:
  - Subject: "RB2B is here"
  - Body: "Hi, first name. I'm thrilled to announce that RB2B is live. You can create your free account by clicking here."
- These people already knew him and followed the journey, so they were primed to sign up.

chunks.heading: Strategy 2: Pure cold outbound (about 21% of revenue)
chunks.text:
**Targeting**
- Source: Apollo.io.
- Filter: US-based SaaS companies with 3 to 200 employees.
- Contacts: founders or marketing roles, which gave over 80,000 contacts.
- Cadence: each person has been emailed twice per month since.

**Best-performing email**
- Subject line: the person's name plus "RB2B".
- Body, in short:
  - "We launched a tool that lets you know when individuals, not companies, are on your site."
  - "We send you their LinkedIn profile on Slack and we don't charge you a dime."
  - "Respond back with yes if you'd like me to send you a link to sign up."
  - PS: "No, I am not kidding. It's an exact match to the individual that visited, not just the company behind the domain. And we will not charge you a penny."

**Why he says it worked**
- Short, punchy copy.
- It sounds like his actual voice, not corporate speak.
- The direct benefit is in the first line.
- There is one clear, simple call to action.

chunks.heading: Infrastructure: deliverability comes first
chunks.text:
- He sends about 160,000 emails per month (the video also says 160,000 per day, which conflicts, so treat the exact volume with caution) off hundreds of domains.
- The stack:
  - Domains are bought through Instantly, with names like "tryb.com" and "therealrb.com". He creates 2 inboxes per domain.
  - Each inbox sends 2 to 10 emails per day.
  - Smart Lead and Instantly are used, and they switch between them depending on what's happening in each platform.
- He credits this combination of many low-volume inboxes with sneaking past Gmail and Hotmail spam filters into the primary inbox.
- He keeps list quality high. Every email passes multiple verification steps, and deliverability metrics are monitored obsessively every day.
- He had 200+ warmed-up domains before sending anything. Warm-up can be done inside Smart Lead or Instantly.
- Taylor Heron runs the sending infrastructure and the copy.
- Result: over 1 million emails in the first 6 months.

chunks.heading: Strategy 3: Website-visitor retargeting with AI (his biggest lever)
chunks.text:
RB2B identifies anonymous site visitors and triggers a personalized email within minutes. The pipeline:

1. **Install the RB2B script.** It identifies the visitor in real time and pushes their full LinkedIn profile: name, title, company and pages viewed.
2. **Clay enriches the data.** It adds company size, industry, tech stack and recent funding, and filters out existing customers via a HubSpot integration.
3. **Clay AI writes the email.** It references the specific pages they viewed and adapts tone to their industry and role.
4. **Push to Instantly.** The email is sent from the rotating domains, while the visitor is still thinking about RB2B.

**Winning message** (the simplest he has written): "Hey, saw you on our site via RB2B. Do you have any questions?"

**Results**
- One campaign converted at 10.4% (about one signup per 9.6 emails). He says overall retargeting converts at around 10%.
- Adam says this is 26x better than average cold email.
- His explanation for why it works: it is simple, direct and contextually relevant, the timing is perfect because they just visited, and the personalization is real because he knows what they looked at. "Timing is everything."

chunks.heading: Testing discipline and overall results
chunks.text:
- He ran 40 campaign variations over a 4-month window. The first few weeks did not tell the full story, and "most founders give up after sending only 500 emails."
- Cold audience conversion: about 1 signup per 250 emails, versus an industry average he puts closer to 1 in 1,000 or worse.
- Pure cold campaigns average a 30% positive reply rate.
- Up to 10 automated campaigns run at once, across about 200 domains rotated through Instantly.
- Cold email accounts for at least 20% of new revenue.
- He calls margins on the channel "incredible".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Adam Robinson explains how a LinkedIn personal brand, a deliberately simple product, AI-run customer support and a fixed-cost data asset let RB2B reach $8.6M ARR with almost no hands-on work. He argues real moats today are distribution, unique data and network effects, and that bootstrapped cash-flow businesses beat chasing VC scale.

chunks.heading: Why Adam built a personal brand on LinkedIn, and how a viral post set the strategy
chunks.text:
- Adam began posting on LinkedIn because he was selling a Shopify app with strong product-market fit and wanted the fastest way to spread awareness. His reasoning: "people follow people, not companies", so he built a public persona.
- He planned to write about his journey as a SaaS founder, since few "build in public" voices were at his stage.
- Over a year he saw that honest posts about the 2023 SaaS downturn (outbound stopped working, layoffs, business-model resets) got roughly 100x the engagement of posts aimed at ecommerce stores.
- Over Labor Day weekend 2023, a post said that BDR (business development rep) outbound wasn't working, that he laid everyone off, and that growth accelerated afterward. It got thousands of likes and many DMs.
- He tested the result by writing three more posts before dinner. His reasoning: if all three went viral, he would know what the algorithm wanted from him. They did.
- He then chose to write for the B2B software audience and to build a B2B version of his product, launching it with that awareness already in place.

chunks.heading: Designing the business around AI from day one
Simple beats complex: "nobody's touched it in a month"
chunks.text:
- Adam says his CTO hasn't touched code in over a month. He posts three times a week on LinkedIn, and not even about RB2B. A teammate built the AI support system. RB2B is at $8.6M ARR and still growing.
- He did not build a sprawling marketing machine and replace people with many task-level agents. He kept the business simple and used AI where it fit.
- He contrasts himself with Amos (Swan AI), who builds the "autonomous business" with many agents. Adam notes Amos spends his days on eight calls and his team works around the clock. In his view RB2B is already the autonomous business, and it was simpler to build than people assume.
- He is skeptical of the Coinbase-style approach (15% layoffs, one-person teams with agent fleets). He called it the complexity-heavy path.
- He expects a billion-dollar one-person company is possible and mentioned a reported two-person company in the compounded GLP-1 space that scaled direct-to-consumer sales with many AI agents.

chunks.heading: Why RB2B survived copycats: awareness, fixed-cost data, and a low price
chunks.text:
- Competitors entered and tried to copy the product. Adam says each hit the same wall that Amos did.
- He is candid about the product's limits:
  - Web traffic is noisy.
  - Persistent ad-tech IDs are inherently inaccurate.
  - Few of an ideal customer profile's site visitors are actually prospects yet.
  - The result is a signal that must be combined with other signals before anyone acts on it.
- Competitors compensated by building many extra features and charging about $20-30K a year, so they fight over the same later-stage startups. They also had venture investors.
- RB2B starts at $79 and $149 a month, with an average subscription around $200. He is self-funded.
- Customers watch their visitors until they no longer want to, then cancel. Churn is "terrible", he says, but he expects it to level off and it is still strong.
- Awareness: no one else could create the same reach, which gave RB2B a very cheap way to acquire customers.
- Data cost: it is effectively a data company with three business lines (RB2B, Retention, and a data arm that sells flat datasets). A shared data team runs one data asset. He puts the cost at about $1M a year across salaries and annual vendor contracts.
- With that fixed cost, resolving a contact, enriching it and sending it to Slack costs no extra money. Competitors pay about five cents per email.
- That combination lets him price below what it costs most B2B competitors to acquire a subscriber.

chunks.heading: Why his thought leadership is hard to copy
chunks.text:
- The writer, the platform and the readers line up:
  - The audience is B2B software people on LinkedIn.
  - Many of them are aspirational followers, either early-stage founders or employees at bigger companies.
  - These readers are also the buyers of what he sells.
  - His credibility as a SaaS founder carries weight with them.
- He says nobody at his level publishes similar content.
- On vibe coding, his view is that if anyone can copy your product, the defensible advantages are:
  - breaking through the noise in marketing;
  - owning unique data that AI agents can act on;
  - network effects (a two-sided market with 10M users on each side cannot be vibe-coded).
- On Greg Isenberg's take that audience is the hard part, with services first and technology later: Adam says that is easier said than done, and he hasn't seen big wins from that content brand yet. His own path was a version of it: he built the audience before the product.
- He would keep posting on LinkedIn even without RB2B and believes in compounding a personal brand.

chunks.heading: The next bet: a contact-data brand for AI agents
chunks.text:
- He is exploring a contact-data business (emails and phone numbers) positioned for Claude and AI agents. It could be API-first or agent-first with no traditional UI.
- The idea: sell data he already owns, at a very competitive price, behind the awareness funnel he has already built. A brand could mean something like "contact data for Claude".
- The market is a competitive commodity: two big players, a few mid-sized ones, and many faceless small ones. His question is whether a disruptive, brand-led approach can win.
- He says he may launch soon, since shipping is cheap now, and pull the product if it doesn't work.
- He is hiring one person to maintain part of RB2B while the three who built it work on the new project.

chunks.heading: Team size, scale and strategy
Summary
chunks.text: Adam explains how he built a large organic LinkedIn following as a founder, and why it works for him. He stresses authentic, vulnerable pain-point writing over AI-generated content, picking the platform where your ICP lives, ghostwriters for the early stage, and using conflict like a 6sense cease-and-desist as marketing for RB2B.

chunks.heading: Why LinkedIn works for Adam, and when it doesn't
chunks.text:
- Adam's LinkedIn growth took about 12 months to find "content market fit" (a term he credits to Devin Reed of Gong). He says it is as hard as product-market fit and needs the same perseverance and curiosity.
- He says he is in a near-perfect situation: his ICP (revenue leaders and SaaS CEOs) lives on LinkedIn, so the profile is literally his marketing channel.
- He would not recommend going all-in to be the best creator on LinkedIn if you sell to, say, hospitals. It still helps with hiring and ecosystem credibility, but won't generate leads.
- His audience: roughly 75% ICP, and about 85% unique engagers post to post (measured by Peter Conforti from his downloaded LinkedIn data). Typical posts get about 50-60k impressions and 200-500 engagements.
- How he picked the platform: he was targeting large Shopify stores, who are more active on Twitter, but Twitter was very competitive. He started on LinkedIn because the ecosystem (vendors, agencies, employees, partners) is there.
- Nine months of posting with a first ghostwriter (Tommy) built ecosystem-level credibility. It helped him reach the brands he wanted because people took him seriously.
- The big shift came when the company decided to build a B2B product. Writing aimed at B2B CEOs, with a different writer (Alec), is when LinkedIn became the main channel.
- Litmus test for any founder: is your audience actually active on the platform? Look at who engages with your posts. He only learned the Shopify founders weren't on LinkedIn by trying.

chunks.heading: Authenticity, vulnerability and the AI "B minus" problem
chunks.text:
- Adam shared an office with the Jasper AI team for two years, before Jasper. Watching it left him with a deep belief that B-minus AI content would multiply roughly a million times, so the most authentic, human, vulnerable content would be amplified even more.
- He calls it "the LIE of AI" to think it can offer perspective. People want a point of view, not generic AI posts.
- What makes his content unique: he describes in "excruciating detail" the pain a CEO of a $20M ARR SaaS company experiences, with transparency and vulnerability. One early team member told him it was the kind of thing you'd tell your wife or best friend.
- He uses video because he believes ChatGPT can't yet replicate him in that form.
- Example: his monthly update said revenue was down 2.3% for the fourth month in a row, the competitive environment was terrible, and "we are deeply in the woods." Other founders said they couldn't send that to their own executive team, let alone post it.
- He says he has no investors, and they probably wouldn't love it. He admits it isn't easy to write: his ego is tied to ARR, as a SaaS founder's is.
- His limits on sharing: he wouldn't name a specific underperforming individual or say he's about to let a customer success person go.
- Payoff: early-stage SaaS founders tell him they read every post and share them with their teams, because he is "actually in the trenches" and reports every detail.
- Controversy rule: he only stirs the pot "when it's real." Trolling for its own sake gets old quickly on LinkedIn.

chunks.heading: Thought leadership as a hiring and team-alignment tool
chunks.text:
- The seed: at a trade show, the president of Kajabi was asked what he'd tell himself to do differently when he joined at $6M ARR. His answer was to start posting on LinkedIn every day. Adam had six employees and about $6M ARR at the time.
- The reasoning Adam took from that conversation: a steady stream of content about why you do things and how you think lets employees opt in rather than being pushed in reluctantly. The Yellowstone example: John Dutton has no mission-values poster, but you know what it's like to work on that ranch from the show.
- Result: the right employees arrive having already read everything. He has "people hurling themselves" at him to work there, even though his Glassdoor rating is a 2 after a layoff (61 to 55 employees, last year).
- He refuses to manipulate review platforms and takes a "this is the authentic me, take it or leave it" stance. He read his negative Glassdoor reviews for the first time on camera in a "Mean Tweets" style post.
- He recommends Dave Gerhardt's book *Founder Brand* for the case for founder-led thought leadership, even if you're not in his ideal situation.
- Even when selling to hospitals, a founder's thought leadership benefits the enterprise.

chunks.heading: Objections, ghostwriters and his current content workflow
chunks.text:
- Two sets of objections: "I don't want to be famous" and "I don't have the time or experience to compete with professionals."
- On fame: you won't become truly famous, just known in a small part of the world, which helps you and your company. Building a parasocial relationship with tens of thousands of people is very good for business.
- A ghostwriter solves the second set: they know the game (hook, credibility, keeping people on the post, a dopamine hit at the end so they react).
- A competent ghostwriter should ask: who are you, what stage is the company, who are you hiring, who do you sell to, are they on this platform, and what pain can you articulate for them.
- Best post structure per Adam: a mini hero's journey. Agitate a pain, share a transformational moment, then give relief and a takeaway. Articulating pain is the most relatable and cuts through.
- Even with a ghostwriter, he believes you'll feel "I don't know what this is doing for me but it's doing something and I like it."
- His current setup: he no longer uses a ghostwriter and writes everything himself. His consultant Alec helps with idea generation, tightens hooks, and edits. Alec also understands the algorithm and what a post should have done versus what it did.
- Idea capture: he jots ideas on a notepad, and sometimes gets post ideas from questions asked on podcasts. He says it's like having another version of himself over his shoulder asking whether this is good content.
- Weekly cadence: a one-hour ideas meeting with Alec on Mondays, and his whole Tuesday goes to content in some form. He says he runs two startups at the same time.
- Advice to founders who say they have no time: if you hire a ghostwriter and get the feeling it works, you'll figure out how to delegate other things.

chunks.heading: Known well vs. well known: two audience-building strategies
chunks.text:
- Strategy 1 (well known): you don't care who engages. You want a big number and use tactics like memes and viral formats. Content is optimized for virality over meaning, and then you funnel interested people to a newsletter or podcast. Chase Diamond is an example (LinkedIn as awareness, newsletter and podcast as trust), and Dan Murray's approach is similar (memes pulled to his newsletter).
- Chase advised Adam to work on distribution: he spends as much time sending his posts to chat rooms of other big accounts (so they engage) as he does creating the post. Adam's own time goes almost entirely into making the content as good as it can be.
- Strategy 2 (known well): use LinkedIn as both distribution and trust platform, writing for a specific audience you know you'll attract. This makes readers feel they know you and are on a journey with you, a deeper trust than viral content gives.
- Adam prefers strategy 2 and calls it more efficient and elegant because you aren't transferring people across platforms.
- Newsletter growth loop he heard about and is trying: post on LinkedIn with the newsletter as the call to action. Even your best post reaches a small share of LinkedIn, so when you send the same content in a newsletter a week later, it hits a largely different audience and drives people back to comment.
- He says LinkedIn lacks a place for people to go deeper, so he started a newsletter and a weekly webinar (a 10-30 minute monologue followed by Q&A) pointing to his Rb2b landing page.

chunks.heading: The 6sense cease-and-desist post as a distribution play
chunks.text:
- Context: his company bought 6sense for about $18K in November, mainly to compare against Rb2b (he notes this technically violates the terms, but "everybody does that"). His salespeople wouldn't use it because it was harder to get value from than Rb2b.
- 6sense emailed that the price was going up 3x, then offered a flat renewal if he renewed six months early. He says that in the Shopify world, a 5% price increase would get him "burnt at the stake."
- He wrote an inflammatory post (no swearing in the hook), giving theories for why they were scared: their data is bad, person-level beats company-level, and they fear the viral expansion of his tool. He framed it as fun but not as fact.
- Four days later at 6pm he got a cease and desist. His reasoning as a marketer: what could be better than an industry leader (6sense raised at $5.2B) acknowledging a small company, and even looking afraid of it?
- Instead of the demands (take the post down, apologize, and tag the 463 commenters), he uploaded the cease and desist as a PDF and wrote that 6sense tried to sue him over a LinkedIn post. He listed what they demanded, said what he did instead, and restated his theories with a David vs. Goliath framing.
- Results: about 1,600 engagements on that post, which was well above his average. Follow-ups also beat average (one about 800).
- Follow-up: the one credible claim was that you can't buy their tech to compare it with yours, so he checked Rb2b and found they had apparently signed up for an Rb2b account too.
- Takeaway he draws: ask what you can say that others can't or won't, without torching the company. He also notes that the cease and desist wasn't the reason they sent it, but it let him credibly say they were afraid of him.

chunks.heading: How he uses LinkedIn for pipeline: the B2B motion and Rb2b
chunks.text:
- The motion he describes from Alec (who works with B2B CEOs): put out great content, get inbound connection requests, accept only ICP requests, ask what caught their attention, wait about 60 days (by then they've seen your posts and see you as a celebrity), then ask if they want to talk about a problem. He says accept rates are very high.
- He hasn't even needed this yet because the content alone worked better than expected. He now has a free offer used to book discovery calls or agency conversations (for example, talking to 100 HubSpot agencies).
- On free offers: he could charge but would plow the revenue back into marketing anyway, so he makes it free.
- Product-led growth: when a high-value lead signs up for the product and doesn't install the script within four days, his LinkedIn team member reaches out to them directly.
- The product he promotes, Rb2b, does person-level website visitor identification rather than company-level reverse IP lookup (the Clearbit, 6sense, ZoomInfo style). Adam says company-level is useful but limited.
- His personal history: his first startup was stuck at $3M for four years. He says he was dying for someone ahead of him to explain what they were doing and why, and that motivates how openly he shares today.
- Where to find him: rb2b.com, LinkedIn, and retention.com (aimed at e-commerce stores).

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Adam Robinson recounts scaling retention.com to $21M ARR, then trying to build a unicorn in a year after watching Jasper's rise, missing targets on churn, competition and spending discipline. He also explains why LinkedIn founder content, free products, and stacking bootstrapped businesses are his core growth bets.

chunks.heading: Getting unstuck: why Adam says "everything works when your product is good"
chunks.text:
- Adam describes his whole entrepreneurial journey as "getting stuck and getting unstuck again."
- His first SaaS (a newsletter app, $40/month subscriptions to very small businesses) sat at about $3M ARR for four years, and he sold it for $10M.
- retention.com (formerly get emails) hit two sticking points: below $3M ARR, and again around $6M.
- When he was stuck, he went to conferences and grabbed any information about what worked for others. His takeaway now: "all of this stuff that people are telling you is working, they just have a better product than you."
- His rule: "When your product is not good nothing works." Getting unstuck means making everything you do better so it clicks into product-market fit.
- He frames his talks around himself at $3M ARR, three years in, and asks what that person wants to know.
- His favorite startup-building book is "Four Steps to the Epiphany." He says following it close to page by page raises your odds of success far above following your gut, even though there are emotional reasons not to.

chunks.heading: Why bootstrapping can beat "bootstrap vs. VC" thinking
chunks.text:
- Adam says most small bootstrapped companies ("the 37signals thing": few employees, $1.5M cash, few problems) are slowly dying. He sold his for $10M.
- His approach is to get a company to that level, put someone else in charge, then tinker on the next thing. Each new product is better and more efficient because of the product-market fit, marketing and product skills from the last one.
- He claims there is a point (maybe $10M, $15M or $20M ARR, if run properly) where a bootstrapped company becomes so profitable that stacking businesses gets "absolutely incredible."
- His numbers at retention.com: $21.7M ARR, fat founder salaries, and another $6M to $8M of profit expected that year, which they would pay out as dividends.
- He pictures a roughly $20M free cash flow business run with friends.
- A bootstrapped company that big is stronger than much larger venture-backed ones: he says he could afford better lawyers than a $5.2B company while taking on a larger competitor, and it gives freedom and flexibility.
- His motivation is the game itself. If given $1B, he would use it to try to turn RB2B into a huge company, because he doesn't yet know whether he can build a $100M ARR company.
- He says he currently runs four efforts: retention.com (55 employees; he is CEO in name but not running it), RB2B, and an enterprise data sales business his COO Santos is assembling.

chunks.heading: What went wrong trying to grow a bootstrapped company like a VC-backed one
chunks.text:
- The inspiration was Jasper AI. Adam shared an office with its founders when they were stuck at $2.5M ARR (he was at $3M with get emails, which was at $3M with six employees and about $1.5M cash). Jasper went from zero to $50M ARR in 12 months, and Adam says seeing that made something bigger feel real.
- Jasper spent about $2M a month on Facebook ads. His reasoning: if he spent $2M a month on sales and marketing, his business would be bigger too.
- By then get emails was at about $8M ARR with six people. Adam and his COO Santos decided to go for it, funded by free cash flow with no fundraising.
- The plan rested on three assumptions:
  - Demo only to large Shopify Plus stores, which he believed would solve churn.
  - Cut the price roughly in half while doubling the value, then double prices on everyone within a year for big revenue expansion.
  - Good sales velocity plus product-market fit in that niche would make it a "unicorn twice over."
- He also made a YouTube show (about 18 episodes, 10 minutes each, over two seasons) and started posting on LinkedIn to maximize awareness.
- Results: he missed the revenue target by over 50% and the unicorn goal by far more (he guessed 80% or 90%).
- What he got wrong:
  - He assumed it would behave like Klaviyo. Systems of record (CRM, data storage) have very low churn because you must put your data somewhere else if you leave. retention.com sells leads and intent data, so turning it off just means the revenue it produced is gone.
  - His loud success brought about five competitors, who used BuiltWith to find his customers and offered more for less at renewal. Revenue contracted at renewal instead of expanding.
  - He lost financial discipline: spending "like a sailor," hiring very expensive people, and not caring what they were paid.
- Operations: they hired 50 people in about 60 days with no processes, and the new hires brought their own ways of working. He later brought in an executive coach to roll out the Entrepreneurial Operating System (EOS).
- He says the euphoric period ran from late September 2022 to roughly April or May 2023, followed by a cleanup. The business now looks like an EBITDA business, which is fine.
- His chief of staff and de facto CFO, Kelly, was more conservative and pushed back the whole time.
- He has had to lay off many people at once twice, which he says were his hardest moments.

chunks.heading: LinkedIn as a CEO-led marketing channel
chunks.text:
- Adam says he spent about 12 months before it clicked and he understood why it worked. Before that it was "okay and really expensive."
- It works best when the buyer lives on LinkedIn. For a product like RB2B (a product that didn't exist two months earlier), he is selling to people who consume his content there. Otherwise it may help only with investors, hiring or partnerships.
- Practice: he posts three times a week, aiming for four, and also publishes video.
- What he writes about: real numbers and difficulties, such as retention.com being down 2.3% for a fourth straight month. His reasoning is to ask why anyone would read your content when AI produces "B minus crap."
- Jasper can't write his real financials, and it can't (yet) produce an authentic talking-head video, so he leans on both.
- His models were people building in public, such as Nathan Barry of ConvertKit. Five years earlier he would have read anything they wrote "like a rabid dog."
- His LinkedIn collaborator, Alec Paul, told him that if he wrote for B2B people, it would work given the effort he was willing to put in. Four posts in a row got about 2.5 million impressions, which showed him what LinkedIn rewards.
- The key benefit: people feel they know him like a friend, so when they need a product that substitutes for something of his, they buy from him.
- Example: at three events in one night during South by Southwest in Austin, strangers approached him. One $1M ARR SaaS founder said he sent every post to his whole team.
- He sees this fandom and affinity as unmatched by paid ads or cold email, and as the most capital-efficient way to spread awareness if you can nail it.
- His strategy for RB2B: invest zero in traditional marketing (one person does cold email, which he says contributes little) and put time, energy and money into this kind of brand, which is unmeasurable. He says no VC would let you do that.
- On employees: they are not the audience, and they knew he'd do this. His chief of staff pushed back, but he says it does more for the company than anything else, and he thinks employees prefer hearing the truth.

chunks.heading: Free as a product strategy
chunks.text:
- RB2B is a free (freemium) product, and Adam says that after this experience he plans to start every product with free.
- His reasoning: "the power of free is so beyond what I think anyone understands." He cites Mailchimp.
- He compares it to burning money like a venture-backed startup: you could charge and then pay for distribution, or make it free so that "literally everybody's going to try it."
- Free also gives a large amount of information about how people use the product and how it might be monetized later.
- He also points to Jotform as an example of a free-product company (bootstrapped about 18 years, he said North of $100M).

chunks.heading: Founder life and personal context
chunks.text:
- Adam spent about 10 years as a credit default swap trader at Lehman Brothers, from age 21 to about 30. He made a lot of money in that boom and bust.
- He decided to try entrepreneurship using his savings. He says it took five years from deciding to paying himself a dollar, and that a startup consumes whatever money you give it, especially for a first-time founder.
- He lived in a New York apartment with the Vimeo founders while they built the site, which changed his view of what entrepreneurship offered.
- He is 43, has a 2-year-old daughter and a second child on the way. His routine: home at 6:00 every day, works during nap time on weekends, and takes Wednesday mornings off until 11:00 for his daughter's music class. He travels mainly for keynotes, sometimes flying in for a day.
- He says his work pace is "11 out of 10," but he constrains it so there is room for family. He is much less social than he used to be.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Adam walks through Robly (17 months), Retention.com (27 weeks) and RB2B (16 weeks), all without outside funding. The thread: find an acquisition channel with no competition, and eventually build an audience first, since cold email no longer works.

chunks.heading: How Adam finds uncontested channels and gets to $1M ARR faster each time
chunks.text:
- Adam bootstrapped three SaaS companies to $1M+ ARR with no outside funding: Robly in 17 months, Retention.com (originally Get Emails) in 27 weeks, and RB2B in 16 weeks.
- His core belief: "what makes acquiring customers expensive is competition." If you have a channel with no competitors and a good offer, acquisition is cheap.
- Each company got its speed from a different uncontested channel: a scraped customer list with a call center (Robly), provocative Facebook ads plus targeted cold email (Retention.com), and a pre-built LinkedIn audience (RB2B).
- He says his advice for the best business decision he's received is "Do not take institutional capital." He argues VCs show up once you have traction with "a lie about how if you sign this piece of paper you're going to be worth $30 million." He wants to show people you can bootstrap to $10M ARR.
- You still need a small pool of starting capital, roughly $50-100k, from savings, an agency, an info product, or friends and family. Adam lived off savings from 10 years as a trader at Lehman Brothers.

chunks.heading: Robly: a scraped list and a call center to $1M ARR in 17 months
chunks.text:
- Robly was an email marketing product competing with Constant Contact and Mailchimp. It launched January 1, 2014.
- Adam's team built a crawler to find websites with Constant Contact signup widgets. Only paying Constant Contact customers would have one, so the list was a targeted list of paying customers of a public company.
- A team in Pakistan manually enriched about 250,000 domains by Google search to find phone numbers.
- A call center (run "out of my apartment") cold-called with the pitch "We can give you 50% more opens for half the price." They then upsold to three quarters of the price and migrated the customer over. Plans were roughly $15-50 a month.
- The economics worked because nobody else called that list, so human sales was viable even at $15-50 a month.
- About 5,000 people switched from Constant Contact this way.
- Onboarding was manual because the "magic moment" was getting a customer to hit send on their first campaign. Customers who did stuck 100% of the time, but busy small-business owners (a coffee shop with one employee) would not do it alone. They started with three customer success people building templates one-to-one. Then they moved to one-to-many onboarding calls, which had a better show rate and felt like a community. A $25 off incentive got people to show up.
- Why it stalled: once the list was burned through, the product wasn't competitive. Mailchimp had a better product and a free offer, and Robly wasn't even cheaper than Mailchimp. Growth stalled in the low single-digit millions of ARR and then shrank, though it stayed cash-flow positive. The company later sold to private equity in an eight-figure exit in 2021 with no outside funding.
- Adam says those lists still work, but now everyone has access via BuiltWith and similar tools. His own verdict: with what he knows now, he "wouldn't start it."
- The cash from Robly funded the experiments that led to the next company, since the idea came from a feature built inside Robly.

chunks.heading: Failed attempts before Retention.com, and the idea that worked
chunks.text:
- Before Get Emails, Adam spent about two years and hundreds of thousands of dollars on things that didn't work.
- Attempt one: a Constant Contact "authorized local expert" style boots-on-the-ground distribution model (Constant Contact had spent about $50M building it). It was a complete failure, wasted a ton of money, and ended with a lawsuit from Constant Contact over the non-compete of the person involved.
- Attempt two: building a product aimed just above Mailchimp's buyer. His co-founder Diana had seen her old company succeed with it, and they hired engineers and spent a year building. At launch, no one cared because 10 other companies were already doing it. Adam calls this the opposite of how he advocates building now: sell before you build.
