- The breakthrough came at a conference (the Traffic and Conversion conference in 2018). The stunt got attention, but conversations glazed over until he asked, "What if I could get you the email address of people on your website who don't fill out a form?" Every person perked up and wanted to buy it.
- He didn't know how to build it and spent about a year and a half digging. It first shipped as a feature in Robly's email app. Users signed up for the email app just to use the identity feature, download the file, and use it elsewhere, so he spun it out into its own product in November 2019.

chunks.heading: Retention.com: Facebook ads and cold email, $1M ARR in 27 weeks
chunks.text:
- Why it worked: there were data companies with similar products, but they had a "pathetic go to market and user experience" and weren't SaaS people. Adam saw that as the opening.
- The ads: Adam and his wife made weekly one-minute Facebook videos that were deliberately inflammatory to privacy-minded people ("how is that legal?") while answering sales questions. The goal was to get people anticipating the ad. The most searched term for Get Emails became "Helen from Get Emails."
- The ads paid back fast because of occasional whales: a click-through PLG plan let someone buy a $5,000-a-month plan by clicking, which happened about once every two weeks and paid back the prior two weeks of ads.
- He also replied to people who called him a scumbag in the comments, using the fights to make better ads. He says that headspace was bad for him personally.
- Targeting was broad interest audiences: Shopify, entrepreneur, Klaviyo, and names like e-commerce influencer Ezra Firestone.
- The problem: the ads brought "atrocious" customers, roughly 15% monthly churn "wannabes." After about eight weeks without a whale, and after spending around $100k on ads, he stopped the ads entirely and focused on high-value users and targeted cold email.
- Cold email worked better. His co-founder Diana prospected to Shopify and Klaviyo user lists, and those customers had substantially lower churn and higher value. MRR grew from about $200k to $600k+ over the next year.
- Adam credits the whole zero-to-one stage to the awareness from the video ads.

chunks.heading: Churn, plateaus and shrinking TAM at Retention.com
chunks.text:
- Retention.com reached about $3M ARR quickly, then sat flat for nine months. Adam was burned out and thought "maybe I'm just a 3 million ARR guy."
- In a high-churn product category with a high-churn buyer persona, you are "always trying to do things to outpace churn."
- The Shopify audience topped out ARR because of churn. Getting to the next level means larger deals with lower-churn customers such as omnichannel retailers. The company is at roughly $21.8M ARR.
- Product-market fit can fade: he once estimated 50,000 Shopify stores could succeed with the product; he now thinks it's about 1,400, and there are more competitors.
- Cold email only worked then because of a scrappy manual setup: five people in the Philippines spent half the day building lists and half sending emails by hand from Gmail inboxes, and Diana's sales assistant replied and booked demos. He says "it literally just would not work today" because more people send more email and spam filters keep tightening.
- His own 2023 attempt to scale a team of BDRs convinced him that having people click buttons and write emails and LinkedIn connections "just isn't working anymore."

chunks.heading: Layoffs and right-sizing the team
chunks.text:
- Adam has done layoffs three times (the third was the day after the recording).
- Robly: they scaled the sales org around a second list of Constant Contact customers that looked promising, but nobody picked up the phone. They dropped from 38 to 6 people. "It was my fault."
- Retention.com 2023: they scaled outbound sales on false signals about TAM and deal size, and customers churned and contracted. The VP of sales quit and instead of replacing him they cut the sales org from 20 to 4. He says it cleaned up the culture and the team started moving faster.
- Latest round: the company was still sized for the market of 18 months earlier. Throughput was low and he realized they could do the work with half the team. He cites running the company with EOS as helping him see what actually moves the needle.
- His view: no one regrets that move, and the day you realize you can do it with half the people you have to make it. It is "the most liberating feeling" for the founder but awful for employees, and the worst part of the job.

chunks.heading: Building a LinkedIn audience from zero to 92,000 followers
chunks.text:
- He started from zero in September 2022 and had about 92,000 followers when recorded.
- The first 12 months didn't work. He posted a daily video with no theme, aimed at Shopify store owners to sell Retention.com. He struggled to explain why an e-commerce store owner would listen to him instead of an e-commerce agency guy. Posts were good but didn't book demos.
- He kept going anyway. Lesson: you find your voice by producing, and the time spent was "learning what not to do."
- The turning point came in 2023. Their scale-up attempt failed, the VP of sales quit, and the sales team shrank by about 75%. He wrote about it and it exploded (3,300 likes in 24 hours, versus 30-50 on a typical post).
- His LinkedIn consultant, Alec, told him to pivot the content to B2B because all his other clients were B2B and none were willing to be this open.
- He then wrote three more hot takes, such as that BDR teams no longer work, and got about 2 million impressions across the three posts. His follower growth rate permanently steepened.
- The formula: work in public, share financials and failures, say what people only say to their spouse behind closed doors, and be as transparent and human as possible. Talk about how go-to-market is changing and how to build SaaS. He tries to be "a dealer of hope" that you can bootstrap to $10M ARR.
- On haters: LinkedIn is more polite than other platforms. The strongest pushback comes from outbound agencies when he says outbound is dead, though most comments agree.
- He says content can't be boring: you need a real point of view.

chunks.heading: Edutainment and audience-first distribution
chunks.text:
- Adam says he is "in the edutainment business and I happen to have a SaaS at the end of the funnel." His job is making entertaining, educational content about building a SaaS and how you can too.
- Organic social is the most efficient way to build trust and sell. Demand for content about startups is higher than for almost anything else.
- LinkedIn Thought Leadership ads let you put spend behind a post that already performed organically. Clicks are cheap because LinkedIn already wants to show the post, and you know it works. He says that if you can create great organic social content and your large competitors can't, "you have 100 times more efficient awareness generation potential than they do."
- The playbook is less clear than cold email's, but he says it is much more powerful.
- He believes B2B may follow the DTC pattern of influencers first, then distributing product into their audience. He points to Greg Eisenberg as building a portfolio of companies audience-first. Field sales (taking a buyer to a Lakers game for a million-dollar deal) won't change, but for point-solution SaaS, distribution is the hard part.
- He recommends Russell Brunson's Expert Secrets for why organic social content is so powerful.

chunks.heading: RB2B: $1M ARR in 16 weeks from a pre-built audience
chunks.text:
- RB2B matches anonymous website visitors to LinkedIn profiles and pushes them into Slack with a business email. It is aimed at SaaS companies with sales teams.
- Pricing: the core product is free for up to 200 leads a month, which is about 85% of signups. Paid plans start around $99 a month, and a mid-market SaaS pays about $750 a month. The idea was to take price off the table: zero-touch, PLG, a "hundred million dollar value proposition that just punches you in the face" that is free and spreads on its own.
- It was deliberately designed in reaction to the death of outbound: Adam asked what the complete opposite of a go-to-market that no longer works would be, and answered with founder-content-led distribution plus a free product.
- Launch prep: between October (when they decided to build) and the March 1 launch, they held about 300 discovery calls and had a beta version with testers giving feedback. By launch day thousands of people were on a waitlist.
- Results: $1M ARR in 16 weeks after the March 2023 launch (he describes 1 to 2 million ARR in six weeks), and it was past $2M ARR a few months later. Adam also does about 10 podcast appearances a week as part of the go-to-market.

Eoin McGuinness: As a founder, how are you able to walk away from an idea that you poured blood, sweat, and tears into for months - or even years? How do you know it's time to pivot?

Me: Because I know what PMF feels like.

Eoin: What do you mean? 

Adam: I spent 3 years stuck at $3m with a product that DIDN’T have PMF. It was miserable. Nothing I tried worked. Then in 2019, we spun out a feature that identified anonymous web traffic. We built it in 8 weeks and in week one I ran $1k of Facebook ads and got $5k MRR back. We were able to get that company to $13m ARR in 2.5yrs w/ 6 people - PRE - AI, and eventually to $23m ARR w/ under 30.

Eoin: Yeah... but how does that make it easy for you to walk away from an idea you’ve chased for months - or even a year - and are SUPER excited about? 

Adam: Because I remember how PAINFUL it was to push on a string. How HARD you can grind and get nothing back. But that experience made me realize that when you have PMF, everything works, it’s NOT a grind … You can still work really hard, but you get back 100x more from every single action than when you don’t have PMF. 

Eoin: What are things that you look for when you are trying to figure out if an idea has the potential for having PMF? 

Adam: I look at facial expressions and mannerisms. If someone is politely nodding their head telling me it sounds smart, it’s a shit idea. If people in the market stop whatever else they are doing, say things like “wait - say that again?” and “when is this out?” and “how can I start using it?” and “how do I buy it?”, I know I’m on the right track. That is what happened with MoltSetsts, which is at $400k ARR, still in beta, no sign up link on site, and we still haven’t invited our entire waitlist.

Eoin: How do you know when to walk away? 

Adam: If 9/10 people that I speak to in the market don’t have some type of “holy shit” reaction to my elevator pitch, at some point I’ll just pull the ripcord on the idea altogether. The length of time depends on my familiarity with the space before I started talking to people. More familiarity is a shorter time, less familiarity, longer time. But the point is - I need UNIVERSAL “HOLY SHIT” reactions to make a product or business out of it. 

Eoin: Have you ever had an idea you regretted walking away from? 

Adam: I regret the 3 years I spent banging my head against the wall as a stuck schmuck at Robly. I WISH I would have had the clarity to realize it wasn’t going to go anywhere no matter what I did. I wish I would have spent time on something that had a chance of actually working. And now, those are the ONLY ideas I spend time on.

The biggest mistake I see at $10m ARR - and I see it ALL the time - is Founders getting caught up in the unavoidable euphoria of real traction and raising VC money for a business that is actually sub-VC scale. It happened to me too.

I totally went for it in 2022-2023 and went from 6 to 60 people in 60 days. Like almost all of the others who made the mistake, I severely misjudged the TAM, got my ass handed to me in 2024, and by a stroke of amazing luck the market for growth equity fell apart in 2023 as my business was also falling apart. 

But many other Founders are not so lucky. They raise when they don’t have to, and trade freedom for the absolute requirement to grow literally forever. They don’t realize they sold their freedom because they only sold 10-15% of their company. But mark my words - you take that money and if you stop growing and you are toast. There is no doing what I did - settling for a much smaller businesses ($35m ARR now) that throws of tons of cash as a consolation prize. 

If you take that money thinking you will be the next unicorn and you are not, you are relegated to a decade of a low paying job, when you could have been a bit more cautious/responsible/whatever you want to call it and preserved a life-changing outcome for yourself no matter what happened. 

You only need to get rich once. I’m begging you to maximize the probability of that before you swing for the fences. 

Just my two cents ✌️

I think HubSpot made a HUGE mistake. They never should have backpedalled on their decision to create the greatest data co-op in the world. 

Here is the simple reality. People would have whined about it on LinkedIn for two weeks, a handful of customers would have left, then everybody would have moved on to the next thing, and HubSpot would have been left with the single greatest data co-op that has ever been created. 

This would have been INCREDIBLE for every HubSpot user. What do I mean? Guess who knows the best contact information for every single business contact in the world??? The 1.4m active HubSpot CRM users, plus a handful of data scientists. 

This could have been an EPIC UNLOCK for HubSpots customers … and now it’s … GONE … and HubSpot is stuck trying to figure out how to keep the data fresh they got in the Clearbit acquisition, when the best source of data they could EVER IMAGINE is … you guessed it … right in front of their nose.

I think they just executed this poorly. Having people opt-in to a co-op has worked REALLY well in the past, even with enterprise companies (Abacus was an enterprise catalog purchaser data co-op that Double Click bought for $1b in 1999, as one example). In the US, if results are demonstrably better from giving up data, and the only way they can get those results is from joining a co-op, people will join co-ops. 

My good buddy Nick Weldon at 5x5 made a killer data co-op against all odds, and the largest publicly traded company in the data space is their largest customer.

I recognize that I am not HubSpot, my market cap is 1/100th of theirs, and I pride myself on taking an aggressive stance on issues like this. But I do believe that A) it was stupid to pull this back, because B) nobody would have cared after a couple weeks, and C) it would have REALLY helped their customers.

It’s a sad day for the small founder. We need all the help we can get.

Bring back the co-op, HubSpot, but make it opt-in.

It will crush.

Last week Recharge acquired Skio for $105m cash. This is an incredibly important acquisition for founders to pay attention to. Here's why:

What is not said in the headline “we only raised $8m and sold for $105m” is the little-known fact that the reason they only raised $8m was several years ago nobody would do a Series A for Skio. 

Which is why their founder Kennan Frost replaced himself as CEO and moved on to build Icon. 

Why is this important for Founders? 

1. Selling a business for $105m when you only raised $8m is LIFE CHANGING

2. For the same reason he couldn’t get the Series A done, I’m not sure a business like that (sticky but sells to small TAM of elite Shopify users at $500/mo) is saleable at $500m+. 

3. Had Kennan been “lucky enough” to get the Series A done and raised at $200-$250m valuation, the exit hurdle would have been raised to $600-750m

4. Recharge likely wouldn’t be a buyer there ($2.1b at absolute peak valuations), not sure if anybody would be … because if you’re buying Skio at $600-750, you think it’s going to $2b.

5. Skio - which would still be the same, GREAT business - would be stuck in a zombie state, pushing for a valuation that is larger than it was meant to be (like so many others).

Ryan Allis once said, “If you have to raise money, keep it at 1x your ARR at the time”. 

Why? Because it maximizes your optionality. 

You can sell a great biz for $100-$150m, then go do whatever you want. 

Or, you can keep running it. 

Or, you can keep the equity, and hire someone else to run it, and go bigger (like Kennan). 

If you’re a founder, keeping a low 9-fig exit on the table is an incredibly smart move.

Kennan did by accident. You should do it on purpose. 

You only need to get rich once. 

My advice is to have as many paths to that place as possible.

Oh and PS… The other reason he was able to sell besides not raising lots of dough??? 

THEY WERE A GROWING, PROFITABLE BUSINESS … 

Why do more people not live life this way!?!?! 

Congratulations, Kennan!

Melissa Kwan is a 3x bootstrapper. Here's what she said are the 11 most shocking surprises on her way to $1m ARR (everyone disagrees with #10 but I swear by it):

1. Everything they thought would make a huge impact, did not.

They got 1 customer from being top 3 on Product Hunt. 18 trials from a 250k person newsletter. Spent 7 months on a huge design update, zero lift.

2. Product-led is 10x harder than sales-led.

PLG is the hardest nut to crack. Getting someone to find you, sign up, try the product, then convert all on their own is HARD.

3. The market wasn't as ripe as they thought.

Given live webinars (her product) have been widely adopted, they thought automating them would be an easy sell. Turns out, it wasn't a concept most people could grasp without a demo.

4. Consumers are more discerning and less forgiving than ever.

Doesn't matter how great your product is and how many features you have, users will find the fringe case you can't solve and bounce.

5. The amount of time they spent on content creation.

LinkedIn, blogs, backlinks, templates, customer stories, podcasting, videos, guest posting, webpages, help articles, workshops, thought leadership.

6. A single user can cause scaling issues and uncover system flaws.

One user sent so many webinar attendees in 10 days into their system that it was 400x the average user. They never imagined a user like this could exist and was unprepared.

7. Plan limitations are for not losing money (not just making money).

Since they didn't have usage limits, they lost $8k in streaming costs due to the incident in #6. They had to put limits in to restrict similar power users.

8. Pricing strategy can be the difference between profit and loss.

They grandfathered existing customers when they increased prices against the advice of our peers. That could have been $30k/m to invest towards platform costs and hiring.

9. Incremental growth month over month amounts to meaningful revenue.

They grew 10-20% MoM in the 1st year, 5-10% MoM in the 2nd, 1-7% MoM in the 3rd. It often felt too slow and was discouraging, but they got there.

10. You don't need all the fancy metrics to know what to prioritize.

The only thing they obsessed over was the voice of customer through support tickets. Issues, requests, feedback and suggestions. Their roadmap was designed accordingly.

11. $83k/month is not a lot.

There always seemed to be another expense, another hire, another investment. They're capital efficient with outsourcing and contractors. CEO/CTO/COO make salary concessions, and they were still below break even.

Koala - DEAD. Warmly - DEAD. Common Room - DEAD. Pocus - DEAD. Unify - PIVOTED. Vector - PIVOTED. “Signal Orchestration” was supposed to be the future of outbound… But the space ended in an acqui-hire frenzy when nobody could raise their next round.

Here are my observations from this decidedly sad state of affairs:

1. MARTECH SUCKS

If you aren’t a CRM, you are high churn. Martech gets tried and ripped out, most of the time it’s not mission-critical. RB2B is the worst of it - leads/intent data sold as a SaaS to a high-churn buyer persona. Couple that with people raising money before the churn kicks in, and you get a bunch of companies that couldn’t raise the next round and were forced to puke to make payroll. 

This paradigm also applies to the zombies of the COVID era (6Sense, Salesloft, Clari), who thought they had large, sticky customers but ultimately did not. If I were in martech (which I am) and were dependent on a capital transaction to realize business value (which I am not), I would be… sad.

2. VC RUINS GOOD BUSINESSES 

A few of these businesses would have been nice bootstrapped, “lifestyle” businesses where the founders could have built cool stuff, had a happy team, and made millions of dollars per year on their own terms… had they set out to do that. Some combination of pre-churn euphoria and easy money, led to an entire space falling. Investors needed the companies to be bigger than they were meant to be, and the founders with either a little or a lot of convincing, agreed with them.

3. LACK OF TRANSPARENCY IS A PROBLEM 

Every “acquisition” gets framed as some positive thing, even though no price is mentioned, which is misleading to other Founders. An acqui-hire and earn-out is not what any of us are doing this for. Yet these are the headlines we see, and we send congratulatory text messages and DM’s. The problem is that this is a bad outcome, and most VC-backed companies either experience something like this or worse. 

What I want to see is a table of who sold for what and what the Founders walked away with. Then compare it to a table of bootstrappers. But we will we never see it, so the show will go on.

4. WHAT ARE YOU DOING THIS FOR???

It’s very easy to get incredibly ambitious with YC, SpaceX, Anthropic, OpenAI buzzing all around you. Investors all want those outcomes, so they all push you to believe it’s possible. For some people, it might be. But in most cases there is a huge amount of luck (along with skill) in becoming one of the 10% (or less) of people that succeeds after taking VC money. 

I have friends who just couldn’t be happy unless their business became enormous. Yes, you need VC for that. But most people who took money did so because it looked like it made sense at the time, and they were selling a small stake in their business so they didn’t think it was a big deal. But it is. It always is.

My sense is that many people out there are feeling the pain of the red dashboard. I wanted to write this post to let you know that I’M FEELING IT TOO. 

And in my experience, red sucks no matter how big the numbers are. I’d rather go from $0-$1 than go from $100 to $99. 

The question is not how much it sucks, but what you should do about it. Everybody on LinkedIn knows my plan by now … I knew RB2B would stall out around $10m ARR given the TAM and how high the churn was, so I’m not going go fight it. I’m going to let it be what it wants to be - a $9 to $11m ARR super-lean biz with a dead simple product. The quickest and easiest path to the site visitor. 

Instead of entering the signal feature war (which ended in bloody death), I’m “weaving another basket” as Felix Dennis says in one of my favorite books about entrepreneurship, How to Get Rich. After two years of dismissing bad ideas (there were six of them), we finally think we’re on to something w/ unlimited contact data api’s for AI agents. 

All of that is a really long-winded way of saying that if you’re seeing red … and many of us most certainly are … there’s really only one thing you CAN do: 

Keep building.

The spreadsheet that almost killed my company looked completely reasonable at the time. I built it in 10 minutes.

Sadly, I've watched dozens of founders make this same mistake.

After years of grinding, you've found early-product market fit.

Growing 20-30% month over month. Mostly inbound until recently. Then you hired 2 salespeople and had them start doing outbound.

And it's working!

More net-new demos than before. Truly incremental activity. And unlike inbound, you can actually MEASURE it. Full speed ahead!

So you open a spreadsheet.

If 2 reps are booking 10 demos a week… what if you had 10 reps doing the same thing? What if you had 20 reps?

You start extrapolating. Year-end revenue. Series whatever. Maybe PE interest.

Then you start hiring more.

(Even writing this is triggering some serious 2023 PTSD for me!)

If you have made this mistake - and I know many reading have - you know what happens next.

Your 10 new reps contribute ALMOST NOTHING to the overall demo booking.

You try everything from incentives, to power hours, to activity targets.

You're eventually forced to give their manager an ultimatum…

And it all blows up and ends in layoffs.

From 2012-2022, using the classic Predictable Revenue playbook, you could put a college kid in front of a laptop, call them an SDR, and they actually WOULD create demand. They would book demos. 

Not today.

Starting in 2023, outbound reps can only CAPTURE demand you've already created… they do not CREATE demand.

Repeat after me.

"Reps do not CREATE demand. They CAPTURE it"

I have the battle scars to prove it.

In order to avoid this painful outcome for your employees, sales leadership, and company, before you grow your sales org, you must do one thing...

You must PROVE that you can systematically expand your ability to generate leads through marketing before you make a single hire. 

Ask yourself:

1/ Are your reps' calendars completely full? If no... 
2/ Fill them without hiring. If yes..
3/ Figure out how to get more capacity by offloading admin.

Step 2 is where everyone skips ahead.

It feels slow and boring. Unsexy compared to building a sales org.

But your company has to learn to CREATE demand before you hire reps to capture it.

That spreadsheet showing what 10 reps could do will always look reasonable.

The founders who survive learn to ask one question first: 

Where is the demand actually coming from?

Everything else follows from that.

I have 2.4 stars on Glassdoor. But over the last year, we've had near-zero voluntary employee attrition. Here's how I retain top talent:

1.  Focus on providing intellectual, interpersonal, and financial capital.

Forget the fancy office, the free lunches, and unlimited PTO. None of that matters. What matters is whether your people are doing the highest-level work possible, alongside the highest-level talent you can attract. And whether they're getting paid well enough to never entertain a recruiter's DM. Amazon can attract great talent without paying well. You can't.
 
2. Get an exec coach to teach you how to communicate clearly.

Two years ago I knew I was a horrible manager. I just didn't know the main skill I lacked was the ability to clearly define expectations and deliverables. Sounds simple. But if you spent 43 years not doing it properly, it's a hard habit to break. Jonathan Shapiro gets the credit for two years of hard work with our exec team, shaping us all into much better managers. Best money I've ever spent.
 
3.  Don’t squirrel.
 
Like any excitable founder, I used to get ideas and start working on them immediately. That works when you are 3 people, but not when you’re 30.  Teams get frustrated when they're told to work on one thing Monday and something completely different by Thursday.

We rolled out EOS (Entrepreneurial Operating System), and the single greatest benefit has been defining the work during quarterly planning sessions and refusing to deviate until the next quarter. 
 
4.  Give excessive recognition when good work is done.

Praising people for good work in a public setting is one of the most rewarding things you can do for your team members. Any time a shout-out is given in a smaller setting, make sure the exec team hears it, and shout out as many people as you can during all hands meetings. 

5. Every once in a while, do something fun.

I haven't done this, but if you asked each of our 35 remote team members what their favorite work moment of the last 12 months was, my guess is over half would say it was either our Cancun or New York offsites. Our global team gets together in person twice per year, stays in nice places, does fun stuff, and eats great food.  Yes, we're bootstrapped. Yes, it's expensive. But I know this small thing is a big reason people stick around.

TAKEAWAY

Finding and keeping a talented employees is like finding and keeping a spouse.

If you want to find a good spouse, you have to first live a life that is worthy of a good spouse.

If you want to find and keep good talent, your company has to be worthy of good talent.

We used Clay + Claude Code + Apify to launch a multi-channel outbound system that self-improves over time. Here's the actual process Alex Fine🌲 and Understory built for us:

Step 1: They fed 569 demo call transcripts into Claude Code via the Fireflies API to extract competitive signal: which tools kept coming up, what specific language frustrated prospects used, what objections stalled deals, and what made someone stay on the call.

Step 2: Claude analyzed all 569 calls and built a competitor displacement map. Nine competitors ranked by how often they appeared and how dissatisfied those prospects actually were, based on the exact words they used. 

Step 3: Every transcript, intake form, strategy session, and past campaign result got indexed into a structured knowledge base. It updates automatically every time a new call comes in. The system gets smarter with every interaction.

Step 4: They connected Apify directly into Claude Code via MCP. Claude identified the right actor, pulled unique data on decision-makers at companies actively using those high-displacement competitor tools, and pushed 9,000+ contacts to a webhook automatically. Absolutely no manual list building.

Step 5: That webhook dropped everything straight into Clay. They enriched, validated, and segmented by firmographic signals and intent data.

Step 6: They wrote the copy based on everything the knowledge base surfaced. Messaging built around the exact language our target prospects use when they're unhappy with a competitor. Every version synced live to Google Docs via the Google MCP so we could see and edit in real time.

Step 7: Campaigns launched via Instantly for email and HeyReach for LinkedIn. Every reply, positive, negative, or neutral, gets analyzed and fed back into the knowledge base. Every LinkedIn response. Every new demo call that books. Claude re-analyzes what resonated, what didn't, and why. The brief updates automatically. The next campaign starts with sharper targeting, better messaging, and fresher signal than the one before it.

Campaign 2 starts smarter than Campaign 1.

Marty Kausas: Why do you hate VCs so much?

Me: How much time do you have?

BACKGROUND:

Marty is a young-buck YC-founder with early traction.

Ed Hallen is the co-founder of Klaviyo, an IPO’d decacorn.

Every Marty is hoping to become Ed someday. Ed has reached the endgame of the life the VC/YC path is selling, he's worth $100’s of mm now, and I spoke to him the other day about this.

Ed: “Most VC-backed founders end up failing. That just sucks for Founders.”

He told me about an article he wrote for the Harvard Business Review about what he calls the “Mighty Middle”.

He concluded sub-VC scale, bootstrapped companies in niche markets had far higher probabilities of creating life-changing outcomes for founders than the VC track...

And therefore are better for the Founders!

But that wasn’t the most interesting part.

When you talk to Ed about Klaviyo, you can tell he doesn’t think of himself and his co-founder as any more capable than their VC-backed peers.

You get the sense that he believes Klaviyo is where it is because of a few breaks that were totally out of their control. Things they NEVER saw coming.

1. Linking themselves with Shopify when it was a $50m valuation, now it’s $150b (a 300x!)

2. Mailchimp got in a fight and killed their integration w/ Shopify in 2018

3. Email is the one positive NRR product in SMB

What would have been the fate of Klaviyo if none of this was true?

We will never know, but my guess is it would be MUCH smaller than the $1.3b run rate (or whatever Klaviyo is now).

The last point Ed made on our call was my favorite.

“Hundreds of millions of dollars has zero utility beyond a number MUCH smaller.”

His point is that most Founders want the freedom to build cool shit, and live the life they want.

A huge amount of money in the bank, and the huge company that young founders think they want, can work AGAINST those goals.

But good luck trying to explain that to a 25yr old paying $3k/mo rent in SF. 'I'll find that out for myself', says the young Founder. Touché.

Last but not least, I always point out the VC path is dependent on transactions with volatile valuations for the Founder to realize the fruits of his labor. 

A decades-long effort of creating a VERY good business most of the time ends up in a very low-paying job with a boss (your investors). Why? Because if you're VC-backed and your business stops growing, your equity is torched. 

Klaviyo was the exception.

Is Pylon?

Only time will tell.

Marty and YC types make the mistake of bucketing Ed’s “Mighty Middle” in the “lifestyle business” category and dismissing us as “playing small”.

It’s not about playing small.

It’s about freedom, and making sure if Marty were to create a great business (and he probably will), the fruits of that labor accrue to Marty (which is unlikely).

So to answer your question, Marty.

Why do I hate VC’s so much?

Because I want YOU to win. And I want you to be free.

But I think by taking $50m, you minimized the odds of both.

13 things I believe about startups:

1. Ideas don't matter, execution is everything. I've watched founders with mediocre ideas execute their way to massive success, and brilliant ideas fail because they couldn't ship. Nobody will sign up to execute your ideas for you.

2. Your skills compound over time. The first year is brutal because you're learning everything from scratch. But every year after that, you get faster at everything. 

3. Focus on profit from day one. Not growth at all costs, not market share --profit. Ten years later, that profit has grown to where we have resources to pursue any opportunity we want. Profit gives you control.

4. Embrace being small and barely profitable for years. Making just enough to keep the lights on doesn't feel glamorous. But being small and self-sustaining will ultimately compound into real profits and the freedom you actually want.

5. Product quality dictates your trajectory. If you have word of mouth, everything you do works. If you don't, nothing works. 

6. No amount of marketing can overcome a bad product. But a great product makes all your marketing work 10x better.

7. Great talent is everything. When I was stuck at $2M ARR with Robly, I had 38 employees running a call center out of my apartment. Today I run multiple companies doing tens of millions in combined ARR with a tiny team. The difference is the people.

8. You need both great product AND great marketing. Technical founders think they can just build something great and customers will come. That almost never happens. Marketers think they can talk their way to success with a mediocre product. That doesn't work either. The founders who win are obsessed with both.

9. Build an organic audience. I went from 4k to 140k LinkedIn followers in 2 years. That audience is what allowed me to scale RB2B so fast. Every founder should be learning how to do this.

10. Design your life for decades, not months. I never interview, hire, or fire anyone. Internal meetings only on Monday. Content Tuesday, marketing Wednesday. By Friday my calendar is empty. Some call that soft, I call it optimizing for the energy to keep at this for decades.

11. Have patience and never give up. I wrote a letter to myself in 2016 describing the life I wanted -- $25M ARR, lean team, total freedom. It took 4 years of hopelessness after that for something to finally work. Relentless focus on one thing over years is what makes you successful.

12. People ahead of you can't give you good advice. They can only share their experiences. The game changes constantly -- what worked 5 years ago might be irrelevant now. They can share experiences so you can pattern match, but don't blindly follow anyone's playbook.

13. Everything compounds. The relationships, profit, brand -- it all compounds. In the beginning, nobody respects you for that small thing you're working on. But if you can get something going and keep doing it for a decade, you'll have the one thing you actually wanted: freedom.

If I had to start a brand new AI company from absolute zero, knowing everything I know now from building 3 software companies to over $35M in combined ARR, this is exactly what I would do:

—
This is a long post, buckle-up
1200 words
[bookmark this]
—

Why Most Founders Fail

Founders fall in love with their idea instead of their customers’ problems.

They build something for 12-18 months before talking to anyone. That’s why 90% of startups don't make it to $1M ARR because all they had was an idea, locked themselves in a room with their co-founders and then showed up waiting for the world to buy it.

But that’s not how this works.

——

Discovery Before Everything

Before writing a line of code, I'd commit to 50 discovery calls minimum.
Your only goal is to find people who will pay you for something that you haven't built yet, and I'm talking about actual payment, not just “Yeah, that sounds interesting.”

My favorite story about this is Barkbox, which is now publicly traded.

Matt Meeker owned a Great Dane and lived in NYC. All the dog stores sold tiny toys for tiny dogs. (This was 2010, pre-Amazon Prime)

Matt took a Photoshop image, showing a monthly delivery of 5 large toys for $29. He showed it to every large dog owner. When they said they were interested, he swiped their card for $29 with a Square reader.

He got 50 purchases the first day before he had a website.

——

Getting Those First Calls

I'd start with my network. People who match my ICP.

Andrew Mewborn uses this message for his company: “Hi [first name]. I was at Outreach, and now I'm building a Highspot and Seismic competitor, 3x cheaper and 10x more user-friendly, and we have around 4,000 active users that love us. Are you be open to giving feedback?”

He gives them with a $100 gift card (and yes, this still works)

You could also offer paid advisory roles to director-level people in your ICP or go to industry events with just a notepad.

Alina Vandenberghe, founder of Chili Piper (now $40M ARR), would go to sales meetups and find the most influential people. She'd approach them with a drawing of her product and ask, “Would you buy something like this? If not, what would we have to change?”

How do you find influential people? She’d look for who’s getting hugged. The person receiving the hug is the one you want to talk to.

——

What I’d Ask On The Calls

I'd lead with my sizzling one-liner that makes people's eyes light up.

For RB2B, it was “person-level website visitor identification.” Before us, there was only company-level. When people heard person-level, they got excited.

Then I’d ask 6 questions:

1. Do you understand the problem I'm trying to solve?
2. Do you have this problem?
3. How are you solving it today?
4. Would you pay for this solution if I could get it to you tomorrow?
5. What else would it need for you to pay for it?

I'm thinking of charging X. Would you pay that?

The goal is to understand their pain so deeply you can solve it better than anyone.

The only metrics that matter at each stage of SaaS:

$0-500K ARR: Weekly MRR growth rate
$1-5M ARR: Weekly MRR growth rate
$5-10M ARR: Churn + Top of funnel growth

Are you growing week over week? If so, by how much?

Churn doesn't matter until $5M+. Before that, you don't have enough customers for the data to mean anything. 

Once you hit $5M, churn starts eating you alive if you ignore it. That's when it matters.

Top of funnel growth becomes the game at $5-10M. You've got the product, you've got retention. Now it's about feeding the machine.

But before $5M…

Weekly MRR growth rate ONLY.

One year ago our churn was over 15%/mo. I was focused on Founder Brand, one-to-many selling, and building a community. Jonathan Shuster, DM’d me and said there was one OBVIOUS thing I was ignoring completely:

Actually talking to my customers. 

(This seems so idiotic in hindsight I’m embarrassed to be even write this)

I finally linked up with Jonathan this summer.

He helped me put together a low-lift churn study and set up a regular cadence of customer interviews. 

While it hasn’t come close to solving the churn problem, it has helped churn, and made me feel much better about the direction we’re going with RB2B. 

Here’s Jonathan’s 5-step guide on who to interview and what to say: 

1. Find your BEST customers. 

- Dig into intercom, stripe, baremetrics, or whatever else you have to find your longest-standing, high LTV customers.
- Pull 35-50 people out of that segment to ask for an interview
- Send them a one-to-one email asking them if they’d talk to you (the CEO) about the product for 15min
- Line up 5 interviews. More than 5 and you will start hearing the same thing over and over again.
- See my copy below (image)

2. Find a few of your your churned customers who you THOUGHT should be high-LTV.

- Enrich your customer list by revenue, industry, employee count, web traffic, and whatever else you use to determine ICP fit
- Find 35-50 churned customers that match your ICP
- Send them an email that says “I am the founder of RB2B and I really, really, really want to understand why you churned. Would you be willing to hop on a 10 min call to discuss?”
- Line up 5 interviews (you only need 5)

3. Ask your best customers five questions like these (modify them for your product)

-  Why did you choose us versus the other solutions out there? What's the rest of your stack look like?
- If we were to disappear tomorrow and you couldn't have us, what would you do?
- When you find a good lead/visitor, how do you know it's a good match?
- What do you do when you find a good lead? How do you route it?
- What do you do when you find a bad lead?

4. Ask your churned customers the following q’s (modified for your biz): 

- How'd you choose to evaluate us? Where'd you hear about us?
- Do you use anyone else to solve this problem now?
- Be brutally honest, what didn't work?
- How do you figure out what is a good vs bad lead
- What would make it so you could use us again?

5. Determine your product roadmap based on what you’re not doing that people want, and your marketing message based on what you ARE doing that people love. 

TAKEAWAY

Most founders will read this, nod along, and never actually do it. 

They'll tell themselves they're too busy building, or that they already 'know' their customers.

Don't be that founder.

Block off 2 hours this week, send those emails, and have those conversations.

Your solutions to churn are hiding in plain sight. 

You just need to ask.

I’ve bootstrapped $0 to $1M ARR three times. If I had to start over with no money and no personal brand, here’s how I’d hit $1M ARR in under 12 months:

1. Hunt whales in their natural habitat.

Alina Vandenberghe told us on UnF*ck My Startup that she went to sales meetups and showed the people in the room who looked like they knew everybody a diagram of what she wanted to build (now $40m ARR Chilipiper). She asked if they’d buy, if not, what else would they need. Then she built it.

2. Turn your journey into content.

The indirect benefit of an audience rooting for you comes in the form of “pull” (rather than push) recruiting, a customer base who are also fans, and improved content creation skills as time goes on. B2B companies are transitioning to a Kardashian era. You may think it's cringe, but it is the future.

3. I’d test different offers with cold email.

4. Obsess over word-of-mouth like your life depends on it (because it does).

5. Ignore every “growth hack” until step 4 is bulletproof.

6. Don’t hire ANYONE.

In the last 30 days, RB2B’s churn has gone from 9.1%/mo to a STILL HORRIBLE 8.8% (down from 15%/mo last September). I’m incredibly confused about what to do next. Here’s why:

1. RB2B is a high-churn product category with a high-churn persona and a high-churn GTM motion (freemium, no sales, no onboarding, etc)

2. The category is also plagued with issues:

- You can’t book a demo by spamming a site visitor
- You can’t book a demo from a site visit if you can’t outbound in the first place
- A low % of traffic is ICP, for most people it’s not a channel on its own

Product improvement is the only REAL way to reduce churn.

So we need to keep improving.

But, how?

———

Product improvement for RB2B is what I’m confused about.

There’s an obvious feature set that the product person in me wants to build:

It’s “RB2B handles the whole site visitor workflow”.

Meaning - someone hits the site, we:

1. Filter for ICP using AI
2. Provide additional qualified contacts at the account
3. Do AI research for personalization
4. AI writes the copy for the sequence
5. We send the LI connection and messages

And if we built that, it would be better to rebuild RB2B from scratch.

———

I think it’s easy to understand why I think that’s what RB2B “should” be.

Here’s why I’m confused:

If you properly filter for ICP, it will eliminate 90% of site visitors.

For MOST of our customers, that would cut lead count.

For the few who are larger, the workflow described above COULD work…

But high-traffic sites want a bunch of OTHER signals to get demos.

Then once we added the OTHER signals and a workflow builder, we would be in direct competition with (and trying to sell to the same GTM teams as) Common Room, Unify, Warmly…

…and the scariest of all, Clay.

No thank you.

———

So what are we going to do?

Rather than compete with the companies who are owning workflows, we are going to try to power them.

1. We’re creating an OEM product where you can put our pixel inside your own and have RB2B’s identity inside your own app

- One pixel for all your customers, one account/credit balance, you route contacts however

2. We’re going to create a set of “Identity APIs”

- There have been IP > company API’s for years, but there has never been an IP > person API. We’re going to build that and others

At the same time, we’re going to improve the experience of RB2B.

- We’re improving the daily email to be meaningful and interesting
- We’re going to provide additional contacts from the account
- We’re going to replace standard lead info w/ session descriptions and source

Things like that.

As horrible as it feels, as I stare at that almost double-digit churn, and realize the implications for future growth (or lack thereof...)

Two weeks ago I said AI Agents are handling 95% of our sales and support and I replaced $300k of salaries with a $99/mo Delphi clone. 25+ founders DM’d me… “HOW?” Here’s the 6 things you MUST do if you want to run your entire customer-facing business with AI: 

1. Create a truly excellent knowledge base. 

Your AI is only as good as the content you feed it. If you’re starting from zero, aim for one post per day. Answer a support question by writing a post, reply with the post. After 6mo you have 180 posts.

2. Have Robb’s CustomGPT edit the posts to be consumed by AI. 

Robb created a GPT (link below) that tweaks posts according to Intercom’s guidance for creating content for Fin. The content is still legible to humans, but optimized for AI.

3. Eliminate recursive loops - because pissed off customers won’t buy

If your AI can’t answer a question but sends the customer to an email address which is answered by the same AI, you are in trouble. Fin’s guidance feature can set up rules to escalate appropriately, eliminate loops, and keep customers happy.

4. Look at every single question every single day (yes, EVERY DAY).

Every morning Robb looks at every Fin response and I look at every Delphi response. If they aren’t as good as they could possibly be, we either revise the response, or Robb creates a support doc to properly handle the question. 

5. Make sure you have FAQs, Troubleshooting, and Changelogs.

FAQs are an AI’s dream. Bonus points if you create FAQ’s written exactly how your customers ask the question. We have a main FAQ, and FAQs for each sub section of our support docs. 

Detailed troubleshooting gives the AI the ability to handle technical questions. Fin can solve 95% of script install issues because of our Troubleshooting section. 

Changelogs allow the AI to stay on top of what’s changed in the app to give context to questins about features and UI as it changes.

6. Measure your AI’s performance and keep it improving. 

When we started using Fin over 1y ago, we were at 25% positive resolutions. Now we’re above 70%. You can actively monitor positive resolutions, sentiment, and CSAT to make sure your AI keeps improving and delivering your customers an increasingly positive experience. 

TAKEAWAY:

Every Founder wants to replace entire teams with AI. 

But nobody wants to do the actual work to make it happen. 

Everybody expects to flip a switch and have perfect customer service. 

The reality? 

You need to treat your AI like your best employee. 

Train it daily. Give it the resources it needs. Hold it accountable for results. 

Here’s the truth that the LinkedIn clickbait won't tell you… 

The KEY to successfully running entire business units with AI?

Your AI is only as good as the content you feed it.

Building in "stealth mode" is the DUMBEST thing a startup founder can do. Here are the top 6 reasons why building in stealth mode is a rookie mistake (and why I won't sign your NDA):

1. No one is going to steal your idea.

Anybody who is capable of executing your idea is already busy doing something else that they believe is more valuable than whatever you share with them. Don’t make people sign NDA’s to talk to you. It makes it clear that you don’t know what you’re doing.

2. You NEED feedback.

People farther along in their journey can often help you avoid mistakes that all entrepreneurs make (and you will make, too!). More importantly, you need to be speaking to your ideal customer profile to figure out if your product is even valuable.

3. Ideas are like assh*les. 

Everybody’s got one. Furthermore, this is hard to believe, but someone is definitely working on whatever your idea is already (if it’s even a halfway-decent idea). That’s just the world we live in.

4. Ideas are just multipliers of execution.

Jeff Bezos and Elon Musk created trillion dollar companies through being the best at execution. Many others had the ideas of online bookstores, electric cars, and rich guys have been trying to go to space (unsuccessfully) forever. A great idea makes great execution go even faster, but is worth nothing on its own.

5. Building in stealth increases the risk of your startup to a point where you will almost certainly fail.

Please read “Four Steps to the Epiphany” by Steve Blank. The ONLY shot a startup founder has is to follow the method in this book. You must be developing the customers for your product simultaneously with the product itself. If no one will buy what you are building, you must stop and start over. The sooner you find out the better. There’s no way to find that out in “stealth mode”.

6. Our intuition is a terrible indicator of market viability.

You simply have no idea what the market is going to want, with the one exception of you building something to solve your own problem. However, that is still a market of one, and you need to go out and validate that others have the same problem to even have a SHOT at succeeding. 

TAKEAWAY:

Don’t build in stealth mode. 

Go get feedback from your ideal prospects.

Talk to founders who are more experienced than you.

Build up your customer base before you start building your product. 

Read “Four Steps to the Epiphany”, and treat it as Gospel. 

But please, pretty please, above ALL ELSE…

Don’t ask me to sign an NDA to hear about your “idea”.

Koala shut down and Unify raised $40m at $260m (on $5.6m ARR) in the SAME WEEK. Two opposite outcomes for two companies trying to solve the exact same problem. How could this happen? Here's one man’s opinion — who is also in the “signals” space 👇

You don’t shut your business down because you are frustrated with how fast it’s growing.

I don’t know the Koala team, nor exactly how they were doing. I can imagine they were struggling with a lot of the same issues we are at RB2B.

Here are 3 big reasons the signal space hasn’t lived up to the hype:

- For MOST B2B companies, there isn’t enough signal for meaningful pipeline
- You can’t just spam a website visitor and get anything back from it
- Once you combine OTHER signals with the site visit, the number of signals drops even more…

Which leads to incredibly high expectations coming from this inspiring narrative in an era where entire channels were being lost (and not replaced) and CAC is headed to the moon in all others.

Not to mention a handful of vendors who were NOT doing signal - ai copy generation, omnichannel outreach - all jumped in because the demand was so high…

All to converge with a very similar product offering solving a nearly identical problem, onboarding hopeful marketers whose expectations become shattered when they realize only ~10% of the expected juice came out of the lemon when they squeezed it.

A reality that is lower than expectations = churn.

Welcome to The Painful World of Signals that I know so well.

That ROUGHLY explains my hypothesis about Koala.

But what about Unify?

How does a 2.5yr old startup doing the exact same thing raise at 42x revenue?

I have a couple theories there, too.

My observation is that “signal stacking” crushes for sales-assisted PLG dev tools and security platforms … Explosive AI tools are the hero users.

1. OpenAI is an investor, which helped them bag other AI decacorns after PMF

2. Everyone wants to be AI decacorns (perplexity, cursor), insane social proof dynamic

3. Late stage venture SaaS have high traffic & growth teams that can make this type of thing work (justworks, sofi)

These three factors - all relatively large deals - plus a semi-credible AI narrative are showing high early growth rates which VCs can spin each other up about.

What are investors missing here?

1. They are so young that churn hasn’t actually happened yet

2. The TAM of the PLG dev/security space isn’t huge, rest of b2b is “meh” with this category

3. This product category doesn't inherently expand in state over time - NRRs will be HARD

To expand, Unify will need to add features to sell into other parts of the org. Signal activation isn’t like a CRM - it’s not a database that people are comfortable paying more for over time.

The biggest problem of all is that prospecting tools like Unify have a “reverse network effect”…

The more adoption they get, the less effective they will be.

CEO Friend: We just crossed $4m ARR bootstrapped, but are break-even, stalling out, and have virtually no cash in the bank. I’m so stressed I can’t sleep. I’m thinking about raising $5-$7m in VC to invest in growth. What do you think about that idea?

Me: I hate that idea.

CEO: Why?

Me: If stress reduction is what you’re after, raising VC for growth will make your stress level even higher.

CEO: What? Why?

Me: There are three buckets you can fill with money - either from investors, or customers. 

Bucket 1: Pay yourself/Your team
Bucket 2: Build up a cash buffer
Bucket 3: Invest in growth

Filling the first two buckets will MEANINGFULLY reduce your stress levels. 

But the 3rd bucket won’t … 

ESPECIALLY if you add an outside partner, and you’re using THEIR money. 

You will be far, far more stressed, because from that day forward, if your business EVER stalls - like it stalled just now - the odds are that it won’t be worth more than the capital that went in. Which means you’re unlikely to see a dollar.

CEO: Hmm. I never thought of it that way. What are my options?

Me: If you were coming to me saying you’re stressed and you were going to take $5-$7m of secondary - investor capital straight in your pocket - that would be a different story.

If you’ve never made money before that would likely eliminate some stress … 

But if you did $10-$15m that would probably eliminate a LOT of stress.

CEO: Yeah … But I can’t really do secondary right now. We’re just not there yet. What then? 

Me: Growth stalling out is a sign of falling out of product-market fit. It happens all the time, to me included. 

When it happens, the only thing you can do is get as small as possible and find a new product-market fit. 

You may have to take a step or two back, but you’ll figure it out, get unstuck, and start moving forward again. 

CEO: Hmm - I didn’t even realize that was an option. I’m going to get smaller, build a war chest, and pay myself and our team w/ customer money. 

Thanks for the advice… I feel my stress level dropping already!

1,850 paying customers, 13 months, $5m ARR, 5 employees. How did we get so far so fast at RB2B? Here's our 6-step startup playbook (and my message to founders who feel STUCK):

1. We created MASSIVE awareness.

Santosh and I spent the six months prior to launch building an audience of buyers. And doing discovery with over 300 of them to validate that what we had was worthwhile.

2. We threw a terrible MVP out there and got feedback.

We set people up with a pixel and emailed a spreadsheet to people and tried to charge them $495/mo. It didn’t work. Some said “I’d pay $199.” Others said “meh”. We kept throwing spaghetti against the wall. 

3. We found a magic moment - the Slack App.

Tate built a beta that pushed site visitors into Slack, with a headshot. I started showing people at dinners and parties on my phone, and saying “this person is actually ON our website right now”. I had never experienced this type of positive reaction to anything I had built in the past. I knew we were on to something.

4. We made that magic moment FREE.

I believe in the immense power of free, ESPECIALLY if you have a magic moment that you can make free. We screwed up on many things related to pricing along the way, but I think we got this one correct. I do not think we would be anywhere near where we are if Slack wasn’t free.

5. We listened to customer problems. But didn’t actually fix much.

If you’ve been following from home, you probably know that we have a churn problem. You may even be thinking “they really haven’t built much over the past year”. Customers gave us tons of feedback on the product and user experience, but I viewed the solutions they were asking for as the first steps to causing other problems. We have much better solutions now (on their way) so I’m glad I waited.

6. We stopped all marketing (besides me posting on LinkedIn). 

I thought the product and experience was so bad that we were just burning leads. I killed every channel but posting - which I’m able to do because we don’t have investors. We are starting to ramp other channels back up. We slowed down, to speed up.

TAKEAWAY

For anybody but an AI coding company, $0-$5m ARR in 13mo with 5 people is exceptional. 

Especially because it’s not just something we’re SAYING we’re doing… 

We actually DID it.

What’s the flip side? 

We’re stuck until we provide an experience that is different than today.

I’ve been stuck 6 times in my career. 

It feels just as bad at $25m ARR as it did when I was stuck at $3m. 

But here’s the good news… 

1. We have gotten unstuck 5 of the 6 times
2. I know how to get RB2B unstuck 

The anxiety of being stuck and the satisfaction that comes from getting unstuck is probably why I like the game so much in the first place. 

If you’re stuck, just know that you CAN get unstuck. 

I was right where many of you were 5 years ago, stuck at $3m for 3 years. 

And I got to $25m. Bootstrapped. Thanks to my lean, hungry team.

You can get there too.

Just keep building.

Most first-time startup founders I talk to set themselves up to fail. Here are the 7 biggest mistakes I see nearly EVERY founder make (myself included):

1. You spend too much money on things you don’t really need

People love getting offices, hiring salespeople, getting VA’s, expensive video equipment, software, and even setting up an entity pre-revenue. In 2013, I bought a VOIP phone system a year before we had a customer! Cash will be EXTREMELY tight at some point, even if it’s not now. Remember that.

2. Hiring people before $1m ARR

This is a hot take. I think there should be a technical co-founder building and a business co-founder doing sales, marketing, and support until $1m ARR - just like Klaviyo did. If you have that discipline, you will be profitable, control your destiny, and emerge with product-market fit.

3. Thinking you are an “ideas guy” and can find an operator

I spit out my drink when I hear this. Just like when I hear someone talking about “stealth mode”. Thinking someone will do the hard work for you at this nearly impossible stage is delusional. Once you get to $10m ARR with under 10 people, you earned it, but until then, no way.

4. Not “doing things that don’t scale” under $1m ARR

First-time founders don't understand how manual getting to $1-$3m ARR is. It’s face-to-face conversations, however you can get them, taking the feedback, and improving product as quickly as possible. Nothing will work until the product is great, so all that “growth hacking” will be a waste of time and money.

5. Thinking seed funding means you have a good business

If you were able to raise money for your idea pre-revenue, it means nothing more than you could sell a vision to investors. The hard part is making a business out of it. Keep that in mind and avoid funding at all costs. You’ll thank me later.

6. Not posting on organic social media starting TODAY

This one took me a decade to realize, and a year after I started to master. Nothing is more powerful in today’s world than being able to create great organic social media content that your prospects have demand for independent of what you’re selling. If you start today, you’ll get zero engagement, followers, or leads, but that’s not the point… You’re one day closer to finding your voice.

7. Thinking you’ll be in and out in 3-5 years

Founders should have a decades long time horizon when they start. People wildly overestimate what they can accomplish in a year, but wildly underestimate what they can accomplish over a decade.

TAKEAWAY:

Being a first-time founder is hard.

Literally everything is working against you.

If we knew how hard it was, most would never start.

But here’s the good news...

As Alex Hormozi so elegantly put it:

Every successful person started with:

0 revenue
0 subscribers
0 customers
0 fans

And the only difference between them and everyone else is they actually start.

But that’s not REALLY the secret.

The successful ones not only start…

They keep building.

It's 2025. If you're a SaaS founder, you're probably screwed. Anything you do that works gets copied, CAC is up, LTV is down. Here are the 7 things I see that ARE working - in a world where most things are NOT:

1. Creating a TRULY AI-first startup

I'm not talking about slapping some LLMs on top of your old-school workflows and calling yourself "AI-native." I mean creating products on top of LLMs that increase productivity by 10x or more. Companies like Cursor, Windsurf, Icon, and Fyxer aren't using AI as a feature - they're using it as their foundation.

2. Word-of-mouth

This has always been true, but it's more critical than ever. With word-of-mouth, anything works. Without it, nothing does. In 2025, costs are up, attention is fragmented, and buyers distrust everything. The startups that are growing have products so good that users can't stop talking about them.

3. Personal brand

The ability to create organic content that your target market has demand for - completely independent of what you're selling - is the most efficient GTM motion that has ever existed. It's an automated trust-building machine, and trust = brand. In 2025, brand is built one post at a time.

4. Cold email ... in specific contexts

Enterprise buyers? Jesse Oulette says they're blocking it completely. But SMB and VC-backed startups? Blast away, but do it correctly. Most founders sending to an audience where it WOULD work can’t get it to work because of bad messaging.

5. Thought leadership ads

If you know how to create bangers on LinkedIn, pick the best ones and put some $$$ behind them. Promoting a post you know LinkedIn already loves is one of the cheapest sources of eyeballs you can get.

6. Cold calls

We had Kevin Dorsey on UnF*ck My Startup this week and he told us the EXACT cold call script that was generating a 12%-13% rate of accepting the pitch on 200 dials/day/rep that is booking him 20-25 meetings/week per rep. Today. In 2025. Calling works.

7. Staying ridiculously lean

I’m seeing startups winning that are running with tiny teams, staying profitable, and controlling their own destiny. Getting to $10M ARR with 10 people is now the gold standard… Not raising a $100M round at a unicorn valuation.

TAKEAWAY:

Startups are hard. They always have been. 

But in 2025, everything seems so much harder.

Most SaaS founders are going to fail this year because they're running playbooks that worked in 2020.

But if you focus on these seven things, you might have a shot.

In the past 6 months I’ve spoken to over 50 founders doing $1m-$10m ARR. 99% of them feel STUCK. Here are the 6 biggest mistakes they’re making that prevent them from unlocking growth to $10m ARR: 

1. They’re trying to be the same but better. 

It’s easy to get early traction when you’re a little bit better than the incumbent. To reach scale, you need to be 10x better than what people are already using to get them to switch.

2. Their messaging isn’t clear enough.

Crystal clear messaging helps everything. Unclear messaging hurts everything. A decent product with subpar messaging can get to a few million ARR. You have to tighten it up to get to $10. 

3. They don’t know who their ideal customer actually is.

Taking money from anyone and everyone is often what you have to do in the beginning. Honing in on an ideal customer and building for them will often get you unstuck.

4. They don’t understand their unit economics.

If you don’t know what’s working and what’s not, you don’t know what to scale and what to pull back on. Many startups do everything in the beginning and stall out because they have no idea what was actually working and what wasn’t.

5. They don’t have word-of-mouth.

If you have word-of-mouth, everything you do will work. If you don’t have word-of-mouth, nothing you do will work. Some startups capture initial excitement but fail to deliver on promises made, and lose this critical tailwind.

6. Their churn is abysmal because the product isn’t there yet.

RB2B is guilty as charged. We’re working every day on a total reinvention, and if you also have abysmal churn at mid-single-digit ARR, you should tirelessly improve your product too.

TAKEAWAY

Startups are hard.

My life for the last 12 years has been getting stuck, then unstuck again.

In fact, I’m stuck right now!

The good news is that no matter how stuck you feel:

A. There are thousands of founders who are stuck right there with you
B. No matter how stuck you are, you can get unstuck, it’s in your hands

I’m here to tell you don't get defeated.

The rewards for blowing past $10m ARR are unimaginable.

Keep building.

Over the past 18mo, I’ve been a guest on over 200 podcasts and we’ve gotten more than 500 LIVE attendees every week on my live video podcast, “UnF*ck Your Startup”. Here are 6 things I wish I knew before I started podcasting: 

1. Use a Run of Show

Have to credit Christopher Merrill with this one. Your audience will have a better experience if you know what you’re going to talk about and stick to segments over pre-determined time slots. Don't wing it.

2. Have a unique point of view OR amazing delivery OR amazing production.

You’ll listen to LeBron talk about basketball all day long, no matter what the quality is. Think comedians for amazing delivery - or my favorite, Founders w/ David Senra. For production, think “Serial”. Make sure you have one of the three, or you’re going NOWHERE.

3. Constantly ask “WHY ARE THEY STILL LISTENING?” 

Your mindset needs to be that you WIN and LOSE attention second-by-second. That mentality shift help you go from a conversation to delivering incredible value. People have infinite options. Make content so good they stick.

4. Get a great mic and lights. Get a decent background. 

Nobody wants to listen to someone talking from a bedroom. My office is a 10x10 prison cell than John Eley made look sweet with $1k worth of stuff from Home Depot. You can get away with a $200 webcam, but make sure to have good lighting and a great mic. NO ONE wants more Zoom-looking Videos.

5. Try to ladder up guests. 

Always try to invite people that have 10% more status than your highest status guests. I’m trying to do that more this year. 

6. Have incredible patience. 

Sam Parr told us that it took literally YEARS for them to build their My First Million audience. He said it was terrible. They were BEGGING for subscribes, and have made over 700 episodes. You have to ask yourself … are you really that committed? 

TAKEAWAY

Podcasting isn’t for the faint of heart.

If you wouldn’t enjoy it as a hobby, you probably shouldn’t start. 

Because realistically you’ll be lucky if you get anything out of it. 

But just like posting on LinkedIn … 

The real reason to start podcasting ISN’T downloads, leads, or deals. 

You start to be one day closer to finding your voice.

Because in 2025, finding your voice is your one true superpower.

Agency CEO: I’m thinking about building a SaaS product. I’ve been talking to people about what I want to build, and a few investors have offered seed funding. Should I raise $1-$2m to start building it? 

Me: Absolutely not.

Agency CEO: Why not? 

Me: Can you fund development from your agency profits? 

Agency CEO: It would be tight, but yes, we could. 

Me: Do that. Period.

Agency CEO: But we’ll probably get good terms. Like $10m valuation or something. 

Me: You should never ever EVER raise money for a product that doesn’t exist yet if you don’t have to, ESPECIALLY if you are building SaaS for the first time.

Agency CEO: Why not?

Me: Product creation is incredibly risky, mostly because human intuition is a horrible indicator of market viability. You will burn through the money and be left with nothing.

Agency CEO: Should I just bag the idea and keep running my agency? 

Me: I didn’t say that… What I DID say is that you should not raise money, at least until you have product-market fit, preferably longer. 

Agency CEO: How do I get product-market fit?

Me: In an ideal world, before you even start building, you start running a proper discovery process. Talk to hundreds of prospects about their days and their workflows, and get a real sense as to how painful the problem is that you’re solving. If you can sell it before you even have it, that’s a very strong sign that you are on your way to PMF. 

Agency CEO: Yeah but where do I even start? How do I find these people?

Me: You dial your messaging in and start doing outreach to your network and to your networks’ network. I’ve had success asking people for feedback. My friend Andy Mewborn gets great traction from offering a $100 Amazon gift card in exchange for that feedback.

Agency CEO: But WHEN? I’m super busy running my agency. 

Me: You need to treat this discovery effort as a side hustle and start working on nights and weekends. Trust me - if you do not do this first, your SaaS will fail.

Agency CEO: That is far less exciting than raising $2m. 

Me: That may be true - but most startups fail. If you actually do it, you’ll have a far greater chance at actually succeeding. 

Don’t raise $1-$2m. 

Run a proper discovery process before you do anything.

You’ll thank me in a few years.

CEO: My startup is at $2.5m ARR after 24mo, and it’s just me and my co-founder. We want to raise $5-7m at around $30m post. What do you think? 

Me: I hate that idea. 

CEO: Why? 

Me: What are you planning on doing with the money? 

CEO: We think we have pretty decent PMF, so we want to build out engineering, sales, marketing, and CS teams so we can speed up.

Me: The reason I hate it is because if it’s just you two right now you don’t have any repeatable processes. So, you’ll go hire all of these people, it will be a total mess, it will slow you down, and you’ll likely end up doing a large layoff to get small again. I’ve been there. Twice.

CEO: That makes sense. What would you recommend doing instead? 

Me: If you can, I’d recommend continuing to bootstrap it, hiring someone in each department first, start delegating, and see how that goes. As that starts to work, hire a couple people under them. 

CEO: I’m doing the math in my head - depending on how quickly that happens, I’ll probably need money for that.

Me: You will - but not $5-$7m. I had Ryan Allis (sold iContact for $169m) on our show last week. He said something I never heard before - NEVER raise more than 1x your ARR.

CEO: Why not?

Me: Because if you do raise 5-10x your ARR and you stall out, EVER, you will join the 80% of VC backed companies where investors get their money back but the founders get nothing. CEO: Sounds like pretty prudent advice. But won’t my valuation be lower if I take less money? 

Me: Yes, but valuation is meaningless unless you are getting a chance to sell significant secondary. I’m talking many many millions. Raising as little money as possible maximizes your probability-weighted financial outcome.

The Two Opposing LinkedIn Audience Building Strategies (explained in 60 seconds):

THEIR WAY: 

- Create posts around generic topics that LinkedIn loves…
- Work-life balance, hiring, mental health, LinkedIn leadgen, AI, checklists
- Ghostwriters are used (most of the time)
- Join engagement circles or hire engagement service to “get in feeds” 
- Post viral content over meaningful content (think memes)
- Have no intention about who the actual members of your audience are
- Do not reply to comments on your own post
- Stay away from work in public, share only wins but not losses
- Use someone else or AI to reply to other peoples’ posts
- Do not analyze quality of your own audience
- The goal is to grow followers to the highest number possible

OUR WAY: 

- Create the best hook possible for that given post
- Write every line so that the reader will be compelled to continue
- Wrap up the post with something coy to create a dopamine hit
- Zero involvement in engagement pods or artificial post inflation
- Affinity is built through true thought leadership and meaningful content
- Know exactly which audience each post will reach (Founder, Sales, Marketing)
- Create talking head videos for most posts to build a stronger connection
- Be wildly transparent about the journey, share numbers and mistakes
- Answer every single comment yourself
- Have high percentage of your audience in the ICP (75% for me)
- Goal is to drive quantifiable sales outcomes (booked demos, signups)

TAKEAWAY:

Agencies tell you they can ghostwrite and grow your followers with just 1 hour of your time a week. 

They can, and they will. 

It’s one way to start building your brand, and you can see SOME benefit.

Here’s the problem... 

The best case outcome is that you’re “well known”. 

I believe the power of LinkedIn is the opposite. 

If you create the best content, and figure out how to reach your ICP, you can become “known well”, which is a far more powerful level of trust.

Trust = brand. 

In 2025, brand is built one post (and one comment) at a time.

I just bootstrapped RB2B to $5m ARR in 13mo with 5 people. I also bootstrapped Retention.com to $13m ARR with 6 people. My secret? What I do is repeatable. Here’s my 7-step playbook to 7-fig ARR with tiny teams:

1. Validate demand before building ANYTHING

- Retention started as a feature in my first startup, Robly. People loved the identity feature but hated Robly, so we knew the demand was there
- RB2B is a B2B version of Retention. We did 300 discovery calls with marketing leaders to validate the market wanted person-level ID for ABM

2. Create a DIFFERENTIATED (albeit terrible) v1 of your product that people will talk about

- Retention was originally a batch spreadsheet of site visitors. Pretty terrible user experience, but it was so different that it got tons of traction
- RB2B is riddled with horrible problems to this day – but 1 year ago we were the only vendor who resolved site visitors to the person-level

3. Create MASSIVE AWARENESS… Through your HUMANITY

- The best way to accelerate word-of-mouth is through social. I did a crazy FB ads campaign for 6mo when we launched Retention. It stopped working, but EVERYBODY in our TAM saw them… That + word-of-mouth + cold email
- For RB2B I was able to create viral LinkedIn thought leadership to our addressable market for the 6mo prior to launch. We had a 3000 person wait list

4. Eliminate sales and onboarding friction

- At Retention, we gave our customers 25 free emails, then forced them to a call with Diana. She did thousands of 5min presentations that answered key questions and got people to do a 2mo paid trail, then upgrade (or drop)
- At RB2B, we did a freemium product to a PLG with a sales rep answering questions and helping with tactical onboarding for high-value users

5. Wait an unreasonably long time to hire ANYBODY

- At Retention, we had the same 6 people at $13m ARR as we did at launch
- At RB2B, Robb has managed to create an AI that supports 40k free users

6. Spend time and money on very few wildly positive ROI things

- At Retention, we had so few people that we had to focus on what mattered. Product, onboarding, cold email, demos, and “wow-ing” our customers
- At RB2B, we cut all paid marketing spend ($100k/mo) and our growth sped up

7. Keep doing steps 1-6 until you hit $10m ARR

- At Retention, not only did we not burn any money, we actually distributed $5m of cash to the co-founders on our journey to $10m ARR
- At RB2B, 12mo in and we are already profitable, with no plans to grow staff or spend on anything until $10m ARR

TAKEAWAY

Yet VCs want Founders to raise money, usually to crash and burn.

I think more people should start startups my way.

If you can bootstrap $10m ARR, you can do ANYTHING you want with your life.

You will be making millions of dollars and playing by your own rules while enjoying total freedom.

You can do it, too.
