Over the past 10 years I’ve read over 250 books about startups. Here are the 8 books that got me from $0-$25m ARR with zero funding (in order of impact) and what I learned from each of them: 

1. Four Steps to the Epiphany by Steve Blank 

If you are an aspiring founder, this is a must read. I re-read the first half of this book each time I start a startup. It’s dense, but there is no better description of the steps to take to reduce your chance of failure to ZERO. Takeaway: Build your audience of buyers before you launch, or you’re screwed.

2. Founder Brand by Dave Gerhardt

This has been more impactful than anything I’ve ever done in business. Yes, I have magical alignment in that I am my ICP and my ICP lives on LinkedIn. Even if you do not have that alignment, Founder Brand content creation is an automated trust-building machine and will pay dividends.

3. ReWork by Jason Fried

The OG SaaS bootstrappers have great takes on the benefits of creating a business outside of the VC ecosystem. You should read this book, then immediately do Y-Combinator’s Startup School, and land somewhere in the middle. (Jason agreed to come on UnF*ck My Startup. Just don’t have a date yet. We can’t wait!)

4. Y-Combinator Startup School

These guys understand the importance of pursuing growth as a key metric, but can skew towards making you think you should try to go big (because many of the biggest went through YC). As I said, land between here and ReWork.

5. The Hard Thing About Hard Things by Ben Horowitz

Such an incredible articulation of the things that make the CEO job difficult. Must-read for any aspiring Founders to know what you’re getting yourself into.

6. The Great CEO Within by Matt Mochary

Read and re-read as you advance along your journey. Different bits will resonate each year. Being a CEO is hard, and creating a balanced life around the job is even harder. Matt rolls out playbooks for inside and outside the company.

7. $100m Offers by Alex Hormozi

“Have an offer so good your prospects will feel stupid not doing it.” Read, and re-read again. Then look yourself in the mirror and ask yourself if that statement is true for you. If not, make it true… And when you do, everything will change.

8. Purple Cow by Seth Godin

Nothing describes the necessity of being different better than this book. Make yourself a Purple Cow so you get talked about. It’s within your control, do it!

TAKEAWAY:

These books have formed my beliefs about how successful startups happen.

You reading this today - and RB2B going from $0-$5m - is the direct result of me picking up Founder Brand by Dave Gerhardt two years ago.

It planted a seed that led to a rabbit hole and I just kept digging.

That's the power of a great book.

If you're a founder and you feel stuck, logoff Linkedin for a bit.

Head over to Amazon and order one of these 8 classics.

Then put 10 minutes a day aside and start reading.

It may change your life.

I sold my first startup for $10m cash. And immediately got scammed out of $1m in banker fees. If you're a founder thinking about selling your company, here's a step-by-step process for closing multi-million deals (w/ $0 in banker fees): 

BACKGROUND

- I had Aye Moah (CEO of Boomerang) on UnF*ck My Startup LIVE
- She bought GQueues for millions, but unlike me …
- She did the deal directly with the Founder, no banker, minimized legal expense
- Early stage SaaS buyers and sellers need to READ THIS POST 👇

Here’s Mo’s 8 playbook to close multi-million deals w/ ZERO banker fees: 

1. Don’t use a banker!

- Contrary to popular belief, if you have the buyer (or seller), you don’t need a banker.
- Lawyers can advise you and create all documentation to get a deal done

2. Hammer out main deal points w/ Founder on the other side.

- This is key for minimizing your LEGAL fees
- Don’t spend billable hours on points that don’t matter

3. Operate from a position of trust. 

- It’s VERY helpful to have a relationship with the counterparty years before
- This was Mo’s situation, my situation when I sold my co, and Jesse Stein’s situation on all 3 of his acquisitions
- You can tell lawyers to ignore inconsequential things… like a $9 payment that occurs after a cutoff time/date that could be wordsmithed infinitely to take care of edge cases

4. Be aligned with values and product philosophy.

- Cultural fit is the most important factor for making post-transaction integration successful
- Make sure both sides care about the “why”, both of the business, and product decisions

5. Find out what MARKET is.

- Tap into your network to figure out transactions that have CLOSED for deals like yours
- Ideas about what market might be (without closes) are not relevant
- You can get a business valuation if necessary

6. BUYERS: Figure out what you can afford to LOSE.

- “If this goes to ZERO, what can I afford to pay and still survive”?

7. Figure out deal structure. 

- Asset vs stock deal, cash vs. equity payout, holdbacks, earnouts, etc.
- Lawyers can help with what is possible, Founders can figure out if it’s appropriate

8. Sell to the RIGHT buyer. 

- These are our babies. You want to sell to the right person
- The acquirer of my business still had ALL employees after the 3 year non-compete

TAKEAWAY:

There are a few lessons here if you’re buying or selling an early stage SaaS.

1. Don’t pay bankers millions of dollars unless they are finding your buyer
2. You can minimize legal fees by hammering out major points w/ Founder
3. You should get to know potential buyers of your startup TODAY

Selling a startup is the ultimate reward for this journey we’re on. 

When you sell (or buy), keep as much money as you can. 

Don’t make the same mistake I did. 

You’ll regret it.

2. They all have an undying commitment to excellence.

In a way, these biographies are simply collections of unique stories about lives dedicated to the pursuit of excellence. Steve Jobs was about tech and film, Michael Jordan was about basketball and fashion, Sam Walton was about retailing.

But what unified them was their extremely high bar for quality and their pursuit of excellence.

Steve Jobs said “Quality is so much better than Quantity. One home run is so much better than two doubles.”

3. They put the best teams around them they possibly could.

The emphasis on collecting “A players” and constantly trying to upgrade talent comes through in every episode. Especially in engineering - Steve Jobs said a great software engineer could be 100x more productive than a good one.

A CEO friend of mine raised $40M at $400M valuation. Two years later? The money’s gone and his ARR is flat. If you asked him the biggest mistake he made he would tell you: hiring salespeople. Here's why:

To be clear, it wasn’t JUST hiring salespeople… It was HOW he hired them.

Another founder buddy of mine recently did a Private Equity (PE) round.

His investors were pushing him to grow his team of reps from 5 to 20. 

Fortunately, my PE backed friend talked to my CEO friend first.

Here's how that conversation went:

PE Backed Friend (PBF): We just raised $25m and they want us to hire a bunch of salespeople.

CEO: Of course they do. But don’t do it yet. That pressure is EXACTLY what smoked me, wasted 2 years and $40m, and very likely shaved 10 years off my life.

PBF: Ok… well… what do I do? 

CEO: Are all of your reps at 100%? 

PBF: Not really. One might be, the rest aren’t. 

CEO: Do not hire ONE MORE REP until ALL of your reps are at 100% capacity. If you build a machine that has slack in it already, you will experience all sorts of cultural and motivational problems. The same amount of demos your marketing machine is creating and reps are capturing will go to even MORE people. Your team will miss numbers week in and week out. You will attempt to solve that problem by demanding reps you hired to be AE’s do more and more outbound. That will not work. Your sales leader will probably either quit or be fired, because you’ll have the exact same productivity on 4x the team size.

PBF: That’s terrifying. Especially now that we’re PE backed.

CEO: Tell me about it.

PBF: What do I do instead? 

CEO: Before you hire a SINGLE REP, make sure all of your reps are at 100% capacity. Make sure your marketing machine can actually produce more pipeline. If and when you can actually flood your reps with activity and the entire team is at 100%… 

PBF: Then I hire reps? 

CEO: NO!!!! Absolutely not. You work on raising the 100% higher. Figure out how you increase the capacity of the existing team to handle the increased pipeline generation. Can you create AI agents that save account research and follow up time? Can you hire sales assistants to do some of the unavoidable repetitive work? ANYTHING to get your already 100% capacity reps more productive. THEN… AND ONLY THEN… Do you start slowly adding reps onto the team.

PBF: I am so glad I spoke to you before I did anything.

CEO: Me too. 

TAKEAWAY

Institutional capital still wants to push founders into rapidly hiring reps to accelerate growth.

While that sometimes works, it’s VERY easy to do it the wrong way.

What’s the RIGHT way? 

1. Make sure your marketing machine can grow
2. Get all your reps to 100% capacity
3. Raise that capacity as much as possible
4. Slowly add reps to THAT machine

Build your team that way and you can’t lose.

Over the past two years, I’ve spoken to 300+ startup founders and DM’d with 1000's more. Most feel stuck, strapped, and stressed. Why? Because they're all making the same startup-killing mistake. Here's the #1 reason founders fail:

They have not done (or do not know how to do) true Customer Discovery. 

This usually plays out one of two ways. 

The FIRST CAMP of Founders raise seed capital for their brilliant idea.

Then lock themselves in a room for months (or years) and build their vision. 

They emerge to find that no one wants or needs what they’ve built. 

Not even the people who said they cared initially.

The SECOND CAMP is even more heartbreaking. 

They’ve read all the YC blog and memorized Four Steps to the Epiphany.

They KNOW they need to be doing discovery. 

They are doing multiple customer interviews per day.

But alas, they launch, and… No one cares, again. 

Not even the people who said they cared initially. 

What happened to these poor, unsuspecting Founders? 

They fell victim to the fact that most people - even during discovery - can’t help but be nice to a hungry Founder who is working his ass off building something. 

They’ll tell you your idea is great. 

They’ll say they have the problem you’re solving. 

The’ll tell you they want the solution your presenting. 

They may even tell you they’ll pay for it when it comes out. 

But here’s the thing… When you go back to them, they won’t buy. 

Why? 

Because you ran your discovery in the wrong way. 

Here's how you run discovery the RIGHT way:

1. You talk prospects about their DAY, not your product
2. You analyze their WORKFLOWS, but don’t mention your solutions
3. You understand what MOTIVATES them, and how they measure success

The idea that you are building a product to solve a problem they have may not even enter the conversation until the last few minutes. 

When it does, here are a couple pro tips: 

- Try to talk far less than a normal conversation.
- Watch for facial microexpressions. People can’t fake those. 
- Try to get them to pay for something you don’t have. GREAT indicator.

I’ve gone $0-$1M 3x times, each time in half the time with half the resources. 

My discovery got twice as good each time. 

The most successful founders I know ALSO ran the best discovery processes… 

Whether they realized they were doing it or not. 

Don’t let a flawed discovery process keep you from the startup you deserve.

Massive success is out there … Waiting for you to come grab it.

Unicorns are born one discovery call at a time.

COO Friend: I’m going to build my own SaaS. Should I raise $2m and quit my job today, or should I work nights and weekends and try to bootstrap it?

Me: I’ll give you the same advice I give everybody who asks me this… DO NOT quit your job until you KNOW you have something worth quitting for.

COO: What do you mean?

Me: Most startups don’t work. If yours does, you’re lucky. I know you’re burned out working for the man, but taking the leap from a stable job when you have a wife and a kid is a very big deal.

COO: But isn’t that what the $2m is for?

Me: In theory, yes. In reality, you will end up burning through the $2m in 18mos. You’ll build too much product without NEARLY enough customer discovery, since neither you or your co-founder have ever taken a product from 0 to successful before.

COO: But I’ve talked to a handful of people in our industry, and they’re all excited about my idea.

Me: One of the BIGGEST reasons founders fail is because NOBODY will be honest about your idea when you present it. They will be nice. A false signal.

COO: How do I make sure the feedback is honest?

Me: I do it one of two ways. The first is not let on that you are building anything, and just try to understand your prospect’s day, their workflows, and how your solution would fit into them.

COO: What’s the second?

Me: I sometimes sell people things that I haven’t started building yet. I get them to put an actual CC into a Stripe form. Or sign a contract. I love this method because it’s the strongest signal… But it comes after discovery.

COO: Won’t people get pissed you bait-and-switched?

Me: My experience is that if you have solved a painful problem, when you say “I don’t have this yet, but when I do, you will be the first one to get it”, they will wait patiently.

COO: That seems like it would be helpful. But my CTO is ready to quit his job too, and he’s a successful AI engineer at well known SaaS. Doesn’t that mean anything?

Me: That means nothing. The dream of being a Founder is too seductive. People only see where I am, they have no idea how hard it has been to get here.

COO: Isn’t the fact I can raise money a good indicator?

Me: Nope. You are a successful, intelligent, articulate dude. Investors are buying that. And they have modeled in a 70% chance that you will fail. That is COMPLETELY unrelated to your prospects wanting your product.

COO: Well, shit. What should I do?

Me: You should have 100s of discovery calls with prospects to validate what you are providing is valuable. Meanwhile, if your CTO wants to start working, figure out one narrow workflow he can hack together that can provide value, and try to start getting feedback from a light version of the product before you do ANYTHING. Try to get people to pay you for something you don’t have yet. If you do all that, you’ll know it's worth quitting your job for.

COO: On nights and weekends?

Me: YES, ON NIGHTS AND WEEKENDS

Don’t quit your job.

Don’t raise $2m.

You’ll thank me in a few years.

Now, let's look at Keap (formerly Infusionsoft).

- Acquired 23 years later for $80m

Rough. 

Why do I advocate for bootstrapping? 

Compare those two outcomes to another startup...

The ACT-ON/Infusionsoft outcome.

I would love to ask the founders of either company one question and one question only…

“Wouldn’t you have rather done it like Maropost?”

I hit rock bottom Thanksgiving 2017. I was sitting in my brother’s living room watching a Digital Marketing 101 course on my laptop. 10 minutes in I started to panic... "There is NO REASON anyone would buy us over MailChimp."

TO SET THE STAGE:

- I was 4 years into building my startup Robly Email Marketing
- We had been stuck at $3M ARR for 2 years
- We got to $3m ARR sales-led, ran out of leads
- I thought I needed to learn about marketing
- I went to DigitalMarketer(.)com and started taking courses

So I sat there on the couch, listening to Ryan Deiss talk about marketing. 

A few minutes in a bright yellow card filled the screen.

At the top it said STATEMENT OF VALUE.

Ryan said, “If you cannot fill out this card for your business, do not do ANYTHING else.” 

He said that if you cannot articulate a clear statement of value for your business… who you serve, how you help them, and why your customers should choose you… Nothing else will work.

So like any bright-eyed founder in their 20’s, I set out to conquer the card. 

60 seconds later I felt a wave of panic in my body.

My face turned red, my heart raced, my breathing accelerated.

As I looked at this VERY simple fill-in-the-blank card… 

“[PRODUCT NAME] enables [CUSTOMER] to experience [OUTCOME]”

I realized I couldn't answer it.

There was nothing I could write down for Robly, my stuck $3m ARR startup.

There was not a single reason ANY group of people would choose us if they knew about Mailchimp. 

1. We weren’t any less expensive. In fact - Mailchimp would have been FREE.
2. We were WAY behind on features, and they were building faster than us. 
3. We had no integrations, and they had over 1,000 of them.

I sat there for an hour, thinking about every customer I had spoken to over the prior 3 years, comparing what we offered them to Mailchimp.

Then a wave of nausea came over me.

Nothing had been working for me because nothing was GOING to work for me.

I didn’t sleep much that night.

At around 2am, I had an epiphany.

One that many startup founders had before me.

“I need to do something COMPLETELY different than what I’m doing right now.”

There was no way we were going to catch up to Mailchimp in the email space.

I woke up with the naive optimism that only a Founder in their 20’s can have.

I was strangely at peace with the fact that what I was working on was dead.

I needed to make a product so differentiated I could fill out this simple card.

At the time, I had no idea how long it would take…

Nor did I realize that the answer would come almost two years later, when I launched GetEmails (now Retention.com).

TAKEAWAY

Go fill out that statement of value card for your business.

Be as brutally honest with yourself as possible.

If you do not have a compelling answer.

More ads and cold email aren't going to help.

P.S.

I started a private community to help $0-1M founders find PMF. Almost everyone is struggling with the “statement of value” problem. If you want to join us, DM me.

As the Founder of Y-Combinator, Paul Graham has invested in 4,000 startups (including 85 unicorns) and helped create over $600B in enterprise value. When he was asked how he would fund a startup if he were starting TODAY, I was shocked by what he said:

PAUL GRAHAM: “I would raise maybe $500k, keep the company small for the first year, work closely with users to make something amazing, and otherwise stay off SV's radar.”

(So the guy who has seen more VC deployed than any human being alive says he basically wouldn’t use VC!)

PAUL GRAHAM: “Ideally I'd get to profitability on that initial $500k. Later I could raise more, if I felt like it. Or not. But it would be on my terms.”

(…Get to profitability?!?!?! Why does no one take his advice?)

PAUL GRAHAM: “At every point in the company's growth, I'd keep the company as small as I could. I'd always want people to be surprised how few employees we had. Fewer employees = lower costs, and less need to turn into a manager.”

(…I have said these exact words over and over to our team … We always want to be the smallest version of ourselves that we can be)

———

I have never felt so validated for the path we have chosen at Retention.com. 

$25m ARR, 40 employees.

I love how people always seem surprised by how small our team is.

I just NEVER would have guessed that Paul Graham - who has seen more intergalactic successes than literally anyone - would share my business building beliefs. 

These are the words of a bootstrapper at heart! 

What’s the takeaway? 

The fundamentals of business are pretty simple. 

Rule #1: Make things people love
Rule #2: Make more money than you spend

The crazy thing is that we exist in the one space in the world where rule #2 not only does not apply … 

The whole VC machine is set up to get young founders excited about how “rich” they are going to be (but most likely not) and have them do the exact opposite. 

I always loved reading Paul Graham’s essays. 

I love them even more now… 

Because he’s got the heart of a bootstrapper.

I’ve written 100+ viral Linkedin posts. That means over 1,000 likes or 100,000 views. Everyone thinks it’s because I sh*tpost about 6Sense or brag about how much money we make. They’re wrong. Here’s how you can unlock LinkedIn virality for your ICP: 

You MUST find your “Prolific Zone”.

What’s the story behind the Prolific Zone? 

I can explain it in three easy steps. 

Step 1: Don’t be mainstream.

Mainstream, down-the-middle content is just noise, ESPECIALLY coming from a small voice. You’ll never break through.

Step 2: Don’t be crazy. 

If you are TOO far out to the right or left of any issue, you won’t be taken seriously. Don’t sound crazy.

Step 3: Find your PROLIFIC ZONE.

Just right or left of middle, but not TOO far out, lies your prolific zone. It’s not crazy, but it just far enough out there where one side LOVES it and the other side HATES it… meaning it’s POLARIZING.

The beautiful thing about social media is that people on both sides engage with prolific content.

Not only do they let YOU know how they feel, they let EACH OTHER know how they feel. 

The best prolific zones are true, authentic to you, and out there enough to bring in both sides to the discussion… 

And they ultimately become your content pillars.

Here were a few of my prolific zones of 2024:  

1. The Predictable Revenue Model is dead 
2. Bootstrapping $10m ARR is the new unicorn 
3. I spend 60% of my time (as CEO) producing content

If you learn one thing from this post, it is to NEVER post anything mainstream.

- We JUST rebuilt our Hubspot integration to filter, route, alert, add to lead score, and start automations within the CRM
- We STILL have not teed up suggested messages using AI (the “what now”?)
- I ROYALLY screwed up our pricing on launch, and cost us 2mo of growth

Even though $10m will be MUCH harder than $5m because of our high churn.

Stupid Simple Sales Signals.

A CEO friend of mine just shut down his startup after 12 years. He raised over $30m in VC, and the co-founders’ families put in $2m. In 2017, he tried to hire me saying they’d “soon be worth $1B.” I was shocked at what he said when I turned him down:

CEO (to me): You’re not ambitious enough.

Me: What???? Why do you say that?

CEO: It's been 5 years, man. You’re wasting your life on your tiny startup. It’s not going anywhere.

Me: Yeah, but it’s MY tiny startup. 

CEO: We’ll be worth a billion soon. A small part of my startup will be worth so much more than your large stake of yours… And you’ll have a bigger impact working for us. 

Me: I have two main objections. First, paradise to me is a mid-20’s ARR SaaS with under 40 people. I don’t know how I’m going to get there, but that’s what I’m going for. Second, even if my startup is worth less and it’s less impactful, it’s MY startup, which your startup is not. You work for the VCs. I’d rather spend my time working on my own thing, even if I stay stuck here.

CEO: You’re too talented to be thinking so small. 

———

You already know how the story ends.

I now have my mid-20 ARR startup with 40 employees.

Here’s the craziest thing: 

We generated $1m in profit the same month he closed his doors. 

Believe me - my friend no longer thinks I’m “not ambitious enough”.

Here’s a few lessons for my fellow bootstrappers: 

1. The world is really hard on you when you’re small. Stay strong.

2. If you’re small but profitable, you can stay in the game.

3. The skills and effort you’re compounding are VERY valuable.

4. If you build skills and stay in the game long enough, the odds that you will get lucky and hit it big skyrocket.

Don’t let people tell you you’re wasting your life. 

Massive success is inside all of you. 

It just takes LOTS of time, and usually a little luck. 

Keep building.

On my run this morning, I was listening to "How to Make a Few Billion Dollars" by Brad Jacobs (founder of 7x billion-dollar businesses). He had an incredible take on hiring A Players vs B Players vs C Players:

The old adage is that A Players hire B Players.

And B Players hire C Players.

So never let B Players hire.

No C Players at all.

Have a short leash with B Players.

And give your A Players everything.

One of my CEO friends raised over $100M. His startup had a $1.2B unicorn valuation in 2021. I always thought he was CRUSHING IT on every observable metric. So did he. 

Then last week we went jogging and he started venting... 

He’s 13 years in, and the last two have been excruciating.

Rocketship to $50m ARR, almost no growth since 2022. 

He told me: “The only choice we have is to try to build literally everything, pitch tool consolidation to our biggest customers, and pray for expansion. The problem is every company in our space is doing it too”.

A few minutes went by before either of us said anything. It was just depressing.

Four years ago, he was running every day, eating well, looked great. 

Today, he’s rocking a chubby face and dad bod.

He broke the silence. 

“We’re completely stuck. IPO is off the table, I don’t know how we could ever get back to $1.2b valuation let alone a 3x from there. Nobody ever told me this was a possibility.”

This is the biggest reason I talk about bootstrapping so much.

So many founders are trapped in the hype-cycle, drowning in VC money, still burning epic amounts of money trying to figure it out.

But for most of them, there’s no way out.

I've been stuck before. I talk about it all the time.

Sometimes you get unstuck, find that killer product and before you know it you're everybody’s darling again.

But most of the time you're not. You're just treading water.

And then you wake-up, you're 50, dad bod, trying to internalize the idea that the likely outcome for your life’s work is selling your baby for less than the VC you raised.

Maybe you took life-changing secondary, and you’re fine with the situation. 

But maybe you didn’t, and you’re sitting there, anxious about how you’re going to get out of this situation, and even more anxious about what’s next.

My CEO friend isn’t unique. 

There’s a whole class of companies that raised at huge valuations, are stuck, and have no idea what to do.

They’re underwater, they know their plan is terrible, yet they can’t admit it to themselves… The consequences are too just too dire. 

This is what no one ever thinks about when they get on the VC treadmill. 

And that’s why I always say…

If you can bootstrap, bootstrap.

Me: I’m killing all our paid spend. Cold email, ads, UGC, SEO, everything.

CFO: WTF. What??? That doesn’t make sense. Didn’t cold emails and Linkedin ads acquire a ton of customers last year? 

Me: Our reporting said it did. And it may have helped… a little. But look at what happened as the year went on. The more we pushed - on ads, email, etc - the more money we spent and we got back less for every dollar. Diminishing returns. It’s not sustainable.

CFO: But if we turn paid off, won’t our growth hit a wall?

Me: In the short term, maybe. But maybe not. Nobody in B2B has the answer because everybody is terrified of turning anything off that “says” it’s working. Personally, I want to find out. And, I also want to spend ALL my marketing time and money creating a deep emotional connection in the mind of the market with the people who AREN’T in the market to buy right now.

CFO: That sounds great in theory, but how will you know it’s working? 

Me: Day to day we won’t. But here’s the thing - at any given time only 20% of our prospects are in market. If our stuff is good enough, it will constantly be in front of the 80% that aren’t ready to buy. We’ll know it’s working in a year or two… If we’re still growing faster than everybody else in our space with a fraction of the team size and zero paid spend (while they’ve ALL burned $10’s of millions of VC).

CFO: So your plan is to create organic social content for the 80% who AREN’T going to buy? 

Me: Exactly. The downside is we don’t have last-click or multi-touch attribution to tell us it’s “working”, but all that is BS anyway. Just because you can measure a click doesn’t mean that was why someone booked a demo. Most of the time it’s just tech getting in the way of something that was going to happen anyway, with vendors claiming credit to justify high pricing.

CFO: I still don’t understand why we wouldn’t focus on people who are ready to buy. 

Me: When people are in market, they are rationally shopping vendors for features and pricing. When they’re not, our organic content becomes an automated trust-building machine. When it comes time to buy, we’ll be who they think of when they are ready to add Person-Level Website Visitor Identity to their stack. Most of the time they’ll come straight to us, at the very least we’ll be in the deal.

CFO: So it becomes a type of moat...

Me: I watched 37 vendors whip up a similar product to ours in the 12 months since we launched last year. With AI, things are only going to move faster. In the future, brand will be this type of trust, built up over months if not years, one post at a time.

CFO: Alright, I’m starting to see where you’re coming from. 

Me: I forgot one more thing... If it all works out, RB2B will be WILDLY profitable. 

CFO: You know I love that. Spoken like a true bootstrapper!

Early-stage startup founders are bad at retaining employees. Here’s what you need to give to retain any employee, at any company, in any situation: 

Interpersonal Capital: 

- Are they working with people they respect and admire?
- Are they working for leaders whose status will be higher in the future?
- Is their contribution respected by the team, do they feel heard/seen?

Intellectual Capital: 

- Are they working on things that are interesting and challenging?
- Do they see a path towards more new and dynamic things?

Financial Capital:

- Are they being compensated fairly vs. peers inside and outside?
- If performance and equity is involved, is that appropriate/fair?
- (I have observed that “fairness” is more important than the number)

TL;DR

1. Interpersonal
2. Intellectual
3. Financial

Always solve for these three types of capital. 

You’ll never lose an employee again.

When scaling a startup, every CEO should focus on 3 things (and it's not revenue, churn, or hiring great talent):

BACKGROUND:

Over the past 10 years, I read "The Great CEO Within" by Matt Mochary 4 times.

Each time I was at a different part of the scaling journey, so each time something different resonated with me.

When I read it recently, one idea stood out WAY more than it had in the past …

The idea that the *emotional burden* of scaling a startup is substantial.

And it's not fair to put the weight of that burden on your family.

You need a support system to deal with it along the way.

That's why I think every CEO scaling a startup should do 3 things:

1. Get a therapist

I finally found a therapist and now we meet regularly. I have been seeing her regularly, and interestingly, my wife thinks I’m less of an as*hole now. Every week my therapist makes me “bring something in” to talk about, and that alone is making me more mindful of the little things on a day to day basis.

2. Get a mentor or coach

Santosh Sharan has served as my main mentor figure for the past 20 months. He was a huge help with some glaringly obvious shortcomings I had around instilling processes.

A while back, I was explaining to Brian Lee🏌🏻 that I was looking for a mentor or coach, and he connected me to Matt Blumberg, who found Jonathan Shapiro. Jon worked with 8 of our executives, and we've rolled out Entrepreneur Operating System. I’m VERY happy I pursued the mentorship path.

3. Get a network of peers.

I was really sold on the idea of meeting with a group of CEO peers regularly. One of my friends joined YPO and said the forum was excellent, so I applied, went through that brutal screening process, and didn’t get in!

I then decided to join Pavilion and Sam Jacobs' CEO group. It’s definitely doing what I was looking for - a group of people at a similar stage to me experiencing a similar pain in a slightly different way.

TAKEAWAY:

Startups are hard.

Maintaining good mental health throughout the journey is even harder.

It’s not fair for your significant other to bear the burden.

I found a therapist, a mentor, and a group of peers to help me along the way.

Being a CEO can be pretty lonely.

But it doesn’t have to be.

Two weeks ago I was having a drink with John Mackey (Founder of Whole Foods), and I nearly spit out my drink when he turned to me and said, “VC’s RUIN great businesses.” Wait… WHAT?!!?

Me: Tell me exactly what you mean by that, John.

Mackey: VC’s need to shoot for the moon. There are a LOT of great businesses that aren’t meant to be trillion dollar company.

Me: But didn’t Whole Foods do $22b in sales last year? 

Mackey: I’m not talking about Whole Foods - I’m talking about the MANY other Founders I’ve watched get on the VC treadmill, only to waste money trying to push a business farther than its natural state, ultimately destroying a huge amount of value.

Me: Funny enough - I see the same thing all the time. With software in particular.

Mackey: Tell me what you mean by that.

Me: I always thought that software businesses had the characteristics to be INCREDIBLE small-to-medium sized cash generating businesses. I’m talking - $50m ARR with $25m profit. We don’t have to move physical goods, so with a good enough product, we should be able to be WAY more profitable. 

Mackey: I agree with you there. 

Me: Yet, I don’t see anybody doing that. I only know of a few examples - Ross Andrew Paquette from Maropost being one of them, who has been generating over $20m profit for more than a decade. Nobody in our ecosystem even knows it’s possible, so they all head down the VC route as soon as they get any traction. Most fail, but even worse, some spend a decade or two creating businesses that are quite valuable, but not actually valuable to THEM.

Mackey: That’s one major problem. The problem I had at Whole Foods was that I needed VCs to fund my acquisitive growth strategy, but after seven or eight years they needed OUT. It forced me to IPO well before I otherwise would have.

Me: What will you do differently? 

Mackey: I’ll be planning for their exit from Day 1.

John Mackey thinks VC ruins great businesses. 

Yet, he’s very open to using VC money again. 

But only using it under the following conditions: 

1. Proven product-market fit of his retail business
2. He’s ready for rapid, international expansion
3. The exit (IPO) is planned from Day 1

Until then… 

He’s a bootstrapper.

In the past 24 months, I’ve spoken to hundreds of $0-1M ARR startup founders and 99% of them are STUCK. Here are the 5 biggest mistakes they're making that prevent them from finding Product-Market Fit:

1. They can’t clearly articulate what they do. 

This seems pretty basic, but under 1% of founders I speak to have nailed this. Why is it so important? A clear one-liner is what you use to get people to talk to you, and conversations (customer discovery) is what gets you from $0-$1.

2. They can’t clearly articulate who they’re for. 

“Small businesses” isn’t good enough. If you can’t tell me the age, gender, geography, income level, habits, and places these people hang out (both digital and IRL), you will get nowhere. 

3. They can’t articulate why someone would pick them instead of someone else.

Most founders are either not different enough or they are building something that if it works will get copied in a nanosecond (I’m guilty here too). Few seek difficult-to-build opportunities or businesses with true network effects.

4. They are trying to do growth hacking way too early.

This is the most common problem I see. “Adam, can I talk to your cold email guy?” or “Can you connect me with your paid ads agency?” from people with less than $1m ARR. You're not there yet.

5. They’re trying to do too many things for too many people. 

Unless your name is Parker Conrad, niching down is the only way to get something from $0-$1m. Be like Nathan Barry and create an Email Newsletter App for Food Bloggers to start. Then slowly expand wider and wider.

TAKEAWAY:

Product-market fit is very difficult to achieve. 

Most startup founders will never get there. 

But here’s the crazy thing… 

The reason most founders won’t get there isn’t because: 

- They aren’t smart enough
- They don’t have a good enough team
- They don’t know enough about sales and marketing

Most founders won’t get to $1m ARR because they aren’t doing the horribly manual customer discovery process that going $0-$1m requires.

On November 22nd, I declared RB2B dead. I cut $100k/mo in marketing spend (cold email, ads, UGC, SEO). Then in January we grew 10% to $4.5m ARR. Here are the 5 changes we made that led to our biggest ARR gains yet:

1. Cut all marketing spend - over $100k/mo

I went from thinking we had PMF in July to thinking we absolutely did NOT in November. When you fall out of PMF, there is only one thing to do - get as small as humanly possible, and find a new PMF.

2. Brought in Diana Ross to help with sales, onboarding, and enablement

Diana has been a part of two journeys to $10m ARR as the only rep (once with me), and her contribution was far beyond just selling. We have a hypothesis that this and other signals can be filtered by accounts in the CRM, they can trigger workflows in the CRM, and sales and marketing teams would rather action these signals from there than build in another platform.

We realized the workflows we sold last year were either put a human in front of a noisy Slack channel, or run leads through Clay as an ICP filter and shoot them out the SPAM cannon.

Slack is hard to action. Clay --> Instantly/Smartlead works GREAT if you’ve got a ton of traffic and a large TAM. But... ABM? Forget about it.

3. We stopped selling “leads” and “demos” as success

I got this REALLY wrong. Traffic is not leads. Demos are not the only measure of success of knowing a named account is on a high intent page. Orienting people towards that in the beginning led to disappointment.

4. We rebuilt our Hubspot integration

We realized in this new world, we needed to integrate w/ Hubspot CRM (not Marketing), we needed to add more fields, and most importantly, we needed to improve our documentation to show people how to alert reps, add to lead scores, trigger automations, all from site visitors, all in Hubspot.

Do you have a sales team that would like to know when a named account is on a high intent page and trigger HS workflows? DM me.

5. We built a Salesforce integration

Similar to #4, we believe that teams who use Salesforce CRM want to have their CRM filter the signal and reps alerted when a named account is on a high-intent page. And that signal can trigger workflows in the CRM.

Not just the first time… Every time the account comes back.

DM me if you want to route the signal into your CRM and alert your reps of a named account on a high intent page… and/or trigger automated outreach.

1. Marketers want their reps to know when a named account is on a high-intent page

- We closed 40 mid-market deals (over 250 employees) since July 1
- We launched RB2B March 1 and ended at $4m ARR with a tiny team
- We adopted EOS, are more focused and more efficient

THE BAD:

- Churn slows us down on both sides of the business
- We do not yet know our ICP for RB2B
- We have 37 copycats at RB2B
- We shrunk 3mo in a row in Q124

THE UGLY:

- We were wrong about how most people should use RB2B
- We did a large layoff in June at R! (reduced headcount 40%)

2024 was a rebuilding year.

Given where we are right now, 2025 will be too.

===

WHY WE ARE STUCK?

We have two business units – Retention and RB2B.

Retention.com:

We’ve been stuck since late 2023 because despite winning the “large Shopify store” market for what we do, we learned:

1. The number of stores we could make successful was smaller than we thought
2. Competitors show up faster than we thought they would
3. Despite fighting churn, there are still 8 reasons you’d turn this off

So, stores drop, but we have a great product, a great brand, an amazing in-person selling motion, and we’re slowly moving upmarket.

Add all that up and we chop around the same spot, ~$21m ARR.

RB2B:

RB2B was a rocket ship until about 5 weeks ago.

$0-$4m ARR in 9mo, with 30-50% monthly growth.

But all of a sudden we hit a wall.

In fact, we’re going backwards.

What the F happened?

1. We sold site visitors as leads, and promised demos (WRONG)
2. We thought the use case was emailing through smartlead/instantly (WRONG)
3. Our free slack app works against us because web traffic is so noisy
4. Credible competitors with other features bolted this on
5. People got stuck at the “what now” moment, we didn’t provide a solution

Meanwhile, our $119/mo plan is 20% churn per month, and some of our larger customers are and saying “we ran this for 6mo and didn’t close any deals”.

That sounds pretty bleak, and in many ways, it is.

And it’s why we’re moving backwards.

Add those things up and guess what you get…

Stuck. With a capital “S”.

===

If you would have told me on Jan 1 that we would end the year +$25m ARR with $12m run-rate profit and RB2B would go $0-$4m ARR in 40 weeks, would I have been happy?

No.

I would have been ecstatic!

Because Dec 31 last year I was stuck, with a shrinking business.

Somehow we had an out-of-body experience with RB2B.

At the same time, we “grew up” as a company and improved our profitability.

Yet as I sit here at my desk on Dec 31, 2025, I find myself just as stuck as Dec 31, 2024.

And just as annoyed.

Despite now having a business that is my moonshot goal from 5 years ago.

So, what did I learn? 

Continued in comments 👇

In 2024, I grew RB2B from $0-$4M in 40 weeks. Here are the 7 biggest mistakes I made along the way (and the ARR ranges I made them):

1. I created a $0 and $495 plan, got 3,000 signups, and 13 paying customers

Revenue Level: $0-$75k

I had the genius idea to give infinite leads and the Slack app away for free, but charge for other integrations. People parsed the Slack app, sent the data wherever they wanted, and laughed at me. We should have done credit-based pricing from the start.

2. I thought running the leads through Clay would work for everybody

Revenue Level: $0-$1.5m ARR

Clay has been an incredible partner and when you have enough traffic and the right agency partner, it really works. I didn’t realize that all of that needed to be true for people to be successful.

3. I sold web visitors as leads, and “success” as booked demos.

Revenue Level: $0-$3m ARR

I didn’t realize that a site visitor wasn’t actually a lead, it was a signal, and that a signal can be very useful even if it doesn’t lead to a booked demo (what if the visitor ALREADY had a demo?). Web visit + other signals and criteria make a visitor worth contacting.

4. I thought people would know what to do with the data.

Revenue Level: $0-$2m ARR

I was surprised when “what now” came back as churn reason #1. We've finally solved this problem and made these signals actionable.

5. I didn’t invest in filtering and routing through the CRM until three weeks ago

Revenue Level: $0-$4m ARR

We tried to build an ICP filter, but couldn’t nail it. Clay does a decent job, but most people don’t want to add Clay just to use this. Running the signals through the CRM for filtering and routing is a relatively easy solution that should have occurred to me sooner, and did not. Thank you Jeremy Horowitz'. Our new Hubspot integration fixes this.

6. I had no idea how many people would copy us.

Revenue Level: $2-$2m ARR

ZoomInfo now jumped on the bandwagon, as copycat number 37. Shame on me for not realizing that any SaaS that works will immediately be copied by 1,000 people in 1 week.

7. I had no idea how bad churn would be.

Revenue Level: $0-$4m ARR

I thought that we would be able to make B2B companies SUPER successful because of how well we do for our larger ecommerce companies. But, we sell a $149/mo plan that churns at 18%/mo. I did not see that coming. Maybe I should have?

TAKEAWAY:

Startups are hard.

RB2B was really hard, too.

I made some big mistakes…

Not the least of which was assuming a site visitor makes a lead.

I hope I don’t make these mistakes again.

What I do know is that I’ll continue to make mistakes.

Just new and different ones!

That's part of the game.

We keep building.

I wasn’t expecting Henry Schuck to come off the top rope and copy EXACTLY what RB2B was doing. But I’m not surprised - he’s the 37th competitor to pop up since launch. So, how do you survive as an early-stage startup in 2025?

- You have to differentiate on brand
- You have to differentiate on distribution
- You have to move faster than anyone else

It’s easy when you think about it that way. 

Your product matters… 

But in 2025, it’s what’s around it that matters most.

In 2016, I was stuck at $3M ARR with my Email Newsletter App for 36 months. Here's the best piece of startup advice I got during that period (and why it ultimately got me unstuck):

“Try to solve a problem in email that hasn’t been solved yet.” 

This sounds obvious in hindsight.

But I couldn't see it.

When I was stuck, I was: 

- Building features my competitors had to catch up
- Trying to do growth marketing w/o product-market fit
- Frustrated that nothing I tried would work

Once I solved an unsolved problem, I was:

- Selling something new that my prospects hadn’t heard of
- Had inbound demand, so didn’t need growth marketing
- Excited to get out of bed because I was having a blast

Try to solve a problem that hasn’t been solved in your vertical. 

Don't just try to do what everyone else is doing better.

Do something different.

It’s the quickest way to get unstuck.

CHURN

I have some bittersweet news. Yesterday, RB2B hit $4M ARR (just 40 weeks post-launch). Sounds great, right? Wrong. Churn has gotten so out of control that I’m officially declaring RB2Bv1 dead. Here’s what comes next:

Here’s what RB2Bv1 was: 

- Person-Level Website Visitor Identity
- Free push to Slack

Churn is higher than new business for four reasons: 

- People need to filter out the noise
- People need to route the signal to a rep
- Reps want to be told what action to take
- And there are now 3,247,892 copycats

Luckily, we’ve solved the first 2 problems, and the 3rd is coming soon.

How? 

We completely rebuilt our Hubspot integration 

We believe it solves the filtering and routing problem. 

Here’s the 5-Step RB2B >>> Hubspot Setup: 

1. Make sure your TAM is in Hubspot 
2. Send the RB2B Lead to Hubspot 
3. If the lead is an named account in Hubspot, HS tags a rep
4. Hubspot either alerts the rep in HS, who lightly tailors a message, or
5. Hubspot sends a slack message with the rep tagged, who gets alerted

There are a few key differentiators from our last HS integration: 

- Repeat signals (which for larger deals are very valuable)
- You don’t get charged $0.50 for a marketing contact
- We are passing LI URLs to the record and pageviews to timeline
- This allows filtering IN HS, and POWERFUL workflows to be built

We believe we’ve solved the filtering and routing problem for HS users, but we still have one more problem to go until we’re at RB2Bv2. 

The “what now” problem. 

Soon, RB2B will tell a rep exactly what to do when a signal comes in from a named account, based on context from the CRM and pageviews. 

“Connect on LinkedIn, and send the following message …” etc

While RB2Bv1 is completely dead, filtering, routing, and “what now” is what our customers are telling us they need. 

(in addition to solving the broken link problem, which should happen this week)

We’re also looking at adding reverse IP lookup for companies (which is worldwide), and adding several other identity vendors for higher coverage. 

That should give us a push to $10-$15m ARR … at which point we’ll probably stall out again and have to re-invent ourselves yet once again.

… RB2Bv1 is dead …

Longlive RB2Bv2!

18 months ago, I attended a birthday party for a founder who just raised $185M (at a $2B valuation) on the rooftop of the Four Seasons and was absolutely HUMILIATED by his incredibly attractive 28-year old blonde girlfriend:

Me: Hey, what’s going on?

Her: Thanks for coming. What do you do?

Me: I have this startup. What about you?

Her: I’m in marketing at UpWork

Me: I LOVE Upwork. We use them all the time.

Her: Cool. How big is your team?

Me: 6 people

Her: Oh... so you’re just getting started

*my internal monologue*

“Wtf… actually we are at $12m ARR, grew 200% this year, and me and my co-founders are making money hand-over-fist… we’ll have more revenue than your boyfriend in 6mo and we’ve PAID ourselves $5m getting here.”

…But I didn’t say that. 

My face turned bright red, but I just swallowed my pride, made my best attempt at smiling, said “yep, just getting started,” and walked away.

Why did this bother me so much?

Why did this feel so humiliating?

Because everywhere you go as a SaaS founder, the first (and ONLY) thing anyone asks you is how big your team is. 

They size you up.

When you say “six people”, you can see it in their eyes. 

It’s an “oh, that’s cute” kind of look.

Or they feel sorry for you. 

They definitely don’t take you seriously.

Most of time they start wanting to give you advice.

They don’t realize that your team of 6 gets more done - and has more ARR - than their team of 60.

Nobody cares that you have $2m ARR per employee. 

Nobody cares that you can do literally whatever you want.

Nobody cares that your stress level is close to zero.

They care about are the headlines about people raising $50m pre-launch.

They want to read press releases about acquisitions, IPOs, and big teams. 

This is the pressure that’s on the bootstrapped founder, every single day, from every angle, the entire journey.

It makes us feel little. 

But it shouldn’t. 

We have beautiful businesses that most VC-backed execs would kill for. 

It’s hard to remember that when your head is about to explode because someone says “you’re just starting out”. 

But you must remember, so you remain unbroken. 

Stay small.

I get hate on Linkedin because I say cold email is dead, while Taylor Haren is saying that he’s sending 100,000 cold emails per month for RB2B and responsible for 42% of our revenue. Here’s the REAL story:

TO SET THE STAGE: 

- I’ve been saying the Predictable Revenue Playbook (born 2012) died in 2023
- That playbook - “Cold Calling 2.0” led to huge SDR armies at tech companies
- The playbook = send 50-100 emails per day led to 5-10 new response per day
- Responses were then worked down the funnel towards a booked demo

____

Point #1: 

When I say “Cold Email is Dead”, I mean the Predictable Revenue playbook, and the teams put in place to roll out that playbook… None of it works anymore.

Why?

Because response rates to cold email were 10-12% in 2012, and now response rates are pretty close to zero (and going lower).

What has happened?

- Automation tools have decimated inboxes
- Personalization is useless because people don’t even see it
- AI tools have swept the leg

Which leads me to...

_____

Point #2:

There’s a new type of cold email - the Smartlead “Inbox Rotation” kind that I think you need to do… ESPECIALLY as an early stage startup.

- Set up a bunch of domains that resemble yours (looks spammy, sadly)
- Set up 2 inboxes per domain
- Use Smartlead to warm the domains and inboxes up
- Use Smartlead to send 10 emails per inbox per day

This is working VERY well for us, in terms of positive replies:

- Average positive reply rate: 1.97%
- Email-to-Signup Rate: 0.57% (1 signup per 200 emails)
- Paying customers we’ve emailed: 21.04% of paying customers
- Site visitors we emailed who became paying customers: 14.91% of customers

But, and this is a BIG BUT, here's why this is working for us...

___

Point #3:

This is crushing it for us because:

- We have an absolutely KILLER offer (100% free website visitor ID)
- Everybody we’re emailing knows me from LinkedIn
- It’s a mass-market product with a HUGE tam and low awareness

This strategy DIDN’T work for Retention.com because:

- The TAM is TINY (we are going upmarket)
- There was no “founder brand” effect
- The offer is more complex and less of a no-brainer

Which brings me to...

___

Point #4: 

Is cold email really responsible for 42% of our revenue? 

If you assume that the only reason they converted was because we emailed them, the answer would be “yes”. 

But we all know that’s not how this works.

Almost all of our customers are there because of Organic Linkedin.

Which is why I keep trying to push it EVEN HARDER.

TAKEAWAY:

Is cold email dead?

Yes and No.

The days of sending 50-100 emails per day w/ a 10% response rate are dead.

Cold Email with “Inbox Rotation” is incredibly valuable, especially if:

- You truly have a killer offer
- Your audience already knows you
- You have a massive TAM, with low awareness

Will it be as impactful as the reporting says it is?

No, you have to look at the full picture.

In 44 months, I grew Retention.com from $0-$20m ARR. Here are the 8 biggest mistakes I made along the way (and the revenue levels where I made them):

1. We sold to anyone who showed up at our doorstep

Revenue Level: 0-$12M ARR

Not focusing on an ICP and running a self-serve app was the story of our first 2.5 years. I didn’t realize how wrong this was until later. Now I know we would have gone *farther, faster* if we sold only to big Shopify stores.

2. We wasted 6 months and $300k working towards a sale that didn’t happen

Revenue Level: $5-$8M ARR

We attempted to sell the entire business in late 2021. Such a waste of time and money. Thankfully we didn’t sell. We’re much more valuable now.

3. I got major FOMO
 
Revenue Level: $14-$17m ARR

I felt like if we didn’t go as fast as humanly possible we were going to miss the opportunity. This led to panicked hiring, a horrible corporate spending culture, and a bunch of wasted time and money trying to “be everywhere”.

4. I thought our sales and onboarding was easier and less complex than it was

Revenue Level: $12-$18m ARR

We thought we could have inexperienced AEs closing 5 deals per day with a 7 day sales cycle and rush people through onboarding. As you can imagine, that wasn't true! We needed alignment on expectations and what success looks like.

5. I set a FY23 revenue target that was 50% too high
 
Revenue Level: $13-$18m ARR

My idea of “We have to get to $50m” led to over-hiring before we truly had a repeatable sales model. Empty AE calendars led to turning everyone to hunters, which didn't work (because most demand is created elsewhere in 2023). Then our VP sales resigned and we shrunk from 15 to 4 reps.

6. I assumed other vendors’ playbooks would work for us

Revenue Level: $12-$18m ARR

Because Klaviyo and Yotpo had a large agency partnership sales motion, I thought we needed one too. We have a great opportunity in the partnerships space, but it doesn’t look like either of their motions. We had to figure out what works for us.

7. We created a $5k/mo unlimited pricing tier
 
Revenue Level: $12-$19m ARR

This just didn’t work to capture mid-mkt market share. Pricing is relatively less important to those companies. What it did create was existing customers contracting down to 5k, capped our upside, made overage impossible to capture, and upgrading non-existent.

8. We oversold people and didn’t realize it for 5 months

Revenue Level: $12-16m ARR

This was my fault for not seeing it coming. The consequences were horrible. It created a euphoria about the opportunity that led to over-hiring and overspending, then on the back-end led to a massive wave of dissatisfaction, contraction, and opt-outs at 60 days. We're doing the opposite now.

TAKEAWAY:

Growing a startup is hard.

I hope I don’t make these mistakes again. 

What I do know is that I’ll continue to make mistakes...

Just new and different ones!

Here's the trick:

Make sure you’re doing 9 things right for every 8 you do wrong.

We’re launching a new brand for RB2B in January. My whole team hates it. Here’s why they’re wrong:

To set the stage: 

- Eli Rubel asked to redo our $79 webflow website that is full of typos
- I told him “nah, this thing is all we need, and I am too lazy to fix things”
- He did one for Dave (which I like, even though it’s not ugly)
- DG told me I should let him do my brand
- So we’ve been on a journey, that started off with me saying... “I want NAILS ON CHALKBOARD”

Here are the 4 things most people in SaaS get wrong about brand:

1. The best branding is about pattern interrupt. 

Seth Godin said that Silk (non-dairy milk) wasn’t selling until they put it in the refrigerator section next to milk. Why? Because on the shelf it was “milk alternative, milk alternative, milk alternative.” In the refrigerator section, it was “milk, milk, milk, NOT MILK.” 

This is how people are wired. 

2. Everybody tries to copy whatever the hottest VC-backed SaaS brand just did. 

The easiest way to not be remembered is to copy - or emulate - branding that is prevalent at the time. It’s tempting to do - and maybe I’d think about it if I knew I had to raise money - but the MOST impactful thing is to be MEMORABLE, and the way you become memorable is to look like nothing before you. 

Anybody remember Mailchimp’s yellow rebrand in 2018? Legendary.

3. It’s OK if the brand image makes you feel uncomfortable or icky inside.

New things don’t feel good. Most of us love more of the same, even though we think we do not, because there is great comfort in familiarity. My team hates the fact that I seek a brand that puts you in a place of unease when you see it for the first time (or second, or third).

4. Your brand story is critically important (but it’s not the story you think it is)

Brand isn’t the story that Oatly writes on the back of their milk carton. Brand is the story that gets told about your company, behind your back, when no involved party is around. Earlier today I got forwarded a text from a founder that said he LOVED both my content and how I was creating a whole new generation of bootstrapped founders. 

RB2B’s REAL Brand Story? That.

TAKEAWAY:

During our first call, the NoBoringDesign team asked me what I was looking for. 

I said, “I’m not sure … but I’ll tell you what I want the OPPOSITE of.” 

…then I shared my screen and typed www(.)6sense(.)com

So where did we end up? 

Time will tell. 

But - this is the logo. I think it’s badass. 

But… like I said earlier… My team hates it. 

Which makes me love it even more.

Nails. On. Chalkboard.

Stay tuned…

In less than 8 years, the best salesperson I ever met went from an intern at Xerox, to closing $1M enterprise deals to becoming the co-founder and CRO of a Unciorn-bound tech startup.

Here are the 9 things that made her a top 0.1% seller:

1. She truly believes what she sells is best for the customer

Call it drinking the KoolAid. The best salespeople are the best because they believe their customers will be far worse off without the solution.

2. She hits her activity goals every day (no matter what else is going on)

Traveling to NYC for meetings? Wake up early and prospect to hit your activity goals. Have a company-wide offsite all week? Stay up late and hit activity goals. Have to work the booth at a trade show? You get the point.

3. She generates her own leads, even when it’s "not her job"

She was always a “full-stack AE”. Even when her job involved a large amount of inbound, she took it upon herself to build systems that were automating outbound for her.

4. She intimately understands what customers care about

She doesn’t just talk, she listens. Over time she develops a deep understanding of who the customer is, what matters to them and what doesn’t. She’s able to cater the pitch to who she’s talking to, and has a deep intuition for personas.

5. She understands the product better than anyone

She developed a unique understanding of what her product does, relative value of its component, and what features should be built. This allows her to emphasize and de-emphasize certain parts of the product depending on the situation.

6. She has a Kobe Bryant-like commitment to excellence

She doesn’t understand when people don’t do things completely and correctly, because that’s what she would do if she were doing it. She expects the same out of the people who work for her.

7. She knows where to spend her time and the company’s money

You only get to #1 if you figure out how to get the maximum amount of revenue from the minimum amount of money and energy spent. Then do it all over again as fast as you can, every single day.

8. She is extremely focused on her craft

Her whole life is family and work. This type of focus is necessary to be successful in anything you do. This may sound depressing, but it’s the reality of what it takes to be #1 in anything. You need to decide if that’s actually what you want.

9. She’s never complained about anything, ever

This quality is present in truly elite sellers that often goes unmentioned. Great sellers don’t have time to complain. They are too busy making sh*t happen.

...

So who is this Hall of Fame seller?

Her name is Diana Ross.

My good friend and CRO at Retention.com + RB2B.

The playbook for sales success isn’t complicated.

It just requires a level of dedication that few people are capable of.

If you follow Diana’s lead, you can be #1 too.

Last week the legendary startup founder Hiten Shah said, “The Celebrity Founder is a Modern Illusion”. Here’s why he’s wrong:

I not only think it’s a modern REALITY.

I think it will soon be a REQUIREMENT for getting a startup off the ground.

Why are Hiten and I on opposite ends of the spectrum?


1. Hiten’s main argument is that it’s impossible to have a personal brand AND relentless focus on improving your product

I disagree.

I’m a living example of the opposite.

In fact, to flip the argument COMPLETELY…

My personal brand is the MAIN DRIVER of the feedback that leads to product improvement.

- We had 0.1% free-to-paid conversion rate. LinkedIn told me what to change. Our free-to-paid conversion rate is now over 10%
- We had 17%/mo revenue churn rate after 6mo. Linkedin told me how to fix it. It dropped to 10.5% (still bad) but I know how to get it to reasonable levels

We have a ton more product improvements coming, which are a combination of conversations with LinkedIn and us eating our own dog food…

We're building something that our team can’t live without.

So, you can build a personal brand and be product-obsessed.


2. The Value of Personal Brand is up-and-to-the-right

I am 100% certain response rates to cold email will be lower in 2025 than in 2024 (and every year thereafter).

I am equally certain that the trust built from organic social media content will be higher in 2025 than 2024 (and every year thereafter).

This is a mega-trend.

Harnessing the power of social and directing that toward your company is the most efficient way to get a startup off the ground.

No, you can't do what I have done without a great product ($0-4m ARR in 8mo)

But you could not have done it without a large personal brand either.

If you would have given me $100m to spend, it would not have matched the reach that the last 12mo of posting created.


3. Hiten says “Fame is expensive”

I didn’t want to be famous.

Until I was famous to my prospects.

And saw it help EVERY PART OF OUR BUSINESS.

Fame has made it so:

- I can work with people I have no business working with
- We have enterprise customers we have no business selling to
- I get invited to speak in front of 100s of people (for free)

I am now trying to figure out ways to grow this affinity.

Will it cause me to lose my focus on product? 

I don’t believe so, because I have spent 5 years on either side of product-market fit, and I know that with a great product everything works and with a bad product nothing works.

Do you know what would have been expensive? 

Growing RB2B like we did if I WASN’T famous.


TAKEAWAY

Relentless focus on product is a requirement for a startup. 

Perhaps young founders who don’t realize that this is their #1 priority as CEO would benefit from reading Hiten’s post.

Because you’re going to fail without relentless product focus.

But, once you internalize that focus… 

There is ONE THING that will move you faster than ANYTHING.

And that thing is “Founder Brand”.

99% of startups think they need to maximize predictable revenue. They're wrong. The next crop of $1B unicorn startups will solve for sales velocity above all else. Here's 9 reasons why velocity will define the new world:

1. Revenue was never actually predictable

Everybody underestimated their revenue in 2021-2022 and overestimated their revenue in 2023... 2024 seems to have either surprised people negatively or positively but certainly hasn’t been what most predicted.

2. Prospects do their own research

The best GTM motions touch the prospects early and often in the research process with timely and relevant content that helps them on their buying journey. Making it easy for prospects who aren’t ready to buy to access and consume your content to wins deals down the road.

3. Outbound channels are maxed out

Automation overwhelm has led to response rates being cut in half over the last 36 months. Inboxes are ruined, LinkedIn is worse, and AI tools will increase problem 100x.

4. The world is set up for a new GTM model

As cold outreach becomes more difficult, the model of the future will be one that warms prospects up through brand, innovative marketing strategies, UGC-generating machines, small events, indirect channels like partner and affiliate, and captures demand VERY low in the funnel. Close rates are 2-3x, sales cycles are 60% less and sales teams will be smaller.

5. “Influencers” will become more powerful

As the era of AI content unfolds, the best, most authentic content coming from the most trusted voices will become even more powerful. Social continues to become the primary method to create awareness, even for SaaS.

6. High-Velocity environments attract the best talent

The best people want to be on teams that prioritize moving FAST. The antithesis of this is a bloated GTM org that values head count above all.

7. You can be profitable (at the expense of predictability)

Running a lean team that captures demand at the bottom of the funnel (and resists the temptation to layer on outbound reps who will simply capture the demand that you are creating elsewhere) will increase focus on capital-efficiency, reduce system-wide dependence on external funding and create a less volatile ecosystem in the long-term.

TAKEAWAY:

“It's never going to work”. That's what a billionaire CEO told me as I was explaining my vision for the next 24 months of my startup. And not only was he right, but it led to me getting sued.

BACKGROUND:

In the spring of 2017, I was sitting on the couch in my New York apartment, sending emails to wrap up my day.

My startup, Robly Email Marketing, had grown from $0-$3M ARR, but got stuck, and at this point, had been stuck for a year.

Looking for answers, I popped over to LinkedIn.

I saw a message that was so intriguing I read it twice.

An employee of the pioneer in Email Marketing messaged me…

This company HATED me because the way I got to $3M was by calling their customers and offering them a better deal.

What intrigued me so much about the message?

The end of the message was this:

“They put $50m into their in-person selling program, and when we got acquired they just chopped it. You’re the perfect guy to swoop in and take it over.”

This was it!

This was how I was going to get unstuck!

I agreed to wait until his non-compete expired and hire him.

___

A few days later, one of my mentors connected me with a billionaire CEO, who agreed to meet with me as a favor.

I was excited to bound my new idea off a legend.

But half way through our meet, the CEO stopped me.

“It's never going to work,” he said.

“Why not?” I asked, flustered.

“I’ll show you.”

He then started writing numbers on a legal pad.

“How many customers do these agencies have, on average, and how much would they charge?”

“Maybe 10-20, and they charge around $1-2k/mo” I said.

“And what does your software cost?”

“$60/mo,” I replied.

“And what affiliate commission do you pay?”

“40% for life.” I proudly said, because it was HIGHER than most.

The CEO laughed and shook his head.

“If you get 100% penetration into the agency’s accounts, you will make them a total of $24 for each account they bill $2k to their agency for. They aren’t going to care about you or your software.”

What did I do?

Did I listen to the most successful founder I had ever spoken to?

Of course not.

Not only did I proceed, I ended up hiring the guy early because the perfect time presented itself to strike, and “non-competes aren’t enforceable in California”.

Fast forward 12 months...

After the initial excitement, the program got zero traction.

Then the competitor sued me and dragged the lawsuit out for a year.

Eventually we settled, and the employee informed me that by California law, I was obligated to pay his legal fees too.

What a kick in the nuts.

TAKEAWAY:

Should I have listened to the billionaire CEO?

Maybe.

Maybe not.

I think many first-time founders fail because they haven’t learned what only being in the game can teach you.

Those hard lessons shape the founder you become.

Total failure, wasting a year of my life, burning several hundred thousand dollars, and a lawsuit were awful…

But I’m a stronger founder for having gone through it.

The key is living to fight another day.

From 2016-2020, my email marketing startup was stuck at $3M ARR. Literally *nothing* I did moved the needle. I was completely demoralized. 

Here's the story of how we hit $20M ARR (and my message to founders who feel like quitting):

BACKSTORY

In 2016, I hit $3M ARR in the highly competitive Email Marketing SaaS space.

To do this, we used a creative data mining/cold calling strategy.

It seemed like leads would flow forever.

Until they didn't...

Things got so bad I was forced to scale back the team. 

It was the hardest day of my life.

I tried to remain optimistic.

But I had no idea what to do.

No move I made worked.

As I scrambled, two unfortunate patterns emerged:

1. I would meet someone who did X and they would convince me that X was my problem and the reason I was stuck. So, I would spend thousands of $ on FB ads or a new website or SEO or a partner program, which never worked.

2. I would meet someone I saw as an expert and they would tell me to sell the company

The problem was no matter who I met, I took their advice WAY too seriously. 

That's how desperate I was.

I had constant anxiety.

I wanted to quit.

My dream-life was collapsing before my eyes.

Then one day I learned something new...

I heard you could resolve anonymous website visitors to an email address. 

This was mind blowing.

Our current customers biggest problem was shrinking email lists. 

"Damn," I thought.

If I can turn anonymous web traffic into emails, I can sell it to anyone. 

It took us 18 months to figure out how to do it. 

I thought it would be a cool feature inside our app.

But then we noticed something...

People were signing up for our app, using the new anonymous ID feature, downloading the data, and using it in another email app and saying it was amazing. 

I read once that if someone is willing to endure a brutal user experience and still give you a high NPS score, that’s an early sign of product/market fit.

So we made a major pivot.

We spun out the anonymous ID feature as its own product.

I got the UI and front-end of v1 done on Upwork. 

Then I ran a $5,000 Facebook ad campaign to promote it.

And something amazing happened...

We got $10,000 back in MRR!

That was the moment Retention.com was born.

Since then, we’ve had A TON of bumps in the road.

But it’s been mostly up-and-to-the-right.

Because when I was stuck, I would have done ANYTHING to hear from a founder who was going through the same.

To read their words, what they were trying, what was working and not. 

I would have done ANYTHING to learn how to get unstuck.

That's why I create all of this content on Linkedin about my business.

That's why I share about the journey.

I’m doing it for the founders who are stuck

I'm doing it for a younger version of myself.

If you're out there and you're stuck... 

Know this:

The breakthrough is around the corner.

It may not feel like it.

You may want to quit.

But just keep building.

Last year I spoke to 50+ top-tier VC firms about investing in my bootstrapped (profitable) $25m ARR SaaS. Here are 7 reasons why I walked away and decided NEVER to take VC money:

1. Dividends are good

If you create a successful startup, you should be rewarded by getting paid millions of dollars every year… Not just some *potentially* huge number at some point MAYBE in the future.

2. The investor value prop is weak (if you don’t need capital)

I listened to pitch after pitch of investors saying their “GTM advisory would be game-changing” for us. This pitch was weak and designed to get founders like me dreaming big dreams that if they panned out would largely be my team’s doing.

3. A new seat at the table is a net negative. Period

At best, investors will slow you down. At worst, they will ruin your life AND destroy your common equity if your business slows down for macro reasons outside your control.

4. Investors are in the portfolio game. You’re not.

Situations emerge - FREQUENTLY - where what is best for your life and company can be usurped by a group of investors wanting a quick 2x. Even if they have a minority position, there are SO many ways they can exert influence and drive the outcome that is best for the fund.

5. I want to do things investors would not tolerate

My strategy for 2024 is to give away a super-valuable product to millions of people using viral distribution strategies and do a lightning-fast PLG. With a team that is unreasonably lean. While continuing to add value to the free offering. THE SECOND any of this plan went sour, I would be told to stop, and if I didn’t, I’d be fired.

6. I don’t believe in measuring things or spreadsheets

This is controversial. The only thing I measure is ARR and churn… and the one and only Nathan Latka and the Founderpath team created a new revenue dashboard that is pretty cool (see below). Unlike other dashboards, they help you estimate what your business is worth (both in a raise and sale) based on relevant deals in the market.

7. Large carrots dangled in front of us lead to bad decisions

An investor’s job is to figure out what number will motivate the founder to transact and get them to attach their identity to that number. We love validation that our beautiful business IS worth $100m, even if it actually lowers the probability-weighted financial outcome for the founder.

TAKEAWAY:

Last year I was seduced by the idea I could take millions off the table and move even faster.

After speaking to an investor a week for all of 2023, I realized those millions would likely change many of the things about my life I value the most.

I’d sacrifice independence, freedom, and it would slow us down.

That's why I'm a bootstrapper at heart.

And I always will be.

- Your work is never done

- Hit people over the head with the value you generate

- There are other ways to provide value than $$$

- You need to understand your metrics as you scale
- Where you deploy capital will soon become the most important thing

Ignore the pomp and circumstance.

3 weeks ago I posted that RB2B’s churn hit 17%/mo at $2.9m ARR. Since then we’ve lowered churn to 10.9% and grown to $3.5m ARR (+20%). Here’s what we learned, what we did, and what we plan to do:


WHAT WE LEARNED

1. Our product is unusable for our ICP (growth stage SaaS w/ sales teams)
 
If you're tiny and get 3 leads a day, it’s great. If you’re an Enterprise with a growth team and know exactly what to do with our feed, RB2B is great.

For growth stage startups with sales teams, filtering and routing is currently impossible without Clay. We are in the process of fixing this in several ways.

2. Our product exposes our customers’ traffic problems

Some people don’t realize how low a % of ICP visitors hit homepages in general. When our product highlights it, the product gets blamed, and in some cases, willingness to pay goes down ("Why should I pay for junk leads?").

3. We have broken LinkedIn links

We are in the middle of a huge database update. This problem will resolve itself in the coming quarter. We've had one public accuracy test done with Clearbit - we were far more accurate - and are having 11 more done now.

4. These aren’t actually leads

I’ve come to the realization that a site visitor isn’t a lead, it’s a signal.

We shouldn’t be selling demos, we should be selling alerts (and how to action them) to sellers that help them move prospects down the funnel.

Booking a demo is only one use case and it’s lower value than ongoing signals to salespeople from accounts they are monitoring and prospecting.


WHAT WE'VE DONE

- Added Hot Leads
- Added URL restrictions
- Changed weekly stats email to be more informative
- Added Zapier (usage is 4x what it was 2 weeks ago)
- Added “the most successful RB2B accounts do these 3 things” email


WHAT WE ARE GOING TO DO

1. Tell Hubspot CRM users EXACTLY how to filter and route in HS

We are going to create a feature that ONLY sends contacts at accounts that are already in Hubspot TO Hubspot, grab the account owner, then send it BACK to Slack with the rep tagged. We believe this will make our product usable for growth stage SaaS on HS.

2. We’re messing around with other delivery methods

We think reps might want this signal delivered to their Gmail (or Outlook) inboxes. If this works, it will eliminate the friction of marketers having to set up a HS workflow.

3. We think the “what now” problem is really a prioritization problem

A rep who carries a quota and/or manages a team has so much going on that they don’t want to take 5 mins to come up with what to write. We think we can use AI to tell the rep what they should say and why they should say it - and cut that to 15 secs.


TAKEAWAY

10.9% churn is absolutely god-awful.
